data.name: ABS
data.summary: Tough, heat tolerant styrenic plastic that can be sanded, glued and smoothed with acetone. It shrinks 1 to 2 percent, so it warps, cracks between layers and lifts corners unless the printer is enclosed and warm. It releases styrene fumes. Choose ASA instead if the part sits in sunlight.
use_for: parts that need acetone smoothing or welding
avoid_for: outdoor parts in sunlight (yellows and turns brittle)
open frame printers without an enclosure

nozzle_temp_c.note: Orca generic and Bambu allow 240 to 280 (Bambu on X1C prints at 270 after a 260 first layer). The Bambu TDS says 240 to 270, Prusa prints at 255 and Polymaker at 245 to 265. Start at 260 and move in 5 C steps.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: Orca generic, Bambu X1C and Prusa Core One all use 260 for the first layer.

bed_temp_c.note: Bambu glue table 90 to 100 (TDS 80 to 100), Prusa 100 (80 to 110 by part size), Polymaker 90 to 100. Prusa smooth sheet profiles use 110. Use 100 and go higher for large flat parts.

chamber_temp_c.note: Passive enclosure (X1C, P1S, P2S, Voron, closed box): the chamber runs well below the active range on bed heat alone (no source gives a figure), so keep the front door and lid closed. Bambu's TDS lists 45 to 60 C as the working range. Active heating (X1E max 60 C, H2D max 65 C, Prusa Core One 55 C at full bed heat): Bambu ships the ABS profile with a 65 C chamber target on H2D and P2S and 0 on X1C and X1E. For X1E, Bambu suggests turning on 60 C only for large or dense parts because chamber heating lowers filter performance. Small parts print fine without it.

enclosure.note: Bambu lists ABS as not recommended on open frame printers and compatible with all enclosed printers. Prusa says the material needs a housing and offers the draft shield only as a partial fix. Polymaker recommends an enclosure to prevent warping. A small part with a brim can succeed on an open printer, a large one will not.

plates.note: Bambu requires glue and lists the low temperature plates as unsuitable for ABS. Bed temperature is far above what the Cool Plate can take.
TDS lists the Engineering plate with glue for ABS at 80 to 100 C.
Glue keeps the sheet clean and helps hold corners.
Prusa says to use the smooth or powder coated sheet with glue stick.
Works with glue. Grips well and releases once the plate is cool.

cooling.note: Bambu X1C uses 10 to 60 percent with 80 on overhangs. Orca generic goes to 80. Prusa runs 10 to 20 percent and Polymaker turns the fan off. Cooling is the enemy of layer bonding in ABS: keep it low and let the enclosure hold the heat. Bambu warns that too much fan and a cold chamber cause splitting.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered

drying.note: Bambu's drying table marks ABS "recommended", not required. AMS 2 Pro is listed as not compatible: it stops at 65 C. Use an AMS HT, an oven with forced air or the heated bed. Take PLA and PETG out of an AMS HT before drying ABS at 80 C. Wet ABS pops and leaves rough walls and weak layers.

nozzle.note: Bambu lists all nozzle sizes as compatible with a brass or stainless nozzle. The glass filled version needs hardened steel.

flow_ratio.note: Bambu 0.95, Orca generic 0.926, Prusa Core One 1.0. Confirm with a flow test.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Bambu ABS on X1C: 16 standard, 25 high flow. On H2D: 20 for 0.4 mm and 25 for 0.6 mm (35 on the high flow hotend). Orca generic: 12 standard, 20 high flow. Prusa Core One and MK4S: 15.

retraction_mm.note: Bambu profiles use 0.4 mm on X1C, X1E, H2D and P2S. The Bambu TDS suggests 0.8 to 1.4 mm for bowden style feed paths. Bowden values come from the printer profile.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: Bambu TDS says 20 to 40 mm/s. Bambu machine profiles use 30, its X1C high flow ABS profile uses 40, Prusa MK4S uses 35.

pressure_advance.note: Prusa ships M572 S0.02 for a 0.4 mm nozzle on Core One and MK4S (0.012 at 0.6 mm, 0.01 at 0.8 mm), and the MK3.5 profile stores 0.02. Bambu printers calibrate flow dynamics per spool. PA is printer specific; calibrate.

smart_layer.quality_mode: Thinner layers (0.12 to 0.16 mm) smooth curved walls and take sanding or acetone smoothing well. Keep the floor near 0.1 mm, because thin layers cool fast and ABS needs each layer hot to bond.
smart_layer.strength_mode: Bias toward 0.2 to 0.28 mm on load bearing parts. A thicker bead holds its heat longer and needs less fan, which helps bonding in a warm chamber. Tests show under 8 percent tensile loss from 0.1 to 0.2 mm, so this is a reliability choice more than a strength gain.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: Minimum layer time (12 s in Bambu profiles) stretches small thin layers. Keep the fan low and add a second part instead of shortening the layer time.

layer_height.note: Bambu ships 0.08 to 0.28 mm presets for a 0.4 mm nozzle and Orca allows 0.08 to 0.3 mm. The X1C allows 0.12 to 0.42 mm on a 0.6 mm nozzle and 0.16 to 0.56 mm on a 0.8 mm nozzle. Polymaker tests ABS at 0.1 mm. The warm chamber benefit of thicker layers is a rule of thumb, not a measured result.

smart_layer.note: ABS prints well from 0.25 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.25 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: Bambu lists under 300 mm/s, Polymaker suggests 30 to 50 mm/s. Real speed is capped by max volumetric speed (see extrusion). No source caps outer wall speed for ABS.
speeds.note: First layer: Bambu Standard preset 50 mm/s, Prusa MK4S preset 40 mm/s, Orca base 20 mm/s.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Bambu holds 100 C from the first layer. Prusa runs 100 C (80 to 110 by part size). If corners lift, raise the first layer bed 5 to 10 C before adding more squish. Let the bed and chamber soak 10 to 15 minutes first.
first_layer.squish_note: Do not squish harder to cure lifting corners (Prusa). A first layer of 0.25 mm or more at 120 percent line width holds better than a thin one (Ellis).

walls.note: Bambu Standard uses 2 walls and its Strength preset 6. Extra walls add stiffness, but thick solid sections build shrink stress in ABS, so stop at 4 for large flat parts.

infill.density_note: 10 to 20 percent for housings and jigs. Bambu Standard is 15 percent grid and Strength is 25 percent.

supports.note: Same material ABS supports weld to the part and leave scars. Bambu Support for ABS is a release interface (support only, enclosed printer, drying optional, limonene dissolvable). HIPS gives a soluble interface on dual nozzle or multi material printers, but Prusa warns ABS and ASA partly dissolve in limonene, so keep the dip short and test a scrap. Prusa soluble presets use a top Z distance of 0 with 3 interface layers.

multi_material.note: Bambu lists ABS as compatible with AMS and not recommended on AMS lite; its ABS guide says ABS, ASA and PC are not compatible with AMS lite. AMS HT can dry ABS.

softening_temp_c.note: Bambu TDS Vicat 94 C, Polymaker Vicat 104 C and Tg 101 C. Orca vitrification is 110 C.

annealing.note: Bambu suggests it but warns parts can deform. Use a forced air oven, never a kitchen or microwave oven. Shrinkage is 1 to 2 percent (Prusa), so expect dimensional change.

safety.note: Releases styrene and other fumes that Prusa and Bambu warn can be a health risk. Print in an enclosure in a ventilated room and avoid drafts on the print. Bambu X, P and H series carry an activated carbon filter for ABS and ASA; enable activate_air_filtration in the filament profile. Carbon adsorbs less when the chamber is very hot.

food_contact.note: ABS is not food safe. Styrene can leach, layer lines trap bacteria and colorants are uncertified.

failure_modes.symptom: Corners or edges lift off the plate, or the base curls

fixes.why: A brim adds contact area so corners hold against ABS shrinkage.
Wide brims resist the pull of a large ABS part. Prusa suggests wide brims for large parts.
A shield wall holds a warmer pocket of air around the part on printers that cannot heat the chamber.

fixes.advice: Preheat the chamber. Close the door and lid, and let the bed sit at 100 C for 10 to 15 minutes before starting. On X1E, H2D or Core One set the chamber temperature.

fixes.why: A slow first layer squishes and bonds better.
Cooling shrinks the top of the part faster than the bottom and drives warping.

fixes.advice: Apply a thin coat of glue stick or PVP glue to the plate. Bambu requires glue for ABS.

failure_modes.symptom: Cracks along layer lines, often high on tall parts

fixes.why: Hotter plastic fuses better with the layer below.
Bambu names excess cooling and a cold chamber as the cause of layer splitting.
A warmer chamber cuts thermal shrinkage stress. Only on printers with active chamber heating.

fixes.advice: Keep the door and lid closed for the whole print, and let the part cool inside the printer.

failure_modes.symptom: Strong plastic smell or irritation during printing

fixes.why: Runs the activated carbon filter during ABS prints on Bambu X, P and H series.

fixes.advice: Run the printer in a ventilated room or vent it outdoors, and stay out of the room for long prints.

failure_modes.symptom: Popping sounds, bubbles, rough or fuzzy walls

fixes.advice: Dry at 80 C for 8 h in a forced air oven or an AMS HT. AMS 2 Pro cannot dry ABS.

failure_modes.symptom: Sagging overhangs and bridges because the fan is low

fixes.why: Boost the fan only on overhangs. Bambu ships 80 for ABS.
Slower bridges give each line time to set.

disagreements.resolution: Default to 260 C. Stay under 270 C unless a specific spool needs more.

positions.claim: 100 C, up to 110 C for large parts

disagreements.resolution: Use 100 C. Go to 110 C only on a smooth sheet for large flat parts.

disagreements.topic: chamber temperature control on X1E and P2S

positions.claim: Off by default for ABS to keep filtration effective; on at 60 C for big or dense parts
65 C chamber target in H2D and P2S ABS profiles

disagreements.resolution: Follow the printer profile. On X1E enable 60 C only for warp prone parts.

positions.claim: Thicker layers hold heat and bond better in a warm chamber (rule of thumb)
ABS tensile strength is 7.57 percent lower at 0.2 mm than at 0.1 mm, and layers thicker than half the nozzle hurt strength (PLA test)

disagreements.resolution: Use 0.2 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle. Go to 0.24 to 0.28 mm only to keep heat in tall parts, and do not go below 0.1 mm.

data.name: ASA
data.summary: ABS style engineering plastic with an acrylic rubber phase that resists UV and weather. It is the material for parts that live outdoors. It prints like ABS: hot bed, warm enclosure, low fan, styrene fumes. Warps a little less than ABS in practice, but large flat parts still lift without an enclosure.
avoid_for: open frame printers without an enclosure
parts that need to flex or take shock loads across layers

nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu profiles use 270 C and a 270 first layer, Prusa 260, Polymaker 240 to 260 and the Bambu TDS 240 to 270. Start at 260 and move in 5 C steps. Cooler ASA gives cleaner detail, hotter ASA gives stronger layers.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu 270, Prusa and Orca generic 260.

bed_temp_c.note: Bambu glue table 90 to 100 (TDS 80 to 100), Prusa 105 then 110 C, Polymaker 75 to 95. Use 100 C, and 110 C on smooth PEI for large parts.

chamber_temp_c.note: Passive enclosure (X1C, P1S, P2S, Voron, closed box): the chamber runs well below the active range on bed heat alone (no source gives a figure), so keep the door and lid closed. Bambu's TDS lists 45 to 60 C. Active heating: X1E maxes at 60 C, H2D at 65 C, Prusa Core One reaches 55 C at full bed heat. Bambu ships the ASA profile with a 65 C chamber target on H2D and P2S, and 0 on X1C and X1E. On X1E, Bambu suggests 60 C only for large or dense parts, since chamber heating lowers filter performance.

enclosure.note: Bambu lists ASA as compatible only on enclosed printers. Prusa says an enclosure is necessary for large parts and offers the draft shield as a mitigation. Polymaker recommends one to prevent warping. Small parts with a brim can print on an open printer in a warm room.

plates.note: Bambu requires glue and lists the low temperature plates as unsuitable for ASA.
TDS lists the Engineering plate with glue at 80 to 100 C.
Glue helps hold corners and protects the sheet.
Prusa: smooth or powder coated PEI with glue stick. Do not put acetone slurry on a powder coated sheet.
Works with glue. Releases once the plate is cool.
Prusa says glass may need a thin layer of ASA or ABS dissolved in acetone.

cooling.note: Bambu holds the fan at 10 to 35 percent (25 to 35 on X1C) with 80 on overhangs. Prusa runs 12 to 25 percent. Orca generic allows up to 80. Polymaker turns the fan off. Keep it low: ASA cracks between layers when cooled hard.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered

drying.note: Bambu marks ASA drying "recommended". AMS 2 Pro is listed as not compatible because it stops at 65 C. Use AMS HT (80 C, 8 h), a forced air oven, or the heated bed. Bambu lists ASA-CF and ABS-GF as needing desiccant in use.

nozzle.note: Bambu lists all nozzle sizes as compatible. ASA Aero foamed ASA is 0.4 mm only. Carbon filled ASA-CF needs hardened steel (see asa_cf).

flow_ratio.note: Bambu 0.95, Orca generic 0.926, Prusament on Core One 1.0. Confirm with a flow test.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Bambu ASA on X1C: 18 standard and 25 high flow. H2D 0.4 mm: 20, up to 35 on the high flow hotend. P2S: 18, up to 25. Orca generic: 12 standard, 20 high flow. Prusament ASA on Core One and MK4S: 15.

retraction_mm.note: Bambu profiles use 0.4 mm on X1C, H2D and P2S. Bambu's TDS suggests 0.8 to 1.4 mm for longer feed paths. Bowden values come from the printer profile.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: Bambu TDS says 20 to 40 mm/s. Bambu machine profiles use 30, Prusa MK4S uses 35.

pressure_advance.note: Prusa ships M572 S0.02 at 0.4 mm (0.012 at 0.6 mm, 0.01 at 0.8 mm) on Core One and MK4S. Bambu printers calibrate flow dynamics per spool. PA is printer specific; calibrate.

smart_layer.quality_mode: ASA keeps its matte finish and UV stability at 0.12 to 0.16 mm, and thin layers show off curved outdoor parts. Keep the floor near 0.1 mm, because ASA splits between thin layers as easily as ABS.
smart_layer.strength_mode: Bias toward 0.2 to 0.28 mm for outdoor brackets and housings. A thicker bead stays hot longer and needs less fan, which helps layer bonding in a warm chamber.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: Minimum layer time is 10 to 12 s in Bambu and Prusa profiles. Keep the fan at 35 percent or less and add a second part when small layers slow down.

layer_height.note: Same limits as ABS: Bambu presets run 0.08 to 0.28 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle and Orca allows 0.08 to 0.3 mm. Polymaker tests ASA at 0.1 mm. The tension data comes from ABS and PLA, and ASA is extrapolated.

smart_layer.note: ASA prints well from 0.25 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.25 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: Bambu lists under 250 mm/s, Polymaker suggests 30 to 50 mm/s. Real speed is capped by max volumetric speed (see extrusion). No source caps outer wall speed for ASA.
speeds.note: First layer: Bambu Standard preset 50 mm/s, Prusa MK4S preset 40 mm/s.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Prusa runs the first layer at 105 C and then 110 C. Bambu holds 90 to 100 C. Raise the first layer bed 5 to 10 C if corners lift.
first_layer.squish_note: Do not squish harder to cure lifting corners (Prusa). A first layer of 0.25 mm or more at 120 percent line width holds better than a thin one (Ellis).
first_layer.note: Prusa profiles keep the fan off for 4 layers, Bambu for 3.

walls.note: Outdoor parts gain more from 3 to 4 walls than from dense infill, and walls also shield the core from weather.

infill.density_note: 10 to 20 percent for brackets and housings, 25 percent for the Bambu Strength preset.

supports.note: Bambu lists Support for ABS as compatible with ABS only, so test it on a scrap before ASA. Same material ASA supports weld and leave scars. Prusa warns HIPS is not suited to ASA supports because ASA partly dissolves in limonene, and a long dip hurts Prusament ASA layer adhesion.

multi_material.note: Material table shows ASA compatible with AMS and AMS lite. Bambu's ABS, ASA and PC guide says these are not compatible with AMS lite, so treat AMS lite as not recommended. AMS HT can dry ASA.

softening_temp_c.note: Bambu Vicat 106 C. Polymaker Tg 97.8 C and Vicat 105 C. Orca vitrification 110 C.

heat_deflection_c.note: Bambu ASA TDS, annealed specimens. Prusa quotes heat resistance up to 93 C.

annealing.note: Suggested by Bambu. Parts can deform and warp, so use a forced air oven and test on a spare part.

uv_resistance.note: Prusa: high UV resistance. Bambu: exceptional UV, weather, mechanical and thermal resistance.

safety.note: Releases styrene fumes that Prusa flags as potentially dangerous. Print in an enclosure in a ventilated room without drafts on the print. Bambu X, P and H series carry an activated carbon filter; enable activate_air_filtration in the filament profile. Carbon adsorbs less when the chamber is very hot. Bambu's data sheet calls ASA odorless when cold, but the print smells hot.

food_contact.note: ASA is not food safe. Colorants are uncertified and layer lines trap bacteria.

failure_modes.symptom: Corners or edges lift off the plate

fixes.why: A brim adds contact area so corners hold against ASA shrinkage.
Wide brims resist the pull of a large ASA part.
Prusa suggests a draft shield on printers without a housing. It keeps a warmer pocket of air around the part.

fixes.advice: Preheat the chamber. Close the door and lid and hold the bed at 100 C for 10 to 15 minutes. On X1E, H2D or Core One set the chamber temperature.

fixes.why: A slow first layer squishes and bonds better.
Less cooling reduces the shrinkage difference between layers.

fixes.advice: Apply a thin coat of glue stick to the plate. Bambu requires glue for ASA.

failure_modes.symptom: Cracks along layer lines

fixes.why: Hotter plastic fuses better with the layer below.
Bambu names excess cooling and a cold chamber as the cause of layer splitting.
A warmer chamber cuts thermal shrinkage stress. Only on printers with active chamber heating.

fixes.advice: Keep the door and lid closed and let the part cool inside the printer.

failure_modes.symptom: Strong smell or irritation during printing

fixes.why: Runs the activated carbon filter during ASA prints on Bambu X, P and H series.

fixes.advice: Ventilate the room or vent the printer outdoors, and avoid sitting next to it for long prints.

failure_modes.symptom: Popping, bubbles, rough or fuzzy walls

fixes.advice: Dry at 80 C for 8 h in a forced air oven or an AMS HT. AMS 2 Pro cannot dry ASA.

failure_modes.symptom: Visible layer lines on a part that needs a glossy surface

fixes.advice: ASA smooths well in acetone vapor and can be wet sanded or welded with acetone. Do this in a ventilated area.

disagreements.resolution: Default 100 C. Use 110 C on a smooth sheet for big flat parts and 90 C for small parts on textured plates.

positions.claim: 240 to 270 C in the Bambu TDS, 260 C at Prusa, 240 to 260 C at Polymaker

disagreements.resolution: Default 260 C. Go to 270 C for layer strength, never above 280 C.
Treat as not recommended.

positions.claim: HIPS dissolves in limonene and is used as a soluble support for ABS and ASA
HIPS supports are not suitable for ABS or ASA because they partly dissolve in limonene

disagreements.resolution: Use a release interface such as Bambu Support for ABS or the same material with a larger Z gap. Use HIPS only with a dip of 10 to 20 s and after a scrap test.

data.name: BVOH (water soluble support)
data.summary: Water soluble support material, a stiffer and better behaved alternative to PVA. Prusa calls it the better but more expensive option, and it is the only practical soluble support for PETG. It prints cooler than PVA and clogs less, but it is still very hygroscopic and must be kept dry. Dissolves in water in hours. Needs a multi material setup.
use_for: support interfaces and bases under PLA and PETG parts
avoid_for: long idle time in a hot nozzle

nozzle_temp_c.note: Prusa uses 215 C for BVOH. Orca generic BVOH profile is 190 to 240 with 220 as its default, and the Bambu wiki lists 190 to 240 for dry PVA and BVOH. Match the temperature to the model filament.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: Orca generic uses 220. Prusa's single BVOH value is 215.

bed_temp_c.note: Prusa uses 60 C. Orca generic sets 40 on the Cool Plate and 55 on PEI plates. BVOH sticks better to a PLA raft than to bare PEI.

enclosure.note: Not needed for warping. Bambu groups BVOH with PVA (softening below 60 C), so open the door or remove the top cover if the bed is above 45 C.

plates.note: Orca sets 40 C. The plate follows the model filament.
Bambu gives no BVOH row, PVA and PLA rows require glue on this plate.
Follows the model filament.
Follows the model filament.
Prusa recommends a 1 to 2 layer PLA raft because BVOH sticks much better to PLA than to PEI.

cooling.note: Orca generic BVOH uses 100 percent fan and 8 s. No manufacturer cooling guidance was found.

oven.note: PVA values used as a proxy, see note.

drying.note: Prusa says BVOH is very hygroscopic and should be kept as dry as possible, ideally printed straight from a dryer or drybox. Bambu's drying tables list PVA but not BVOH, so PVA numbers (55 to 85 C, 8 to 12 h in an oven, humidity below 20 percent RH, calcium chloride desiccant) are a proxy. BCN3D dries its BVOH 4 to 16 h at 60 C in a hot air dryer or vacuum oven and stores it sealed with desiccant. Follow the spool label first.

nozzle.note: Bambu lists dry PVA and BVOH as not compatible with 0.2 mm nozzles. Prusa says it clogs less than PVA but more than standard materials.

flow_ratio.note: Orca generic uses 1.0. Confirm with a flow test.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Orca generic BVOH is 8, double PVA's 4. Reduce it if the extruder clicks or the interface is rough.

retraction_mm.note: No BVOH specific figure. This is the printer default (Bambu 0.8 mm, Prusa MK4S 0.7 mm), not material data.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: No BVOH specific figure. Bambu machine profiles use 30 mm/s and Prusa MK4S uses 35.

pressure_advance.note: No BVOH specific value is published. Use the printer default or the paired filament's value.

smart_layer.quality_mode: BVOH only forms the support interface, so its layer height follows the model. Thin layers under PLA or PETG give a smoother underside, but BVOH under extrudes if forced thin.
smart_layer.strength_mode: Strength does not apply. BVOH is dissolved away, so use the layer height the model needs.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: BCN3D runs the fan at 50 to 100 percent and Orca generic at 100 percent with an 8 s minimum layer time. BVOH softens below 60 C, so keep the chamber cool and the fan on.

layer_height.note: BCN3D lists a layer height of 0.15 to 0.4 mm, which exceeds the 0.28 mm Bambu and Orca limit for a 0.4 mm nozzle. Forward AM says nozzle 0.4 mm or larger.

smart_layer.note: BVOH (water soluble support) prints well from 0.25 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.3 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: BCN3D prints BVOH at 20 mm/s and Forward AM at 30 to 60 mm/s. Orca generic allows 8 mm3/s (see extrusion). No source caps outer wall speed. Interface layers run slower than the rest of the support.
speeds.note: Prusa's soluble interface preset runs its interface at 40 mm/s with a 40 mm/s first layer on the MK4S.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Prusa runs the bed at 60 C and BCN3D at 45 to 90 C. Follow the model filament's bed temperature. BVOH sticks much better to a 1 to 2 layer PLA raft than to bare PEI.
first_layer.squish_note: No BVOH specific squish guidance. BCN3D says to use Magigoo adhesive for reliable bed adhesion when BVOH touches the bed.

structure.note: BVOH is only used as a support interface or base. Wall and infill settings follow the model.

supports.note: BVOH dissolves in water about twice as fast as PVA and leaves less residue. Prusa pairs it with PLA and calls it the only practical soluble support for PETG, and BCN3D also lists ABS, PA and PAHT CF15. Warm water speeds dissolving. Keep the spool sealed with desiccant, expect a larger purge on tool changes, and clean the hotend after long BVOH prints. Prusa's soluble interface preset uses a top Z distance of 0, 3 interface layers and 0.1 mm interface spacing.

multi_material.note: Bambu lists dry PVA and BVOH as compatible and says damp PVA or BVOH is too soft for the AMS path. Use a sealed dry box for the whole print. Prusa notes frequent changes need higher purge volumes to avoid PLA contamination. For PETG, BVOH is practically the only soluble support choice.

softening_temp_c.note: Orca temperature_vitrification is 45 C. Bambu groups BVOH with PVA as softening below 60 C.

dissolving.water_ratio: About 20 ml of water per 1 g of BVOH.
dissolving.time: Hours. Warm water is faster but should not be very hot.
dissolving.note: Prusa gives 1 g per 20 ml and says dissolution time depends on temperature and material to water ratio.

safety.note: Prusa describes it as non toxic and odorless.

food_contact.note: Not for food contact.

failure_modes.symptom: Extrusion stops or clicks, bubbly output

fixes.advice: Dry the spool and print from a sealed dry box or dryer.

fixes.why: A slower flow reduces jams.

fixes.advice: Do not leave BVOH parked hot in the nozzle. Purge or retract it during pauses.

failure_modes.symptom: Support peels off the plate or model

fixes.advice: Print a 1 to 2 layer PLA raft under the soluble support.

fixes.why: Prusa recommends 0 mm distance for soluble supports.

failure_modes.symptom: PLA or PETG specks in the soluble support

fixes.why: Prusa says frequent changes need larger purge volumes.

failure_modes.symptom: Hairs and bubbles at the interface

fixes.advice: Re-dry the spool and reseal it.

fixes.why: Less ooze.

failure_modes.symptom: Soluble support fails when paired with PETG
causes: PVA does not survive PETG temperatures

fixes.advice: Use BVOH for PETG supports. Prusa says practically only BVOH works with PETG.

positions.claim: BVOH is stiffer, behaves better, prints at 215 C and clogs less
Orca generic profile prints BVOH at 220 C and 8 mm3/s with soluble flag 0

disagreements.resolution: Use 215 to 220 C. Orca's filament_soluble flag is 0 for BVOH but is_support is 1, so it may need to be marked soluble manually in the slicer.

positions.claim: no BVOH row in the drying tables, PVA listed
keep as dry as possible, no numbers

disagreements.resolution: Use the spool label. If missing, start with the PVA numbers at the low end.
Use 215 C only when the model filament needs it, as Prusa does. On a cooler model material such as PLA, 195 to 210 C is what the BVOH makers list.

positions.claim: 55 C for 8 h (Bambu lists PVA and BVOH together)
60 C for 4 to 16 h in a hot air dryer or vacuum oven

disagreements.resolution: Use 55 to 60 C for 8 h and keep it under 60 C to avoid softening.

data.name: HIPS
data.summary: High impact polystyrene. Prints at temperatures close to ABS with much less shrinkage, and dissolves in limonene, so it is used as a soluble support for ABS and ASA on dual extruder or multi material printers. As a model material it is light and easy to sand but soft and low heat. Bambu has no HIPS data in its wiki, so most numbers come from Prusa and Orca generic.
use_for: soluble support for ABS and ASA
parts that will be sanded or acetone smoothed
avoid_for: ABS or ASA parts printed with long limonene dips (Prusa warns they partly dissolve)
PETG parts (no maker pairs HIPS with PETG)

nozzle_temp_c.note: Orca generic allows 220 to 270 and prints at 240. Prusa says 225 to 255. Start at 240 and move in 5 C steps. If used as ABS support, match the ABS temperature within about 10 C.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: Orca generic uses 240.

bed_temp_c.note: Prusa says 100 to 110 C. Orca generic uses 90 C on the engineering, smooth and textured plates. Use 100 C.

enclosure.note: Prusa says HIPS shrinks much less than ABS and its page does not require an enclosure. When HIPS supports an ABS or ASA part, the printer runs in the ABS enclosure anyway. A closed printer still keeps drafts off and helps large parts.

plates.note: Orca sets no Cool Plate temperature for HIPS.
Orca sets 90 C for the engineering plate. Bambu has no HIPS row, so use glue as for ABS.
Orca sets 90 C. Glue is a sensible barrier as for ABS.
Prusa: smooth PEI gives the best adhesion.
Prusa: powder coated textured and satin sheets also give the best adhesion.
Prusa lists satin sheets among the best surfaces for HIPS.

cooling.note: Orca generic runs the fan at 0 to 60 percent, 80 on overhangs, minimum layer time 6 s. When HIPS supports ABS, follow the ABS fan settings since both share the fan.

drying.note: No manufacturer drying figure was found for HIPS. Bambu's drying table does not list it. Start with the ABS figure (80 C for 8 h, AMS HT or oven) only if the filament pops or strings. Prusa asks for at least 24 h of drying after a limonene bath, which is a different matter.

nozzle.note: Orca generic requires HRC 3 (brass is fine).

flow_ratio.note: Orca generic 1.0. Confirm with a flow test.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Orca generic: 8 standard and 13 high flow.

retraction_mm.note: No HIPS specific figure. This is the printer default (Bambu 0.8 mm, Prusa MK4S 0.7 mm), not material data. Tune by strings, and match the ABS value when HIPS supports ABS.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: No HIPS specific figure. Bambu machine profiles use 30 mm/s and Prusa MK4S uses 35.

pressure_advance.note: No HIPS value in Prusa or Bambu profiles. Calibrate.

smart_layer.quality_mode: As a model, HIPS sands well and smooths in acetone, so 0.12 to 0.2 mm is plenty. As a soluble support it follows the layer height of the part it holds.
smart_layer.strength_mode: HIPS is a soft, low heat plastic and rarely the structural choice. When it is a model, 0.2 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle bonds well and prints faster than thin layers.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: Orca generic runs a 6 s minimum layer time with the fan at 0 to 60 percent. When HIPS supports ABS, follow the ABS fan settings since both share the fan.

layer_height.note: No HIPS layer height source. Numbers come from Orca machine limits and the standard 0.4 mm presets. Prusa's soluble support presets also run at 0.2 mm.

smart_layer.note: HIPS prints well from 0.25 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.3 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: Flashforge tested HIPS at 50 mm/s and 230 C. Orca generic allows 8 mm3/s on a standard hotend and 13 on a high flow hotend (see extrusion). No source caps outer wall speed. As a support it runs at the speed of the ABS it holds.
speeds.note: The 30 mm/s lower bound is a conservative choice, not a maker figure. First layer: Bambu Standard preset 50 mm/s, Prusa MK4S preset 40 mm/s.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Prusa recommends 100 to 110 C. All standard Prusa sheets give the best adhesion, and a brim helps on small contact areas.
first_layer.squish_note: No HIPS specific squish guidance. Treat it like ABS.

walls.note: As a model, 3 walls keep the soft plastic from denting. As a support, walls follow the ABS part.

infill.density_note: 10 to 20 percent as a model. Support structures use their own pattern.

supports.note: HIPS dissolves in limonene with no residue (10 to 20 s dip, then dry the part 24 h) and prints at ABS temperatures, which is why it is the classic ABS support on dual nozzle or multi material printers. Prusa warns ABS and ASA partly dissolve in limonene and rates printing HIPS supports as challenging. Prusa's soluble interface preset uses a top Z distance of 0 and 3 interface layers, Bambu's default is 0.2 mm. HIPS is not water soluble. Bambu Support for ABS is a non-soluble alternative.

multi_material.note: Bambu lists no HIPS row. Prusa rates printing HIPS supports as challenging and warns that ABS and ASA partly dissolve in limonene. Prusa recommends against long limonene exposure of ASA parts because it can hurt layer adhesion.

softening_temp_c.note: Orca vitrification temperature. No sourced data sheet HDT.

heat_deflection_c.note: Flashforge data sheet, printed at 230 C. Water absorption is 1 percent in 24 h.

solvent.name: limonene
solvent.note: Prusa: 10 to 20 s in limonene is enough to dissolve a support layer, then dry the part for at least 24 h. Long limonene exposure can hurt some filaments such as Prusament ASA.

safety.note: Prusa's HIPS page has no fume warning. HIPS is a styrene based plastic like ABS, so ventilate the room and use activate_air_filtration on Bambu X, P and H series. This is an inference. Limonene is a solvent: use it in a ventilated area and away from flames.

food_contact.note: Not food safe as printed. Support material is not certified.

failure_modes.symptom: HIPS support stays stuck after a limonene bath

fixes.advice: Prusa says 10 to 20 s is enough. Agitate, and for thick interfaces repeat the dip. Dry the part 24 h afterwards.

failure_modes.symptom: HIPS interface does not bond to the ABS part or peels early

fixes.why: A small gap with soluble support gives a clean face. Tune between 0.08 and 0.2 mm.

fixes.advice: Match the nozzle temperature and bed temperature to the ABS side, and keep the enclosure closed for the HIPS and ABS combination.

failure_modes.symptom: Corners lift

fixes.why: A brim adds hold. HIPS warps far less than ABS but not zero.
A modest brim is enough for most HIPS parts.
Lower cooling reduces warping.

failure_modes.symptom: Smell during printing

fixes.why: Runs the carbon filter during printing on Bambu X, P and H series.

fixes.advice: Ventilate the room.

failure_modes.symptom: Main part weakens or crazes after the limonene bath
causes: main material is attacked by limonene

fixes.advice: Prusa warns not to leave ASA parts in limonene too long. Keep the dip short and test a scrap piece first.

disagreements.resolution: Use 100 C. Match the ABS bed if HIPS is a support.
Use 240 C.

disagreements.topic: HIPS as support for ABS and ASA

positions.claim: HIPS dissolves completely in limonene and works as a support material
Not suitable for ABS or ASA supports because they partly dissolve in limonene

disagreements.resolution: Keep the dip short (10 to 20 s), test a scrap of the model filament, and prefer Bambu Support for ABS where a dual nozzle is not available.

data.name: Nylon 12 (PA12)
data.summary: Flexible, impact resistant nylon with lower moisture uptake and less warping than PA6 or PA66, so it holds size better in humid air. It still needs dry filament, a glue layer and a closed printer, and it prints slowly with the fan off. Sourced numbers here are thin: most manufacturer data is for the carbon fiber grade, and unfilled PA12 has no sourced data sheet in this base.
use_for: parts that live in humid places
avoid_for: parts that need high stiffness (use PA12-CF or PA6-CF)
first time nylon users who have no dry box
open frame printers in a cold room

nozzle_temp_c.note: Polymaker's wiki gives 240 to 260 C for PA12. Its PA12-CF runs 260 to 300 C and Orca's generic PA allows 260 to 300 (default 280). Start at 260 for unfilled PA12 and follow the spool label.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: No PA12 specific figure. Use the main nozzle temperature. Orca generic PA uses 280.

bed_temp_c.note: Polymaker PA12-CF specifies 25 to 50 C and warns not to exceed 50 C. Orca's generic PA uses 100 C. Follow the spool maker, and start cool for Polymaker style grades.

chamber_temp_c.note: Polymaker PA12-CF asks for 25 to 50 C and says not to exceed 50 C, so a passive enclosure is enough and chamber heating above 50 C can hurt that grade. Bambu's X1E guide defaults PA to 60 C chamber for its own high temperature nylons. Do not apply 60 C to a Polymaker style PA12.

enclosure.note: PA12 warps less than PA6 (Polymaker wiki), and its PA12-CF wants only 25 to 50 C ambient. A closed printer still keeps drafts off and helps large parts. Bambu treats all nylons as enclosed printer materials.

plates.note: No Bambu Cool Plate route for PA, and glue is needed.
Bambu lists the Engineering plate with glue for nylon.
Polymaker: almost any surface with a thin PVP glue or Magigoo PA coat. A flex plate helps release.
Polymaker suggests garolite or PVA glue for nylon.

cooling.note: Polymaker says turn the cooling fan off for PA12-CF and print at 30 to 60 mm/s. Orca generic PA allows 0 to 60 percent with 30 on overhangs.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered. Bambu PA figure, not a PA12 figure.

drying.note: Polymaker dries PA12-CF at 80 C for 12 h in a convection oven, only if it has absorbed moisture, and says it is less sensitive to moisture and should be stored in a dry box. Bambu's PA figures (80 C for 8 to 12 h, AMS HT 85 C for 12 h) are the safe fallback. AMS 2 Pro is not compatible with nylon drying. Do not over dry: Polymaker says extremely dry filament can hurt processing.

nozzle.note: Unfilled PA12 is not abrasive. PA12-CF is: use hardened steel. Orca generic PA lists 40 HRC, probably inherited from the filled profile.

flow_ratio.note: Orca generic PA 1.0. No PA12 specific value. Confirm with a flow test.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Orca generic PA: 8 standard and 12 high flow. Prusa MK3.5 generic PA: 11. Polymaker PA12-CF prints at 30 to 60 mm/s.

retraction_mm.note: No PA12 source. Bambu's nylon data sheets suggest 0.8 to 1.4 mm. Tune by strings.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: No PA12 source. Borrowed from Bambu's nylon data sheet (20 to 40 mm/s) and the Bambu machine default of 30.

pressure_advance.note: Prusa's generic PA profile stores 0.02 on MK3.5. Klipper and Ellis both say to calibrate per filament.

smart_layer.quality_mode: Unfilled PA12 can print at 0.1 to 0.16 mm for detail and holds thin features better than PA6 because it shrinks less. Dry it first.
smart_layer.strength_mode: PA12 bonds well between layers. Use 0.2 to 0.28 mm for functional parts, and keep the chamber warm rather than adding air.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: Polymaker runs PA12-CF with the fan off. Profiles use a 2 s minimum layer time, so small layers slow down rather than needing fan.

layer_height.note: No maker gives a layer height for PA12. Numbers come from Orca machine limits and the standard 0.4 mm presets. Polymaker says PA12 has fewer warping issues than PA6.

smart_layer.note: Nylon 12 (PA12) prints well from 0.25 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.25 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.35 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: Polymaker gives 30 to 60 mm/s for PA12-CF, used here as a proxy for unfilled PA12. Real speed is capped by max volumetric speed (see extrusion).
speeds.note: First layer: Bambu Standard preset 50 mm/s, Prusa MK4S preset 40 mm/s.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Polymaker runs PA12-CF with the bed at 25 to 50 C on a garolite sheet or PVP glue. Bambu's general nylon guidance is 100 to 120 C on glued plates. Use the surface's own range.
first_layer.squish_note: No PA12 specific squish guidance was found. Glue stick or garolite matters more than nozzle height.

walls.note: PA12 is tough and flexible, so 3 walls suit most functional parts. Extra walls help under bending load.

infill.density_note: 15 to 30 percent. PA12 warps less than PA6, so denser infill is less risky.

supports.note: Nylon welds to nylon supports. Bambu lists Support for PA/PET (now discontinued) for CF and GF nylons and PET-CF and names Bambu ABS and ASA as alternatives. Bambu does not list PA12, so treat this as a proxy. BCN3D lists BVOH as compatible with PA, but BVOH must be kept dry and needs a multi material printer.

multi_material.note: No PA12 rating. Bambu only lists its PA-CF and PAHT-CF as AMS compatible.

density_g_cm3.note: Orca generic PA value. Not a PA12 data sheet figure.

heat_deflection_c.note: PA12-CF (carbon filled), annealed at 80 C for 6 h. Unfilled PA12 is lower.

annealing.note: Polymaker recommends annealing PA12-CF parts at 80 C for 6 h. Tensile strength rises from 43.6 to 71.6 MPa and bending strength from 48.2 to 110 MPa in its test.

moisture.note: Polymaker: lower moisture absorption than PA6 and PA66, and PA12-CF keeps its properties after moisture conditioning. No numeric figure sourced.

relative.scale: 1 to 5, Bambu star ratings for PA in general, not PA12 specific

safety.note: Prusa says a ventilated room or enclosure is a must for nylon because of odor and ultrafine particles. Ventilate and use activate_air_filtration on Bambu X, P and H series.

food_contact.note: Not food safe as printed.

failure_modes.symptom: Corners lift or the base curls
causes: bed too hot for this grade

fixes.why: A brim adds hold against shrinkage.
Wider brims resist corner lift on large nylon parts.
Polymaker prints PA12 with the fan off.
A slow first layer bonds better.

fixes.advice: Use PVP glue or Magigoo PA. Polymaker PA12-CF wants the bed at 25 to 50 C and not above 50 C. Follow the spool label for other brands.

failure_modes.symptom: Steam, popping, foamy extrusion, rough walls

fixes.advice: Dry at 80 C for 12 h. Store in a dry box.

failure_modes.symptom: Strings and ooze

fixes.why: Nylon is runny when hot.
More retraction relieves pressure before travel.

failure_modes.symptom: Support will not come off cleanly
causes: part left exposed to moist air

fixes.advice: Polymaker says to remove self-support structure right after printing, before the part absorbs moisture and the support bonds hard.

positions.claim: 25 to 50 C, do not exceed 50 C

disagreements.resolution: Use the spool maker's number. No unfilled PA12 data sheet is sourced here, so ask the user for the brand.

positions.claim: 25 to 50 C ambient, do not exceed 50 C
60 C default for PA in Bambu Studio on X1E

disagreements.resolution: Cap chamber at 50 C unless the spool label says higher.

data.name: Nylon 6 (PA6) and PA6/66 copolymers
data.summary: Tough, wear resistant, slightly flexible polyamide. Unfilled PA6 pulls moisture from the air within hours, shrinks a lot and warps hard. Dry it before every print, print it from a dry box, and give it a warm enclosure and a glue layer. PA6/66 copolymers such as Polymaker CoPA trade some strength for lower warping and a much cooler bed.
use_for: parts that take repeated impact or flex
avoid_for: parts that must hold tight dimensions in humid air
large flat parts without a brim
anything that needs a matte cosmetic finish without drying

nozzle_temp_c.note: Orca generic PA allows 260 to 300 and prints at 280. Prusa recommends 285. Polymaker's CoPA runs 250 to 270 and its wiki quotes 250 to 270 for PA6 and 240 to 280 for nylon in general. Follow the spool label first. Start near 270 and move in 5 C steps.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: Orca generic uses 280 for the first layer. Prusa recommends a single 285 for its PA profiles.

bed_temp_c.note: Sources split into two camps. Hot bed: Prusa 110, Orca generic 100, Polymaker's PA66 note 80 to 100, Bambu's glue table 90 to 110 for PA. Cool bed: Polymaker CoPA specifies 25 to 50 C on a PC or textured PEI plate. Use the maker's number for that spool. With no data, start at 80 C and glue the plate.

chamber_temp_c.note: Passive enclosure: Polymaker's CoPA asks only for a closed chamber at ambient temperature, and Prusa says a high ambient temperature "helps a lot" and that a temporary enclosure works. Active heating: Bambu's X1E guide turns 60 C on by default for PA and other high temperature filaments (H2D max 65 C, Prusa Core One 55 C at full bed heat). Use active heating for large or dense parts.

enclosure.note: Bambu requires an enclosed printer for PA. Prusa says pure polyamide is prone to warping and an enclosure helps a lot, and that a well ventilated room or an enclosure is a must for odor and ultrafine particles. Polymaker's CoPA needs a closed chamber, but its wiki says Polymaker nylon does not require an enclosure. Treat it as required for large parts.

plates.note: Bambu glue table gives no Cool Plate route for PA and the plate cannot take the bed temperature.
Bambu lists the Engineering plate with glue for its PA family. Liquid glue is not recommended for PA.
Bambu recommends Smooth PEI or High Temp plate with glue for PA6-GF.
Polymaker CoPA prints on PC or textured PEI with glue when needed, at a 25 to 50 C bed.
Polymaker names garolite or PVA glue for nylon, bed from room temperature to 100 C depending on the maker.
Prusa users report success on the stock steel sheet with plenty of glue stick. Prusa's own advice is its PA Nylon sheet.

cooling.note: Orca generic PA runs 0 to 60 percent with 30 on overhangs. Polymaker CoPA says fan off. Prusa forum users print with fans off. Low fan keeps layers bonded and reduces warping. Turn it up only for overhangs and bridges.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered, flip the spool

drying.note: Bambu's table marks PA drying and desiccant required: 80 C for 8 to 12 h in a forced air oven, 85 C for 12 h in AMS HT, 90 to 100 C for 12 h on the heated bed. AMS 2 Pro is not compatible because it stops at 65 C. Polymaker dries CoPA at 100 C for 8 h. Prusa says at least 4 h below 90 C. Print from a sealed dry box under 20 percent humidity. Wet nylon steams, strings, foams and prints weak and rough.

nozzle.note: Unfilled nylon is not abrasive. Orca's generic PA profile sets a 40 HRC requirement, probably copied from the CF profile, and Polymaker says brass nozzles wear on CoPA quite often. Use hardened steel if the spool is filled. Bambu's table only lists the CF and GF grades.

flow_ratio.note: Orca generic 1.0. Bambu's filled PA uses 0.96. Confirm with a flow test on a dry spool.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Orca generic PA: 8 standard and 12 high flow. Prusa MK3.5 generic PA: 11. Polymaker CoPA quotes 50 to 200 mm/s print speed.

retraction_mm.note: Bambu's data sheet for PA6-CF suggests 0.8 to 1.4 mm at 20 to 40 mm/s, and its X1C profile uses 0.8. Unfilled PA6 has no Bambu profile.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: Bambu's PA6-CF data sheet says 20 to 40 mm/s and Bambu machine profiles use 30. Unfilled PA6 has no maker figure.

pressure_advance.note: Prusa's generic PA profile stores 0.02 on MK3.5, and its PA-CF profile ships M572 S0.05 at 0.4 mm on Core One. PA is printer specific; calibrate.

smart_layer.quality_mode: Unfilled nylon has no fiber to limit detail, so 0.1 to 0.16 mm works, but nylon looks matte at any height and wet spools ruin thin layers. Dry first.
smart_layer.strength_mode: Nylon fuses well between layers when it is hot and dry. Use 0.2 to 0.28 mm for load bearing parts, which also cuts the warping that comes from many thin layers.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: Profiles run the fan at 0 to 30 percent with a 2 s minimum layer time. Nylon warps when cooled, so keep the fan low even on small layers.

layer_height.note: No maker gives a layer height for unfilled PA6. Numbers come from Orca and Bambu machine limits and the standard 0.4 mm presets. Prusa and Polymaker only say PA6 warps unless the chamber is warm.

smart_layer.note: Nylon 6 (PA6) and PA6/66 copolymers prints well from 0.25 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.25 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.35 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: No unfilled PA6 data sheet exists in the sources. The cap is borrowed from Bambu's nylon family (under 100 mm/s). Real speed is capped by max volumetric speed (see extrusion).
speeds.note: Proxy value. First layer: Bambu Standard preset 50 mm/s, Prusa MK4S preset 40 mm/s.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Prusa recommends 110 C. Bambu says 100 to 120 C with glue stick on PEI or the Engineering plate. Garolite works at low or no bed heat with PVA glue (Polymaker).
first_layer.squish_note: Nylon bonds chemically to a matched surface, so use glue stick on PEI and keep the nozzle at normal height. Wet nylon gives a foamy first layer that no squish setting fixes.
first_layer.note: Bambu PA6-CF keeps the fan off for 3 layers, Prusa nylon profiles for 4.

walls.note: Nylon is tough and flexible, so 3 walls give a good balance. Add walls for parts under bending load.

infill.density_note: 15 to 30 percent. Nylon absorbs impact well, and dense solid infill mostly adds warping.

supports.note: Nylon welds to nylon supports. Bambu lists Support for PA/PET (now discontinued) for PA6-CF, PAHT-CF, PA6-GF and PET-CF, and names Bambu ABS and ASA as the alternatives. Bambu does not list unfilled PA6, so treat this as a proxy. BCN3D lists BVOH as compatible with PA, but BVOH must be kept dry and needs a multi material printer.

multi_material.note: Bambu only rates its PA-CF and PAHT-CF as AMS compatible. AMS HT can dry PA at 85 C. Nylon stiffens and swells in a humid AMS, so keep spools sealed.

density_g_cm3.note: Polymaker CoPA 1.12. Orca generic PA carries 1.04.

softening_temp_c.note: Orca vitrification temperature. Polymaker CoPA HDT is only 70 C at 1.8 MPa.

heat_deflection_c.note: Polymaker CoPA data sheet. Plain PA6 and PA66 are not covered by a sourced data sheet here.

annealing.note: Polymaker anneals CoPA at 80 C for 6 h. Anneal in a forced air oven, dry. Nylon parts shrink and can warp when annealed.

relative.scale: 1 to 5, Bambu star ratings for PA

safety.note: Prusa says a well ventilated room or an enclosure is a must for odor and ultrafine particles. Ventilate, close the enclosure, and enable activate_air_filtration on Bambu X, P and H series. Chamber heating reduces carbon filter performance.

food_contact.note: Nylon is not food safe as printed. Additives and layer lines make it unsuitable.

failure_modes.symptom: Corners lift and large parts curl off the plate

fixes.why: A wide brim gives nylon more area to hold against its strong shrinkage.
Nylon shrinks hard. A 10 mm brim resists corner lift.
Keeps a warmer pocket of air around the part if the printer cannot heat the chamber.
A slow first layer squishes and bonds better.
Cooling drives warping. Polymaker and Prusa print nylon with the fan off or low.

fixes.advice: Glue the plate: PVP glue, Magigoo PA or a thick coat of glue stick. Prusa recommends its PA Nylon sheet.
Preheat the chamber. Close the door and lid, hold the bed at temperature for 15 minutes. Use chamber heating at 45 to 60 C on X1E, H2D or Core One for large parts.

failure_modes.symptom: Steam, popping, foamy or hairy extrusion, brittle rough parts

fixes.advice: Dry at 80 C for 8 to 12 h (Bambu) or 100 C for 8 h (Polymaker CoPA). AMS 2 Pro cannot dry nylon.
Print from a sealed dry box with desiccant. Nylon takes on water within hours.

failure_modes.symptom: Thin strings and ooze between features

fixes.advice: Dry the spool first. Wet nylon strings no matter what the settings are.

fixes.why: Nylon is runny when hot. Go down 5 C at a time.
A little more retraction pulls pressure out before travel.

failure_modes.symptom: Part splits along layers

fixes.why: Hotter plastic fuses better with the layer below.
Less cooling keeps layers hot long enough to bond.

failure_modes.symptom: Parts change size or get soft after a few days

fixes.advice: Prusa notes nylon stays hygroscopic after printing. Expect it to swell slightly and go less stiff in humid air. Store parts dry and design in clearance.

positions.claim: 80 to 110 C on a glued hot bed
25 to 50 C on PC or textured PEI (CoPA)

disagreements.resolution: Follow the maker of the spool. Default to 80 C with glue when there is no data.

positions.claim: Polymaker nylon does not require an enclosure

disagreements.resolution: Use an enclosure for anything larger than a small part.
Use 80 C for 12 h in a forced air oven or AMS HT at 85 C. Go hotter only if the spool maker says so.

data.name: Carbon fiber nylon (PA6-CF, PAHT-CF, PA12-CF)
data.summary: Stiff, strong, heat resistant nylon filled with chopped carbon fiber. The fiber cuts warping and shrinkage compared to plain nylon, but the filament still drinks moisture, wears brass nozzles in a few hundred grams, and needs a hot bed, glue and (for Bambu grades) a warm chamber. Use a hardened nozzle, prefer 0.6 mm, and dry every spool.
avoid_for: printers that cannot reach 260 to 290 C
parts that must flex or take impact across layers
AMS 2 Pro users who cannot dry it

nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu allows 260 to 300. PA6-CF prints at 275 in its profile, PAHT-CF at 290 (280 first layer on some printers, 290 on X1C), and both data sheets list 260 to 290. Prusa's PA11-CF profile prints at 285 after a 275 first layer. Polymaker PA12-CF runs 260 to 300. Prusa says composites cover 240 to 285. Start at 275 for PA6-CF and 285 to 290 for PAHT-CF.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu PA6-CF 275, PAHT-CF 290 on X1C and 280 in the base profile, Prusa PA-CF 275.

bed_temp_c.note: Bambu TDS 80 to 100, glue table 90 to 110, profile 100. Prusa uses 100 on the textured sheet and 115 on smooth, and its nylon page says 110. Polymaker PA12-CF is the outlier at 25 to 50 C and not above 50.

chamber_temp_c.note: Passive enclosure (X1C, P1S, P2S closed): Bambu's data sheets list 45 to 60 C and the X1C PA6-CF profile leaves the chamber target at 0, so the chamber just follows bed heat. Keep the door and lid closed, cover the top vents if possible, and use glue and a brim. Active heating: Bambu profiles for PA6-CF and PAHT-CF on X1E, H2D and P2S set 60 C (PAHT-CF on X1C also 60). H2D max is 65 C and Prusa Core One reaches 55 C at full bed heat. Chamber heating cuts warping and raises interlayer strength. Exception: Polymaker PA12-CF wants 25 to 50 C and says not to exceed 50.

enclosure.note: Bambu lists PA-CF as an enclosed printer material, recommended on enclosed printers and not recommended on open frames. Prusa says CF nylon does not warp nearly as much as plain nylon and can be printed without an enclosure. For small parts on an open printer with glue and a brim that can work, but larger parts still curl.

plates.note: Glue is required and the low temperature plates cannot take 100 C.
Bambu TDS names Engineering plate with glue. Liquid glue is not recommended for PA.
Bambu lists High Temperature plate with glue.
Works with glue. The PAHT-CF TDS lists Textured PEI and Prusa's PA-CF profile prints on it.
Bambu recommends Smooth PEI with glue for PA6-GF. Prusa's profile uses 115 C on smooth sheets. Prusa also sells a PA Nylon sheet.

cooling.note: Bambu PA6-CF and PAHT-CF use 10 to 30 percent with 40 on overhangs. The PAHT-CF data sheet allows 0 to 40 and PA6-CF 0 to 60. Prusa PA-CF runs 15 to 20. Polymaker PA12-CF says fan off. Keep the fan low; more air raises warping and weakens layers.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered, flip the spool every 6 h

drying.note: Bambu's table for PA6-CF, PAHT-CF and similar: required drying and desiccant. Oven 75 to 85 C for 8 to 12 h (80 C in its material table), AMS HT 85 C for 12 h, heated bed 90 to 100 C for 12 h. AMS 2 Pro is not compatible (stops at 65 C). Polymaker PA12-CF dries at 80 C for 12 h and is less moisture sensitive. Bambu's saturated absorption: PAHT-CF 0.88 percent, PA6-CF 2.35 percent. PAHT-CF is the one designed to keep strength when wet.

nozzle.note: Bambu: hardened steel or tungsten carbide only, 0.6 mm nozzle recommended, 0.4 mm compatible, 0.2 mm not compatible, 0.4 mm high flow nozzle not recommended. Prusa requires a hardened nozzle and says 0.4 mm with 0.2 mm layers is the minimum. Polymaker says PA12-CF can wreck a brass nozzle in a few hundred grams. Orca profiles set 40 HRC.

flow_ratio.note: Bambu PA6-CF and PAHT-CF 0.96, Prusa PA11-CF on Core One 1.05. Confirm with a flow test.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Bambu suggests a maximum of 8 mm3/s for PAHT-CF and speeds under 100 mm/s (PA6-CF TDS says under 100 mm/s). X1C profiles: PA6-CF 8 standard and 10 high flow, PAHT-CF 8 and 12. Prusa PA-CF on Core One: 6.5.

retraction_mm.note: Bambu X1C profile 0.8 mm (0.6 mm on a 0.6 mm nozzle). Data sheets suggest 0.8 to 1.4 mm at 20 to 40 mm/s.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: Bambu data sheets for PA6-CF and PAHT-CF both say 20 to 40 mm/s, and Bambu machine profiles use 30.

pressure_advance.note: Prusa ships M572 S0.05 at 0.4 mm and 0.025 at 0.6 mm for PA-CF on Core One, and the MK3.5 generic PA-CF profile stores 0.05. Bambu printers calibrate per spool. PA is printer specific; calibrate.

smart_layer.quality_mode: Chopped fiber limits fine detail and raises clog risk below about 0.15 mm on a 0.4 mm hardened nozzle. Keep the floor at 0.15 mm. A 0.6 mm hardened nozzle at 0.2 to 0.3 mm is Bambu's first choice.
smart_layer.strength_mode: Push toward 0.2 to 0.3 mm. Fibers align along each bead, so layer bonds are the weak plane. Fewer, thicker layers mean fewer bond planes, and hot dry filament matters more than layer height.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: Bambu PA-CF profiles use a 2 s minimum layer time and Prusa PA-CF 20 s. Keep the fan at 30 percent or less, since cooling weakens nylon layer bonds.

layer_height.note: Bambu says 0.15 to 0.3 mm at about 100 mm/s on a 0.4 mm hardened nozzle and prefers a 0.6 mm hardened nozzle. Prusa says layers of at least 0.2 mm. The X1C allows 0.12 to 0.42 mm on a 0.6 mm nozzle.

smart_layer.note: Fiber filled nylon clogs at thin layers; keep at least 0.15 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: Bambu PA6-CF and PAHT-CF data sheets say under 100 mm/s, and the Bambu wiki caps CF and GF filaments at about 100 mm/s on a 0.4 mm nozzle. Polymaker gives 30 to 60 mm/s for PA12-CF. Volumetric limits of 6.5 to 10 mm3/s (see extrusion) set the real speed. No source caps outer wall speed.
speeds.note: First layer: Bambu Standard preset 50 mm/s, Prusa MK4S preset 40 mm/s.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Prusa runs PA-CF at 115 C on smooth PEI and 100 C on textured sheets. Bambu holds 100 C on glued plates. Use glue stick on all PEI.
first_layer.squish_note: Fiber filled nylon bonds hard to glued PEI, so normal nozzle height is enough. Do not squish harder to cure lifting corners (Prusa).
first_layer.note: Bambu keeps the fan off for 3 layers and Prusa for 4.

walls.note: Fibers align along each bead, so walls carry the load and infill adds stiffness cheaply but little strength. CF parts gain little from denser infill.

infill.density_note: 15 to 25 percent. Spend material on walls and top and bottom shells first. Lightweight parts do fine at 10 to 15 percent.

structure.note: No source tests wall versus infill for PA-CF. The advice follows from fiber alignment and Prusa's note that composites gain stiffness but lose layer adhesion.

supports.note: Bambu lists Support for PA/PET (280 to 300 C, hardened nozzle, dry required, now discontinued) for PAHT-CF and PA6-CF, and names Bambu ABS and ASA as the alternatives. It is a support interface only. BCN3D lists BVOH as compatible with PAHT CF15, but BVOH must be kept dry and needs a multi material printer.

multi_material.note: Bambu rates only its PA-CF and PAHT-CF as AMS compatible. Its glass and carbon nylon guides list AMS lite as not compatible. PA6-CF is not on the AMS list, so use AMS HT or an external spool. AMS HT dries PA-CF at 85 C for 12 h. Use Bambu Support for PA/PET as support.

softening_temp_c.note: Orca vitrification 170 to 180 C. Bambu PAHT-CF Vicat 220 C, Tg 70 C.

heat_deflection_c.note: Bambu PAHT-CF 194 and 170 C, PA6-CF 186 and 164 C (0.45 and 1.8 MPa). Polymaker PA12-CF 105 C at 1.8 MPa after annealing at 80 C. PA12-CF is much lower.

annealing.note: Bambu PAHT-CF and PA6-CF: 80 to 130 C for 6 to 12 h. Polymaker PA12-CF: 80 C for 6 h, which raises tensile strength from 43.6 to 71.6 MPa in its test. Parts can warp, so use a forced air oven and test on a spare.

relative.scale: 1 to 5, Bambu star ratings for PA-CF and PAHT-CF

safety.note: Prusa says nylon needs a ventilated room or enclosure because of odor and ultrafine particles. Carbon fiber dust from sanding is a lung irritant, so wear a mask. Enable activate_air_filtration on Bambu X, P and H series when the chamber is not held at 60 C.

food_contact.note: Not food safe. Carbon fiber and additives are not certified.

failure_modes.symptom: Corners lift, base curls, layers split near the bottom

fixes.why: A brim gives nylon more hold against shrinkage.
Wide brims resist corner lift.
Holds a warmer pocket of air around the part if the chamber cannot be heated.
A slow first layer squishes and bonds better.
Bambu profiles cap the fan at 30 percent for PA-CF.

fixes.advice: Glue the plate and keep the door and lid closed. On X1E, H2D, P2S or Core One preheat the chamber to 55 to 60 C (not above 50 C for Polymaker PA12-CF).

failure_modes.symptom: Popping, steam, rough or fuzzy surface, weak layers

fixes.advice: Dry at 80 C for 8 to 12 h in an oven, 85 C for 12 h in AMS HT, or 90 to 100 C for 12 h on the heated bed. AMS 2 Pro cannot dry PA-CF.
Print from a sealed dry box. Bambu marks desiccant during use as required.

failure_modes.symptom: Under extrusion or clog after a few spools, or brass nozzle wear

fixes.advice: Use a hardened steel or tungsten carbide nozzle, and 0.6 mm if possible. Prusa says a poorly set first layer raises clog risk.

fixes.why: Hotter plastic flows more easily through a small nozzle. Stay inside the range.

failure_modes.symptom: Part snaps along layers

fixes.why: Hotter plastic fuses better with the layer below.
Less cooling helps interlayer bonding. Prusa notes composites lose layer adhesion.

fixes.advice: Orient the part so main loads run along the layers, not across them. Prusa says fiber filled materials reduce layer adhesion.

failure_modes.symptom: Support fuses to the part

fixes.advice: Bambu recommends its Support for PA/PET as the support material for PAHT-CF. Remove any nylon self-support before the part absorbs water.

positions.claim: CF nylon warps far less than plain nylon and can print without an enclosure

disagreements.resolution: Enclose for parts larger than a small bracket. Open printers only for small parts with glue and a brim.

positions.claim: Bed and chamber 25 to 50 C, do not exceed 50 C (Polymaker PA12-CF)
Bed 80 to 100 C and chamber 45 to 60 C (Bambu PA6-CF, PAHT-CF)

disagreements.resolution: Each spool follows its maker. Ask which grade before applying Bambu numbers to a Polymaker PA12-CF spool.
Use 80 C for 12 h.

disagreements.topic: layer height for carbon fiber nylon

positions.claim: 0.15 to 0.3 mm on a 0.4 mm hardened nozzle, about 100 mm/s
layer height of at least 0.2 mm

disagreements.resolution: Use 0.2 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle, which sits inside both, and prefer a 0.6 mm hardened nozzle.

data.name: Glass fiber nylon (PA6-GF, PAHT-GF)
data.summary: Nylon filled with glass fiber. Stiff, heat resistant (Bambu PA6-GF holds 182 C at 0.45 MPa), dimensionally stable and cheaper than carbon nylon, with a matte surface. Glass is abrasive like carbon: use a hardened nozzle, prefer 0.6 mm, dry every spool and print in a warm enclosure with glue. Only PA6-GF has a Bambu profile and data sheet. PAHT-GF is covered as a family member and follows PAHT-CF settings.
use_for: parts that need stiffness and heat resistance without carbon cost
avoid_for: parts that need impact toughness across layers
AMS 2 Pro users with no way to dry

nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu profile allows 260 to 300 and prints PA6-GF at 265 on X1C (280 in the base profile). The data sheet lists 260 to 290 and its specimens print at 265. Bambu's table groups PAHT-GF with PAHT-CF at 260 to 300 (plus or minus 10). For PAHT-GF start at 285 to 290 as for PAHT-CF (that is an inference from the shared row).

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu X1C 265, base profile 280.

bed_temp_c.note: Bambu TDS 80 to 100, glue table 90 to 110, profile 100.

chamber_temp_c.note: Bambu's data sheet lists 45 to 60 C and ships the PA6-GF profile at a 60 C chamber target on X1C, H2D and other enclosed printers. On a passive enclosure (X1C, P1S, P2S closed) the chamber runs below that target and depends on the bed, so keep the door and lid closed. Active heating (X1E 60 C max, H2D 65 C max, Prusa Core One 55 C at full bed heat) reduces warping and raises interlayer strength. Bambu's guide says glass filled grades warp much less than plain nylon.

enclosure.note: Bambu: requires an enclosed printer, not compatible with P1P or A1. Glass fiber cuts warping compared with plain nylon but does not remove it.

plates.note: Glue is required. Bambu says PA6-GF is not compatible with the Cool Plate SuperTack.
Bambu lists PA6-GF as not compatible with the Cool Plate SuperTack.
Glue stick is required. Liquid glue is not recommended for PA.
Bambu recommends Smooth PEI or High Temp plate with glue applied.
Recommended by Bambu, with glue.
TDS lists Textured PEI with glue.

cooling.note: Bambu profile runs the fan at 10 to 30 percent with 40 on overhangs. The data sheet allows 0 to 60 percent. Keep it low for interlayer strength and less warping.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered, flip the spool every 6 h

drying.note: Bambu: PA6-GF 80 C for 8 to 12 h in a convection oven, 90 to 100 C for 12 h on the heated bed, 85 C for 12 h in AMS HT. AMS 2 Pro is not compatible. Bambu warns wet PA6-GF gives bubbles, stringing and weak layers, and marks desiccant during use as required. Saturated water absorption is 2.56 percent.

nozzle.note: Bambu: hardened steel or tungsten carbide only. Use 0.6 mm (recommended). 0.4 mm is compatible, 0.4 mm high flow is not recommended and 0.2 mm is not compatible. Prusa: hardened nozzle required, 0.4 mm and 0.2 mm layers minimum.

flow_ratio.note: Bambu 0.96. Confirm with a flow test.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Bambu suggests 10.5 mm3/s at speeds under 130 mm/s for PA6-GF. Its X1C and H2D profiles both use 10.5. PAHT-CF equivalents use 8 to 12.

retraction_mm.note: Bambu's data sheet suggests 0.8 to 1.4 mm at 20 to 40 mm/s. The printer profiles inherit the machine default.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: Bambu's PA6-GF data sheet says 20 to 40 mm/s and Bambu machine profiles use 30.

pressure_advance.note: No PA6-GF value sourced. Prusa's PA-CF profile ships M572 S0.05 at 0.4 mm and 0.025 at 0.6 mm on Core One, a sensible starting point. Calibrate.

smart_layer.quality_mode: Glass fiber roughens the surface, so thin layers gain little. Keep the floor at 0.15 mm on a 0.4 mm hardened nozzle. Bambu recommends a 0.6 mm hardened nozzle for PA6-GF.
smart_layer.strength_mode: Push toward 0.2 to 0.3 mm. Glass fibers align along each bead and layer bonds are the weak plane, so fewer thicker layers and a hot, dry spool matter most.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: Bambu PA6-GF uses a 2 s minimum layer time and a fan of 10 to 30 percent. Keep the fan low, since cooling weakens nylon layer bonds.

layer_height.note: Bambu says 0.15 to 0.3 mm on a 0.4 mm hardened nozzle for CF and GF filaments and prefers a 0.6 mm hardened nozzle. Prusa says layers of at least 0.2 mm. The X1C allows 0.12 to 0.42 mm on a 0.6 mm nozzle.

smart_layer.note: Glass filled nylon clogs at thin layers; keep at least 0.15 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: Bambu's PA6-GF data sheet says under 130 mm/s, while the Bambu wiki caps CF and GF filaments at about 100 mm/s on a 0.4 mm nozzle. Bambu's PA6-GF profile allows 10.5 mm3/s (see extrusion), which sets the real speed. No source caps outer wall speed.
speeds.note: Lower bound borrowed from Polymaker's 30 mm/s for fiber nylon. First layer: Bambu Standard preset 50 mm/s, Prusa MK4S preset 40 mm/s.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Bambu holds 100 C on glued plates and lists glue stick as required. Use the same bed temperature for every layer.
first_layer.squish_note: Glass fiber nylon bonds hard to glued PEI, so normal nozzle height is enough. Do not squish harder to cure lifting corners (Prusa).

walls.note: Glass fibers align along each bead, so walls carry the load and infill adds stiffness cheaply but little strength. GF parts gain little from denser infill.

infill.density_note: 15 to 25 percent. Spend material on walls and shells first.

structure.note: No source tests wall versus infill for PA-GF. The advice follows from fiber alignment and Prusa's note that composites gain stiffness but lose layer adhesion.

supports.note: Bambu lists Support for PA/PET (280 to 300 C, hardened nozzle, dry required, now discontinued) for PA6-GF and names Bambu ABS and ASA as the alternatives. It is a support interface only. BCN3D lists BVOH as compatible with PA, but BVOH must be kept dry and needs a multi material printer.

multi_material.note: Bambu: PA6-GF is not compatible with AMS lite. Bambu's AMS table lists only PA-CF and PAHT-CF as compatible. AMS HT dries PA6-GF at 85 C.

softening_temp_c.note: Orca vitrification. Bambu Tg 67 C and melt 219 C.

annealing.note: Bambu suggests it and warns parts can deform. Use a forced air oven.

relative.scale: 1 to 5, Bambu star ratings for PA-CF and GF

safety.note: Prusa says nylon needs ventilation or an enclosure for odor and ultrafine particles. Glass fiber dust from sanding is an irritant, so wear a mask. Enable activate_air_filtration on Bambu X, P and H series if the chamber is not held at 60 C.

food_contact.note: Not food safe.

failure_modes.symptom: Corners lift or the base curls

fixes.why: A brim adds hold against nylon shrinkage.
Wide brims resist corner lift.
A slow first layer bonds better.
Bambu's PA6-GF profile caps the fan at 30 percent.
Holds a warmer pocket of air when the chamber cannot be heated.

fixes.advice: Apply glue stick to the plate (required by Bambu) and close the door and lid. Preheat the chamber to 55 to 60 C if the printer can.

failure_modes.symptom: Bubbles, stringing, weak layers, rough surface

fixes.advice: Dry at 80 C for 8 to 12 h in an oven, 85 C for 12 h in AMS HT, or on the heated bed at 90 to 100 C for 12 h. AMS 2 Pro cannot dry it.
Print from a dry box or AMS HT. Bambu marks desiccant in use as required.

failure_modes.symptom: Under extrusion, wandering line width or clog after a few spools

fixes.advice: Use hardened steel or tungsten carbide, and 0.6 mm if possible. Bambu says 0.6 mm gives better quality with both glass filled materials.

failure_modes.symptom: Part splits along layers

fixes.why: Hotter plastic fuses better with the layer below.
Less cooling helps interlayer bonding.

fixes.advice: Orient the part so loads run along the layers. Fiber filled materials lose layer adhesion (Prusa).

disagreements.resolution: Default 265 C, raise to 275 to 280 C for layer strength or high flow.

positions.claim: Bambu's material table groups PAHT-CF and PAHT-GF in one row
No PAHT-GF profile or data sheet in Bambu's Orca profiles

disagreements.resolution: Use pa_cf PAHT-CF settings and the spool label for PAHT-GF.

disagreements.topic: print speed for glass fiber nylon

positions.claim: about 100 mm/s maximum for CF and GF on a 0.4 mm nozzle

disagreements.resolution: Cap at 100 mm/s on a 0.4 mm nozzle and allow up to 130 mm/s on a 0.6 mm hardened nozzle if the extruder keeps up with 10.5 mm3/s.

disagreements.topic: layer height for glass fiber nylon

positions.claim: 0.15 to 0.3 mm on a 0.4 mm hardened nozzle
layer height of at least 0.2 mm

disagreements.resolution: Use 0.2 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle, which sits inside both.

data.name: Polycarbonate (PC)
data.summary: Strong, tough, high heat polycarbonate. It needs a 270 to 290 C nozzle, a 100 to 115 C bed, a hot enclosure and dry filament, and it warps and cracks easily. Prusament PC Blend is a modified grade that absorbs less moisture and prints more easily than plain PC. Pure PC is the hardest filament in this set for beginners.
avoid_for: cold rooms (Prusa fails below 18 C ambient)
large parts with sharp corners and no brim

nozzle_temp_c.note: Orca and Bambu profiles allow 260 to 290 and print at 280 after 270 for the first layer. The Bambu TDS says 260 to 280, Prusa says 275 (PC Blend on Core One also 275). Polymaker's wiki quotes 280 to 310 for its own grades. Start at 275 to 280.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu 270, Prusa 275.

bed_temp_c.note: Bambu glue table 100 to 120 (TDS 90 to 110), Prusa 110 first layer and 115 after, Orca and Bambu X1C 110, Bambu P2S 100. Use 110 C.

chamber_temp_c.note: Passive enclosure (X1C, P1S, P2S closed): the chamber runs well below the active range on bed heat alone (no source gives a figure). Keep the door and lid closed, and expect corner curling on large parts. Bambu's TDS lists 45 to 60 C. Active heating: X1E maxes at 60 C and Bambu's guide turns it on by default for PC. H2D maxes at 65 C. Prusa Core One reaches 55 C at full bed heat. Bambu ships PC profiles with a 60 C chamber target on X1E, H2D and P2S. Polymaker's wiki asks for 50 to 60 C ambient. Chamber heating lowers carbon filter performance, but PC fumes are milder than ABS.

enclosure.note: Bambu lists PC as not recommended on open frame printers and compatible with enclosed ones. Prusa says an enclosure helps and that printing fails below 18 C ambient (bed thermal runaway). Polymaker calls an enclosure required at 50 to 60 C.

plates.note: Glue is required and the Cool Plate cannot take 100 C or more.
Bambu TDS names Engineering plate with PVP glue. Liquid glue is not recommended for PC in the glue table, glue stick works at 100 to 120 C.
Bambu approves it with glue. Prusa warns PC can damage smooth PEI, so always use a separation layer.
Prusa says avoid smooth PEI because adhesion can damage it.
Best option: Prusa recommends powder coated TXT or satin sheet with glue stick, Bambu lists Textured PEI with PVP glue. PC Blend on satin may work without glue if used occasionally.

cooling.note: Bambu X1C uses 10 to 40 percent with 60 on overhangs. The Bambu TDS allows 0 to 60. Prusa PC Blend runs 12 to 25 percent. Keep the fan low and cool slowly. Polymaker warns slow cooling is crucial or PC prints crack.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered

drying.note: Bambu marks PC drying and desiccant use required. AMS 2 Pro is not compatible. Use an AMS HT, forced air oven or heated bed and keep it in a sealed box under 20 percent humidity. Prusa says PC is extremely hygroscopic and that PC Blend absorbs much less. Wet PC bubbles, strings and loses layer strength. Bambu's TDS lists saturated water absorption at 0.25 percent.

nozzle.note: Bambu marks 0.2 mm as not recommended for PC, and P2S and X2D cannot use it at all. All larger sizes are compatible with a brass or stainless nozzle.

flow_ratio.note: Bambu 0.94, Prusa 1.0 on Core One and 0.94 on MK4S. Confirm with a flow test.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Bambu PC on X1C: 18 standard, 29 high flow. X1E: 18. H2D 0.4 mm: 20, up to 35 on the high flow hotend. Orca generic: 12 standard. Prusament PC Blend: 12 on Core One and 8 on MK4S.

retraction_mm.note: Bambu H2D profile 0.4 mm. The Bambu TDS suggests 0.8 to 1.4 mm. X1C and P2S profiles leave it to the printer default.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: Bambu TDS says 20 to 40 mm/s. Bambu machine profiles use 30, Prusa MK4S uses 35.

pressure_advance.note: Prusa ships M572 S0.05 at 0.4 mm and 0.025 at 0.6 mm for PC Blend on Core One, and 0.02 on MK4S. The MK3.5 generic PC profile stores 0.05. Bambu printers calibrate per spool. PA is printer specific; calibrate.

smart_layer.quality_mode: Thin layers (0.12 to 0.16 mm) suit clear or glossy PC and small detail. They cool quickly at 270 to 280 C, so they need a warm chamber to avoid cracking between layers.
smart_layer.strength_mode: Bias toward 0.2 to 0.28 mm. A thicker bead keeps more heat and fuses better, and PC splits between layers when it cools fast or the chamber is cold.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: Bambu PC uses a 2 s minimum layer time and Prusa PC Blend 20 s. Keep the fan at 10 to 25 percent and let small layers slow down instead of adding air.

layer_height.note: No maker states a PC layer height. Bambu ships 0.08 to 0.28 mm presets for a 0.4 mm nozzle. Bambu and Polymaker both tie PC layer splitting to fast cooling and a cold room.

smart_layer.note: Polycarbonate (PC) prints well from 0.3 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.3 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.35 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: Bambu lists under 300 mm/s. Real speed is capped by max volumetric speed (see extrusion), and Prusa PC Blend runs 8 to 12 mm3/s. No source caps outer wall speed for PC.
speeds.note: No maker gives a lower bound. First layer: Bambu Standard preset 50 mm/s, Prusa MK4S preset 40 mm/s.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Prusa runs 110 C first layer and 115 C after. Bambu says 100 to 120 C with glue stick on its plates. Use 110 C, and go to 115 to 120 C if corners lift.
first_layer.squish_note: PC shrinks hard, so a clean, level bed and steady first layer matter more than extra squish (Prusa). Use glue stick as a release layer on PEI.
first_layer.note: Prusa profiles keep the fan off for 4 layers, Bambu for 3.

walls.note: PC is tough enough that walls carry most of the load. Add walls before adding infill, and avoid large solid blocks that build shrink stress.

infill.density_note: 15 to 25 percent for functional parts. Solid or very dense infill raises warping in PC.

supports.note: No maker lists a release or soluble support for PC. Same material PC supports bond hard, so widen the top Z gap to 0.25 to 0.3 mm or use tree supports to limit contact. Bambu names ABS and ASA as its support filaments for nylon and PET based materials, but does not list PC.

multi_material.note: AMS lists PC compatible, but Bambu's ABS, ASA and PC guide says PC is not compatible with AMS lite. AMS HT can dry PC at 80 C for 8 h. Keep PC out of a humid AMS for long.

softening_temp_c.note: Bambu TDS Vicat 119 C and Tg 145 C. Orca vitrification 120 C.

heat_deflection_c.note: The Bambu wiki lists 117 C at 0.45 MPa. The TDS prints 117 C at 1.8 MPa and 112 C at 0.45 MPa, which looks swapped. Expect about 110 to 117 C.

annealing.note: Bambu annealed and dried its PC specimens at 80 C for 12 h but gives no annealing recommendation for prints. Polymaker's wiki suggests an oven treatment after printing. Anneal below the Tg and use a forced air oven.

blends.name: PC Blend (Prusament)
blends.note: Modified PC grade. Prusa says it absorbs much less moisture than other polycarbonates, is significantly easier to print and can print on powder coated satin without a separation layer.

blends.name: PC-ABS and PC-PBT
blends.note: No sourced settings in this knowledge base. Follow the maker's data sheet. Expect settings between ABS and PC.

blends.name: PC FR (Bambu)
blends.note: Flame retardant V-0 polycarbonate with its own TDS. Same printer requirements as PC. Heat resistance 113 C at 0.45 MPa.

safety.note: Prints hot with a mild odor and ultrafine particles. Print in a ventilated room, keep the enclosure closed, and enable activate_air_filtration on Bambu X, P and H series if the chamber is not heated to 60 C. Chamber heating reduces carbon filter performance.

food_contact.note: Polycarbonate can release bisphenol A. Do not use printed PC for food or drink.

failure_modes.symptom: Corners lift or the base curls, especially on large parts

fixes.why: Prusa recommends a brim for small contact areas. It also holds corners on large PC parts.
A wide brim resists the strong pull of PC.
Prusa notes denser infill raises warping risk on large models.
