fixes.advice: Preheat the chamber. Keep the door and lid closed and heat the bed to 110 C for 15 to 20 minutes first. On X1E, H2D or Core One set the chamber to 55 to 60 C.
Round sharp corners in the model. Prusa says rounded edges warp less than sharp ones.

fixes.why: A slow first layer bonds better on a hot bed.

fixes.advice: Apply glue stick or PVP glue. Bambu requires glue for PC.

failure_modes.symptom: Cracks between layers, often high on the part
causes: cooling too fast after the print

fixes.why: Hotter plastic fuses better with the layer below. Stay under 290 C.
Less cooling keeps layers hot long enough to bond.

fixes.advice: Let the part cool inside the closed printer. Polymaker warns fast cooling cracks PC.

failure_modes.symptom: Popping, bubbles, stringing, rough walls

fixes.advice: Dry at 80 C for 8 h in an AMS HT, forced air oven or on the heated bed. AMS 2 Pro cannot dry PC.
Print from a sealed box with desiccant. Bambu marks desiccant use as required for PC.

failure_modes.symptom: PC bonds too hard and tears the coating of a smooth PEI sheet
causes: PC bonds strongly to smooth PEI

fixes.advice: Prusa says to avoid smooth PEI. Use textured PEI or the Engineering plate with a glue layer.

failure_modes.symptom: Printer stops with a bed thermal runaway error in a cold room

fixes.advice: Prusa printers cannot hold 110 C on the bed below about 18 C ambient. Warm the room or enclosure first.

positions.claim: 117 C at 1.8 MPa and 112 C at 0.45 MPa

disagreements.resolution: Quote about 112 to 117 C and design parts to stay under 100 C.

positions.claim: High Temperature Plate with glue is approved
Avoid smooth PEI, it gets damaged

disagreements.resolution: Textured PEI with glue is the safe default. Use smooth PEI only with a full glue layer.
Default 275 to 280 C, and stay under 290 C.

data.name: PETG
data.summary: Tough, slightly flexible polyester with good layer adhesion and moderate heat resistance. The default choice for functional parts that PLA would creep or crack on. Strings more than PLA and bonds very hard to smooth PEI.
avoid_for: parts that need a glossy crisp surface without stringing

nozzle_temp_c.note: Orca generic allows 220 to 260 (default 255). Bambu lists 240 to 270 for PETG and 230 to 260 for PETG HF, each plus or minus 10 C. Prusa prints at 240 after a 230 first layer. Start at 240 to 245 and move in 5 C steps.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: Prusa and Bambu PETG HF use 230 for the first layer; Orca generic uses 255.

bed_temp_c.note: Bambu runs 60 to 80 (profile 70). Prusa runs 85 first layer then 90. Both work; the higher value helps on open frame printers in cold rooms.

enclosure.note: Not needed to stop warping. Bambu recommends an enclosed printer for PETG so a cold room does not weaken layer bonds, and recommends removing the top glass cover when the bed is above 70 C to avoid heat creep.

plates.note: Listed as not recommended for PETG.
Glue stick works as a release layer at 60 to 80 C.
Smooth PEI grips PETG hard enough to tear the sheet. Use glue stick as a separation layer.
Prusa warns PETG can damage smooth PEI; apply glue stick first.
Best general surface for PETG. Releases once cool.

cooling.note: Bambu uses 10 to 40 percent with 90 percent on overhangs. Prusa MK4S uses a 40 percent max and the Core One 30 to 60. Orca generic allows up to 100. Less fan means stronger layers; more fan means cleaner overhangs and bridges.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered

drying.note: Bambu's material table says 70 C for 8 h in an oven, its drying page says 60 to 65 C. PETG HF and translucent PETG are marked drying required. Wet PETG strings, pops and leaves rough walls.

flow_ratio.note: Bambu 0.95, Orca generic 1.0. Always confirm with a flow test.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Generic PETG: 10 standard, 18 high flow. Bambu PETG Basic on X1C: 15. High flow PETG (PETG HF) on X1C: 21 standard hotend, 29 high flow hotend. Prusament PETG on MK4S: 12.

retraction_mm.note: Bambu PETG Basic on X1C 0.4 mm, Prusa 0.8 mm, Klipper suggests about 0.75 mm once pressure advance is tuned. Bowden values come from the printer profile, not the filament.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: Bambu PETG Basic and HF TDS say 30 to 60 mm/s. The Bambu printer profile uses 30 and Prusa MK4S 35.

pressure_advance.note: Prusa ships M572 S0.053 for a 0.4 mm nozzle on MK4S and Core One (0.032 at 0.6 mm). Klipper's typical range is 0.05 to 1.0 with the high end for bowden. Bambu printers measure it per spool with flow dynamics calibration instead of a fixed value. PA is printer specific; calibrate.

smart_layer.quality_mode: PETG rounds off fine detail and strings on small features, so very thin layers buy less than in PLA. Use 0.12 to 0.16 mm on curved tops and keep 0.2 mm elsewhere. Bambu uses 0.1 mm with a wider 0.5 mm line for translucent PETG.
smart_layer.strength_mode: PETG layer bonding depends on heat, not layer thinness. Thicker layers (0.2 to 0.28 mm) keep more heat in the stack and tolerate the low fan PETG wants. Stay at or under 0.7 of the nozzle diameter.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: Bambu sets a 12 s minimum layer time for PETG and a low fan, so thin layers on small parts slow down a lot. Printing several parts at once keeps the nozzle moving and reduces blobs.

layer_height.note: Bambu tests 0.08 to 0.28 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle and Prusa allows 0.07 to 0.30 mm on the MK4S. CNC Kitchen tested layer height on PLA only, so the strength rule is carried over from that test with less certainty.

smart_layer.note: PETG prints well from 0.2 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.2 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: Bambu PETG Basic is rated under 200 mm/s and PETG HF under 300 mm/s. Speed is capped by max volumetric speed; see extrusion. Bambu suggests about 90 mm/s if the outer wall shows dents from speed changes.
speeds.note: First layer speed is not stated by a maker. PETG bonds hard to PEI, so a slower first layer of about 30 mm/s is a practical default (Bambu asks for 30 or less when the first layer fails, Prusa MK4S uses 40).

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Prusa runs the bed at 85 C for the first layer and 90 C after, with a 230 C nozzle first layer and 240 C after. Bambu runs 60 to 80 C, profile 70 C, for every layer.
first_layer.squish_note: Do not squish PETG. Prusa says PETG bonds strongly to smooth PEI and needs glue stick as a separator, and a nozzle that is too low causes blobs and burnt specks. Raise Z offset a little if the first layer looks glassy and rough.

walls.note: Bambu says raise strength with walls up to 6 and infill up to 50 percent, and warns that more of both raises warping risk. Prusa says use more perimeters instead of more infill for solid parts.

infill.density_note: 15 to 30 percent is enough for most parts. Above 50 percent adds warping without adding much strength (Bambu).

interface_materials: Bambu PETG Basic or PETG HF (own support)

soluble_pairing.dissolve: water, several hours; PVA is not compatible with PETG

supports.note: PETG welds to its own supports, and Bambu says PETG supports on a PETG model are harder to remove and can mark the surface. Raise the top Z gap from the 0.2 mm default to about 0.25 mm (expert value) or use an interface filament with a zero gap: Support for PLA/PETG, or PLA Basic as interface only. Bambu says PVA is not compatible as support for PETG.

softening_temp_c.note: Orca temperature_vitrification 70 C. Prusa says fine for use below 80 C.

safety.note: No enclosure filtration needed for normal use. Ventilate the room as with any hot plastic.

food_contact.note: PETG resin is often called food safe, but no printed part is by default. Layer lines trap bacteria, colorants are usually uncertified, and brass nozzles can contain lead. For food contact use a stainless steel nozzle and a food safe coating, or treat the part as single use.

failure_modes.symptom: Thin hairs between features

fixes.why: Cooler PETG is less runny between moves. Go down 5 C at a time, not below 230 C.

fixes.advice: Dry the spool (65 C for 8 to 12 h). Wet PETG strings no matter what the settings are.

fixes.why: A little more retraction pulls pressure out of the nozzle before travel. Stay under 1.5 mm on direct drive.
Faster travel gives the nozzle less time to ooze.

failure_modes.symptom: Part tears chunks out of a smooth PEI sheet
causes: PETG bonds chemically to smooth PEI

fixes.advice: Switch to textured PEI, or put glue stick on smooth PEI as a release layer.

failure_modes.symptom: Blobs and burnt brown specks on the part
causes: PETG sticks to the nozzle and drops back later

fixes.advice: Raise the Z offset slightly (0.02 to 0.05 mm) and clean the nozzle with a brass brush while hot.

fixes.why: Very high fan can make PETG stick to the nozzle skirt instead of the part.

failure_modes.symptom: Part splits along a layer line

fixes.why: Hotter plastic fuses better with the layer below.
Less cooling keeps layers hot long enough to bond.

fixes.advice: Print with the enclosure closed or out of drafts.

failure_modes.symptom: Sagging overhangs and bridges

fixes.why: More air only where it is needed keeps the rest of the part strong.
Slower bridges give each line time to set.

disagreements.resolution: Default 70 C on Bambu plates, 85 to 90 C on Prusa sheets. Both are inside the material's working range.
Use 65 C. It sits in both ranges and stays well under the softening point on most spools.

disagreements.topic: support Z gap for PETG on PETG

positions.claim: 0.2 mm default gap in Bambu and Prusa profiles
PETG supports on PETG bond harder and are harder to remove; use an interface filament with zero gap

disagreements.resolution: Use an interface filament when the surface matters. With same material supports use about 0.25 mm, an expert value that needs a test print.

data.name: PETG-CF (carbon fiber PETG)
data.summary: PETG filled with chopped carbon fiber. Stiffer than PETG, with a matte finish, less stringing and lower shrink. Layers bond a bit worse than plain PETG. The fibers are abrasive and destroy brass and stainless nozzles, so a hardened steel nozzle is required. Bambu recommends an enclosed printer.
avoid_for: any print with a brass or stainless nozzle
parts that must flex or take shock

nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu 240 to 270 (profile 255). Orca generic PETG-CF 220 to 260 at 255. Fiberon PETG-rCF 240 to 270 at 270. Start at 255 and move in 5 C steps. Prusa notes a hardened nozzle may need more heat than brass.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu and generic use 255. Fiberon uses 270.

bed_temp_c.note: Bambu lists 60 to 80 on every plate except the Cool Plate. Profile 70.

enclosure.note: Bambu lists an enclosed printer as recommended for PETG-CF so cold rooms do not weaken layer bonds. Remove the top glass cover when the bed is above 70 C to avoid heat creep. Not needed for warping.

plates.note: Listed as not recommended for PETG-CF.
Glue stick as a release layer.
Smooth PEI bonds PETG hard enough to tear the sheet. Use glue stick as a separation layer.
Prusa's PETG guidance: apply glue stick first.
Best general surface. Releases once cool.

cooling.note: Bambu X1C uses 5 to 40 percent with 100 on overhangs. The Bambu base uses 0 to 30 with 90 on overhangs. Generic uses 5 to 40. Less fan gives stronger layers.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered

drying.note: Bambu's material table says 70 C for 8 h, its drying page says 60 to 65 C for PETG and PETG-CF. Use 65 C.

nozzle.note: Hardened steel only. Bambu says no 0.2 mm nozzle and rates 0.4 mm hardened as first choice for its own PETG-CF and 0.6 mm for other CF blends. Bambu high flow 0.4 mm is marked not recommended. Prusa says 0.4 mm minimum. Cold pull before printing.

flow_ratio.note: Bambu 0.95, generic 1.0. Confirm with a flow test.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Bambu PETG-CF on X1C is 11.5 standard and 20 high flow. Bambu base 10, generic 11.5, Fiberon 12. The Bambu high flow 0.4 mm nozzle is not recommended for PETG-CF, so 20 applies to a 0.6 mm or larger high flow nozzle.

retraction_mm.note: Bambu X1C high flow profile uses 0.8 mm. PETG Basic uses 0.4 mm. Klipper suggests about 0.75 mm after tuning PA.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: Bambu PETG-CF sheet V2 says 20 to 40 mm/s and V3 says 30 to 60 mm/s. The Bambu printer profile uses 30.

pressure_advance.note: No CF specific number exists. Prusa ships M572 S0.053 for PETG at 0.4 mm on MK4S and Core One. Calibrate per spool.

smart_layer.quality_mode: Carbon fiber hides layer lines, so thin layers add little. Keep the floor at 0.2 mm on a 0.4 mm hardened nozzle: Prusa says composites clog more with thinner layers and smaller nozzles. On a 0.6 mm nozzle the same band is about 0.3 to 0.42 mm.
smart_layer.strength_mode: Fibers weaken the bond between layers, and PETG bonding depends on heat. Prefer 0.2 mm or thicker with a hot nozzle and low fan, and orient loads along the layers.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: Bambu sets a 6 s minimum layer time and a fan of 5 to 40 percent (V3 sheet 0 to 60). Thin layers on small parts lose less to cooling than in PLA-CF but will still string if the nozzle waits.

layer_height.note: Prusa gives 0.2 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle as the lowest optimal setting. A Bambu store excerpt lists 0.12 to 0.28 mm with 0.2 mm typical and prefers a 0.6 mm hardened nozzle; that page could not be fetched directly, so it is low confidence.

smart_layer.note: Prusa gives 0.2 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle as the lowest optimal layer for carbon fiber PETG, so sleipnir has little room to go thinner.

speeds.volumetric_note: Bambu rates PETG-CF for under 200 mm/s on both TDS versions. The 0.4 mm high flow nozzle is not recommended, so 11.5 mm3/s is the practical cap on a standard 0.4 mm hardened nozzle; see extrusion.
speeds.note: No maker states a CF specific outer wall cap. First layer speed is a practical default.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Bambu: 65 to 75 C, profile 70 C, with glue. Prusa lists 70 to 110 C for composites depending on the base plastic.
first_layer.squish_note: Prusa: the first layer must be perfect or the nozzle clogs. PETG-CF still bonds to smooth PEI, so use glue stick on smooth sheets. Cold pull before printing and use a hardened nozzle of 0.4 mm or larger.

walls.note: Fibers align along the walls, so walls add stiffness. Extra infill gives little, and layers bond worse than plain PETG, so orient the load along the layers. Fibers cut warping, so more walls are safe.

infill.density_note: 15 to 25 percent. Walls and orientation decide stiffness; Bambu's PETG guide advises walls of 6 or fewer and infill of 50 percent or less.

structure.note: Expert rule of thumb built on the Prusa statement that composites bond worse between layers.

supports.note: Bambu's PETG guide names Support for PLA/PETG for PETG-CF and says PVA is not compatible with PETG. The mutual PLA and PETG interface guide excludes PETG-CF. Use a wider Z gap than for PLA if you support with PETG-CF itself, because it welds to its own supports.

multi_material.note: AMS compatible, AMS lite not recommended. Abrasive fibers wear the AMS PTFE feed channels over time.

softening_temp_c.note: Orca temperature_vitrification is 70 C. Bambu rates heat deflection at 3 of 5 stars.

safety.note: Sanding or cutting cured parts releases carbon fiber dust. Wear a mask and avoid dry sanding.

food_contact.note: Not for food contact. Fibers and colorants are not certified.

failure_modes.symptom: Extrusion stops or thin under-extruded lines
causes: small or high flow 0.4 mm nozzle

fixes.advice: Use a 0.4 mm or larger hardened steel nozzle (0.6 mm is safer) and cold pull before printing.

fixes.why: Lower flow lowers jam risk.
Hotter plastic flows around the fibers.

failure_modes.symptom: Lines get wider and quality falls after a few spools

fixes.advice: Change to a hardened steel nozzle. A worn nozzle cannot be restored.

failure_modes.symptom: Part splits along layers

fixes.why: Hotter plastic fuses better.
Less cooling keeps layers hot long enough to bond.

fixes.advice: Print in an enclosure or out of drafts. Orient layers parallel to the main load.

failure_modes.symptom: Fuzz and hairs

fixes.advice: Dry the spool at 65 C for 8 to 12 h.

fixes.why: Less ooze. Stay at or above 240 C.

failure_modes.symptom: Part tears chunks out of smooth PEI
causes: PETG bonds chemically to smooth PEI

fixes.advice: Use textured PEI or put glue stick on smooth PEI.

disagreements.resolution: Use 65 C. Same reasoning as plain PETG.

positions.claim: 0.4 mm high flow not recommended, 0.6 and 0.8 mm high flow compatible
X1C profile lists 20 mm3/s for the high flow variant

disagreements.resolution: Only trust the higher flow on a 0.6 mm or larger hardened nozzle.

disagreements.topic: PETG-CF retraction and fan on the Bambu sheets

positions.claim: V2 sheet: fan 100 percent, retraction 0.6 to 1.0 mm at 20 to 40 mm/s
V3 sheet: fan 0 to 60 percent, retraction 0.8 to 1.4 mm at 30 to 60 mm/s

disagreements.resolution: Follow the newer profile values in extrusion: fan 5 to 40 percent, retraction near 0.8 mm at 30 mm/s. Lower the fan further if layers split.

data.name: PLA
data.summary: The easiest and cheapest filament to print. Stiff, crisp, low warp and happy on almost any plate. It softens around 55 to 60 C, is brittle under impact, and degrades in sun, so it suits display and prototype parts rather than anything left in a hot car or outdoors.

nozzle_temp_c.note: Orca generic and Bambu list 190 to 240 (profile 220). Prusa prints at 210 to 215. Start at 220 and move in 5 C steps. Fast prints need the top of the range to keep up with flow.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: Orca generic uses 220, Prusa KB 215, the Prusa MK4S profile 230.

bed_temp_c.note: Bambu Cool Plate 35 to 45, PEI plates 45 to 65 (profile 55). Prusa uses 60 on PEI sheets.

enclosure.note: Not prone to warping. On an enclosed printer with the bed above 45 C, open the door or remove the top glass cover so heat does not soften the filament in the extruder.

plates.note: Standard choice for PLA on Bambu printers.
Orca generic sets 45 C for SuperTack. Let the plate cool fully before removing.
Orca generic sets 35 C. Bambu does not publish a separate row for this plate.
Bambu marks glue as required on the Engineering Plate for PLA.
Smooth PEI. Wait for it to cool and the part releases.
Prusa lists satin or smooth PEI as the best PLA surfaces.
Best adhesion per Prusa.
Grippy and easy to release once cool. Bottom surface takes the texture.

cooling.note: PLA wants strong cooling. Bambu and Orca use 100 percent. Prusa MK4S uses 70 to 100 and the Core One 85 to 100. Bambu H2D uses 60 to 80 with a strong auxiliary fan. Minimum layer time is 4 s (Orca and Bambu), 6 s (MK4S), 8 s (Core One).

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered, flip every 6 hours

drying.note: Bambu's material table says 55 C for 8 h in an oven, its drying page says 50 C for PLA Basic and Matte. Stay at or under 55 C: PLA softens near 55 to 60 C and a spool can fuse or deform. Static drying in an AMS is not advised for PLA. Wet PLA strings and pops but is more forgiving than PETG or nylon.

flow_ratio.note: Orca and Bambu use 0.98, Prusa Core One 1.0. Always confirm with a flow test.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Generic PLA is 12 standard, 21 high flow and 40 extra high flow. Bambu PLA Basic on X1C is 21 standard and 29 high flow. Prusa MK4S and Core One use 15. The hotend, not the filament, is usually the limit. PLA High Speed profiles raise generic to 18 and 25.

retraction_mm.note: Bambu profiles use 0.4 mm. Generic PLA Matte uses 0.8 mm and Klipper suggests about 0.75 mm after tuning PA. Bowden values come from the printer profile.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: Bambu TDS says 20 to 40 mm/s and the Bambu printer profile uses 30. Prusa machine profiles use 35 (MK4S) and 45 (Core One). It is a printer setting; filament profiles rarely override it.

pressure_advance.note: Prusa ships M572 S0.036 for a 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.025 at 0.5 mm, 0.02 at 0.6 mm (0.022 on Core One) and 0.014 at 0.8 mm. Klipper's typical range is 0.05 to 1.0 with the high end for bowden. Bambu printers measure it per spool. PA is printer specific; calibrate.

smart_layer.quality_mode: PLA holds fine detail well, so thin layers (0.08 to 0.12 mm) pay off on domes, slopes and curved tops. Below 0.08 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle Bambu does not test quality and gains nothing.
smart_layer.strength_mode: Layer adhesion in PLA is weaker than in-layer strength. Keep layers at or under half the nozzle diameter (0.2 mm on a 0.4 nozzle). Going thinner does not bond better, going thicker than 0.3 mm loses about half the layer strength.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: Thin layers on small parts hit the minimum layer time, so the printer slows down. Add a second part or raise the minimum layer time only if overhangs curl.

layer_height.note: Bambu tests 0.08 to 0.28 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle. Prusa MK4S allows 0.07 to 0.30 mm. CNC Kitchen found 0.15 mm strongest in Prusament PLA and a strong drop past half the nozzle diameter.

smart_layer.note: PLA prints well from 0.2 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.2 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: Bambu PLA Basic is rated under 300 mm/s. Real speed is capped by max volumetric speed; see extrusion.
speeds.note: First layer: Bambu X1C profile 50, Prusa MK4S 40, Bambu's spaghetti guide asks for 30 or less when the first layer fails.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Bambu profile: 35 C on Cool Plate, 55 C on PEI. Prusa holds 60 C on PEI for every layer.
first_layer.squish_note: Default first layer height is 0.2 mm on Bambu and Prusa. Ellis suggests 0.25 mm or more with a wider first line for a forgiving first layer. Fix adhesion by cleaning the plate before adding squish.

walls.note: Bambu and Prusa default to 2 walls. PLA is stiff and brittle, so load bearing parts want 4 or more walls before more infill.

infill.density_note: Bambu default is grid at 15 percent and Prusa uses crosshatch at 15. The Bambu Strength preset goes to 6 walls and 25 percent. Gyroid works for even strength in all directions.

soluble_pairing.dissolve: room temperature or warm water (under 50 C for PLA), several hours

supports.note: PLA on PLA supports need a Z gap of about one layer, and they peel off with tools. Bambu Support for PLA and PVA allow a zero gap for a cleaner underside. PLA and PETG do not bond well to each other, so either can serve as the other's interface.

softening_temp_c.note: Orca temperature_vitrification is 45 C. Prusament PLA HDT is 55 C. Prusa says it deforms above 60 C. Bambu advises against use near 50 C.

safety.note: Mild sweet smell. Ventilate the room as with any hot plastic.

food_contact.note: PLA itself is a food grade polymer, but a printed part is not automatically food safe. Layer lines trap bacteria, colorants are usually uncertified, and brass nozzles can contain lead. Use a stainless steel nozzle and a food safe coating, or treat the part as single use. PLA also softens in hot drinks and dishwashers.

failure_modes.symptom: Thin hairs between features

fixes.why: Cooler PLA is less runny between moves. Go down 5 C at a time, not below 200 C.

fixes.advice: Dry the spool (50 to 55 C for 8 h). Wet PLA strings and pops even with tuned settings.

fixes.why: A little more retraction pulls pressure out of the nozzle before travel. Stay under 1.5 mm on direct drive.
Faster travel gives the nozzle less time to ooze.

failure_modes.symptom: Extruder clicks or jams a few layers in, mostly with a warm bed and closed enclosure
causes: PLA softens above the heat break
weak cooling of the cold end

fixes.advice: Open the enclosure door or remove the top glass cover when the bed is above 45 C.

fixes.why: Less heat travels up the heat break.

failure_modes.symptom: Sagging overhangs, curled edges, rough bridges
causes: layers too fast for the fan

fixes.why: PLA needs full cooling to freeze quickly.
Maximum air on overhangs and bridges.
Small layers get more time to cool before the next pass.

failure_modes.symptom: Corners lift, or the first layer does not stick

fixes.advice: Wash the plate with dish soap and hot water. Do not use acetone on textured PEI.

fixes.why: A slow first layer squishes and bonds better.

failure_modes.symptom: Part snaps at layer lines or under light flex

fixes.why: Walls carry most of the load. Infill adds little strength.

fixes.advice: Use PLA+ or PETG if the part must flex or take impact.

positions.claim: 50 C for 8 h (PLA Basic and Matte)

disagreements.resolution: Use 50 to 55 C. Higher risks deforming spools and softening the filament.

disagreements.topic: bed and nozzle for Prusa versus Bambu

positions.claim: 220 C nozzle, 35 to 45 C on Cool Plate, 45 to 65 C on PEI

disagreements.resolution: Both fit inside the working range. Default 220 C and 55 C on PEI. Go lower on the nozzle for detail, higher for speed.

positions.claim: 30 mm/s or less when the first layer fails

disagreements.resolution: Default 40 mm/s. Drop to 30 or lower when corners lift or the first layer is uneven.

data.name: PLA-CF (carbon fiber PLA)
data.summary: PLA filled with chopped carbon fiber. Stiffer and more dimensionally stable than PLA, with a matte finish that hides layer lines and very little warping. The fibers are abrasive and wear brass and stainless nozzles in hours to days, so a hardened steel nozzle is required. Layers bond worse than plain PLA, so parts are stiff but brittle.
avoid_for: any print with a brass or stainless nozzle

nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu PLA-CF profile 210 to 250, printing at 230 on X1C, and its wiki table says 210 to 240. Orca generic PLA-CF 190 to 240 at 220. Polymaker PLA-CF TDS 190 to 230. Prusa's composite guide notes a hardened nozzle may need a few degrees more than brass.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: 230 on X1C, 220 in the generic profile.

bed_temp_c.note: Bambu lists 45 to 65 on all its plates including the Cool Plate (profile 45 there, 55 on PEI). Polymaker TDS says 25 to 60.

enclosure.note: Low warp. Open the door or remove the top glass cover when the bed is above 45 C.

plates.note: Bambu's table gives PLA-CF a higher Cool Plate temperature than PLA.
Bambu profile sets 50 C.
Glue required on the Engineering Plate.
Smooth PEI.
Prusa's PLA guidance. No composite specific plate note.
Good bond, easy release once cool.

cooling.note: Bambu uses 100 percent fan, 8 s layer time and turns the auxiliary fan off. Bambu's page lists 50 to 100 percent. Prusa MK3.5 uses 10 s.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered

drying.note: Bambu's table says 55 C for 8 h, its drying page 50 to 60 C. Polymaker says 55 C for 6 h. Wet CF PLA strings and shows rough walls.

nozzle.note: Carbon fiber wears brass and stainless nozzles quickly. Use hardened steel. Bambu says never use 0.2 mm, prefers 0.6 mm hardened for most composites, and lists a 0.4 mm hardened nozzle as first choice for its own PLA-CF (layer height 0.15 to 0.3 mm, about 100 mm/s maximum). Prusa says 0.4 mm minimum and layer height at least 0.2 mm. Do a cold pull before printing. The nozzle and extruder gears need more frequent maintenance.

flow_ratio.note: Bambu 0.98, X1C high flow 0.975, generic 0.95. Confirm with a flow test.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Bambu PLA-CF on X1C is 15 standard and 25 high flow. On a 0.8 mm nozzle it is 18 and 25. Bambu base is 12. Generic is 12 standard and 18 high flow. Prusa MK3.5 uses 12. Small nozzles clog above these.

retraction_mm.note: Bambu X1C high flow profile uses 0.8 mm. Keep retraction short to avoid pulling fibers back into the melt zone and jamming.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: Bambu PLA-CF TDS says 20 to 40 mm/s. The Bambu printer profile uses 30 and Prusa Core One 45.

pressure_advance.note: Prusa has no CF PLA specific PA. Prusa's generic PLA M572 S0.036 at 0.4 mm is a starting point. Calibrate per spool.

smart_layer.quality_mode: Carbon fiber gives a matte finish with almost invisible layer lines, so thin layers gain little. Do not go below 0.15 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle: Prusa says composites clog more with thin layers and small nozzles.
smart_layer.strength_mode: Fibers weaken the bond between layers, so keep layers near 0.2 mm and print hot. Thicker layers on a 0.6 mm hardened nozzle (0.3 to 0.4 mm) help feed and clog less.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: PLA-CF needs full fan except where Bambu turns the auxiliary fan off. Thin fast layers on small parts hit the minimum layer time, so allow 8 s or more.

layer_height.note: Bambu gives 0.15 to 0.3 mm for its 0.4 mm hardened nozzle, capped at 0.28 mm by its machine profile. Prusa says layer height should be at least 0.2 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle. The higher the layer and the wider the nozzle, the lower the clog risk.

smart_layer.note: Carbon fiber PLA clogs and gains little below about 0.15 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: Bambu rates PLA-CF for under 200 mm/s and its product page says about 100 mm/s maximum for best results. Speed is also capped by max volumetric speed; see extrusion.
speeds.note: TDS 200 mm/s and product page 100 mm/s disagree; see disagreements. Prusa says the first layer must be perfect or the nozzle clogs, so run it slower than plain PLA.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Bambu lists 35 to 45 C with glue on Cool Plate, and profiles use 45 on Cool Plate and 55 on PEI.
first_layer.squish_note: Prusa: the first layer should be perfectly fine, otherwise the nozzle clogs. Do a cold pull before printing and use a hardened steel nozzle of 0.4 mm or larger.

walls.note: Fibers align along the walls, so walls carry the stiffness. Extra infill adds little to a CF part. Layers bond worse than plain PLA, so orient the load along the layers.

infill.density_note: 15 to 20 percent is enough. Walls and orientation decide stiffness, not infill density.

structure.note: Expert rule of thumb built on the Prusa statement that composites are stiffer but bond worse between layers.

soluble_pairing.dissolve: room temperature or warm water (under 50 C), several hours

supports.note: Bambu TDS lists Support for PLA. A CF surface hides support marks well. The mutual PLA and PETG support guide does not cover PLA-CF.

multi_material.note: Bambu lists only its own PLA-CF as AMS and AMS lite compatible. Other CF brands can be too rough or brittle for the feed path. Abrasive fibers wear the AMS PTFE channels over time.

softening_temp_c.note: Polymaker PLA-CF HDT is 50 C at 1.8 MPa and 54 C at 0.45 MPa. Orca temperature_vitrification is 45 C. Carbon fiber does not raise heat resistance much.

safety.note: Sanding or cutting cured parts releases carbon fiber dust. Wear a mask and avoid dry sanding.

food_contact.note: Not for food contact. Fibers and colorants are not certified.

failure_modes.symptom: Extrusion stops, clicking extruder, thin under-extruded lines
causes: fibers jam in a 0.2 mm or small nozzle

fixes.advice: Use a 0.4 mm or larger hardened steel nozzle and do a cold pull before printing.

fixes.why: Lower flow reduces jam risk on small nozzles.
Hotter plastic flows better around the fibers.

failure_modes.symptom: Nozzle bore grows, lines get wider, quality drops after a few spools
causes: brass or stainless nozzle with abrasive fill

fixes.advice: Switch to a hardened steel nozzle now. A worn brass nozzle cannot be restored.

failure_modes.symptom: Part snaps easily along layers, even though it feels stiff

fixes.why: More heat improves layer fusion.
More walls give more bonded perimeter.

fixes.advice: Print with layers parallel to the load. CF PLA is weak across layers.

failure_modes.symptom: Fuzz and hairs on the surface

fixes.advice: Dry the spool at 55 C for 8 h.

fixes.why: Less ooze.

failure_modes.symptom: AMS feed jams or PTFE tube grinds down
causes: abrasive fibers rub the feed path

fixes.advice: Feed CF spools from an external spool holder when the AMS is not rated for them. Only Bambu PLA-CF is listed as AMS compatible.

positions.claim: 210 to 250 C profile, 210 to 240 C wiki table

disagreements.resolution: Default 230 C. Polymaker's CF PLA is printed cooler. Follow the spool label for non Bambu brands.

positions.claim: 0.4 mm hardened first choice for Bambu PLA-CF, 0.6 mm hardened for composites in general

disagreements.resolution: Use 0.4 mm hardened minimum, 0.6 mm for fast or high fill parts. Never 0.2 mm.
Plan around 100 mm/s on a 0.4 mm nozzle and treat 200 mm/s as an upper limit for a larger hardened nozzle.

data.name: PLA Matte
data.summary: PLA with a flat, low glare finish that hides layer lines and small defects. It prints like standard PLA, slightly stiffer and more brittle, and often hides flaws well enough to skip fine tuning. Filled with mineral additives on some brands, so nozzles wear a little faster on 0.2 mm sizes.

nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu, Panchroma, eSUN and generic matte all use 220 inside a 190 to 240 range. Bambu lists matte with PLA.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu matte uses 220. Prusa's generic PLA profile uses 230.

bed_temp_c.note: Follows PLA. Bambu Cool Plate 35 to 45, PEI 45 to 65 (profile 55).

enclosure.note: Not prone to warping. Open the door or remove the top glass cover when the bed is above 45 C.

plates.note: Bambu groups matte with PLA.
Bambu profile sets 45 C.
Glue required for PLA on the Engineering Plate.
Smooth PEI.
Prusa lists smooth or satin PEI as best for PLA.
Best adhesion per Prusa for PLA.
Adds texture to the bottom face.

cooling.note: Bambu, generic and Panchroma matte use 100 percent fan and 4 s. eSUN uses 6 s.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, cover the spool, flip every 6 hours

drying.note: Bambu lists PLA Basic and Matte together at 50 C for 8 h in an oven (its material table says 55 C for PLA). Use 50 C.

nozzle.note: Bambu counts matte as standard PLA and lists it 0.2 mm compatible. Some brands add mineral fillers, so check the label for other brands.

flow_ratio.note: 0.98 for Bambu and Panchroma, 0.99 for eSUN. On X1C high flow, Bambu uses 0.985.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Bambu Matte on X1C is 22 standard and 29 high flow. Generic matte is 11 standard and 19.5 high flow. Bambu base 12, Panchroma 16, eSUN 8. Start at 12 for an unknown brand.

retraction_mm.note: Bambu Matte on X1C high flow uses 0.4 mm. Generic PLA Matte uses 0.8 mm.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: Bambu matte TDS says 20 to 40 mm/s. The X1C high flow profile uses 40 and the base machine 30.

pressure_advance.note: No matte specific number exists. Prusa's generic PLA M572 S0.036 at 0.4 mm is a starting point. Calibrate per spool.

smart_layer.quality_mode: Matte finish hides layer lines, so a plain 0.2 mm layer looks finished. sleipnir pays off only on shallow slopes where the stair step still shows. Going to 0.08 mm rarely improves what the eye sees.
smart_layer.strength_mode: Same as PLA: keep layers at or under half the nozzle diameter. Matte fillers can lower layer bonding slightly, so favor 0.2 mm over 0.28 mm for parts that carry load.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: Matte PLA prints fast (Bambu rates it under 300 mm/s). Thin fast layers on small parts hit the minimum layer time first, so add parts or accept the slowdown.

layer_height.note: No matte specific layer range was found. The band follows PLA and Bambu's tested 0.08 to 0.28 mm range for a 0.4 mm nozzle.

smart_layer.note: Matte PLA hides layer lines, so thin layers pay off mostly on shallow slopes and domes.

speeds.volumetric_note: Bambu rates matte for under 300 mm/s. Speed is capped by max volumetric speed; see extrusion.
speeds.note: Matte hides speed related surface differences better than silk or standard PLA, so an outer wall cap is not needed.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Bambu TDS: 35 to 45 C with PVP glue. PEI plates take 45 to 65 C.
first_layer.squish_note: Matte hides first layer blemishes on the visible bottom face less than on side walls. Use the PLA first layer and a clean plate.

walls.note: Matte parts are stiff and brittle like PLA. Use 3 or 4 walls for parts that carry load.

infill.density_note: 15 percent covers display parts. Matte hides infill show through better than glossy PLA.

structure.note: Expert rule of thumb; no maker states a matte wall count. Ironing (Bambu default 10 percent flow, 0.15 mm spacing, 30 mm/s) smooths flat tops but polishes them, which can undo the matte look, so test on scrap first.

soluble_pairing.dissolve: room temperature or warm water (under 50 C), several hours

supports.note: Bambu lists Support for PLA for matte. The Support for PLA/PETG mutual pairing guide does not cover PLA Matte. Contact scars are less visible on a matte surface than on gloss.

softening_temp_c.note: Orca temperature_vitrification is 45 C for Bambu and 61 C for Panchroma Matte.

relative.scale: 1 to 5, Bambu star ratings for PLA (the table groups matte with PLA)

safety.note: Ventilate as with any hot plastic.

food_contact.note: Matte additives are not certified for food. Do not use for food contact.

failure_modes.symptom: Hairs between features

fixes.why: Cooler PLA oozes less. Do not go below 200 C.

fixes.advice: Dry the spool at 50 C for 8 h.

fixes.why: More retraction removes pressure before travel.

failure_modes.symptom: Under-extrusion on small nozzles with mineral filled matte

fixes.advice: Use a 0.4 mm or larger nozzle. Perform a cold pull if flow drops.

failure_modes.symptom: Matte surface shows glossy stripes or patches

fixes.why: Even, strong cooling keeps the matte finish uniform.
Ironing polishes top surfaces and makes them glossy.

failure_modes.symptom: Part splits between layers

fixes.why: Better layer fusion.
More walls, more strength.

failure_modes.symptom: Sagging overhangs

fixes.why: Full air on overhangs.

disagreements.resolution: Default 12. The lower value is brand and printer specific. Test with a max volumetric speed print.
Use 50 C, the matte specific row.

data.name: PLA+ (tough PLA)
data.summary: A family of impact modified PLA blends sold as PLA+, Tough, or Pro. PLA+ is not a standard. Each brand uses its own additives, so temperatures, speed and heat resistance differ from spool to spool. Expect somewhat better toughness than plain PLA, with about the same low heat resistance.
avoid_for: outdoor or in a parked car
anything needing PETG or ABS level heat resistance

nozzle_temp_c.note: Brand dependent. Bambu PLA Tough+ 220 to 250 (profile 245). eSUN PLA+ TDS 210 to 230 (Orca profile 220, range 190 to 240). Polymaker PLA Pro 210 to 230 in Orca, 210 in the TDS. Read the spool label first. With no label, start at 225 and step by 5 C. eSUN states PLA+ prints about 20 C hotter than plain PLA.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu Tough+ 245, eSUN 220, PolyTerra PLA+ 230.

bed_temp_c.note: Bambu Tough+ 35 to 65. eSUN TDS 45 to 60. Orca profiles use 35 on Cool Plate and 55 on PEI.

enclosure.note: Not prone to warping. With the bed above 45 C, open the door or remove the top glass cover. Bambu lists a 25 to 45 C chamber for Tough+.

plates.note: Follows the PLA row of the Bambu table.
Bambu Tough+ profile sets 45 C.
Glue required for PLA on the Engineering Plate.
Smooth PEI.
Prusa recommends smooth or satin PEI for PLA.
Best adhesion per Prusa for PLA.
Follows the PLA row of the Bambu table.

cooling.note: All three profiles use 100 percent fan. Layer time is 8 s for Tough+, 6 s for eSUN and 4 s for PLA Pro. Bambu Tough+ adds 80 percent auxiliary fan.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered

drying.note: Drying values come from the Bambu Tough+ data sheet (55 C for 8 h). The Bambu drying page lists 45 to 55 C for PLA types. Other brands may soften earlier, so follow the spool label if it gives a lower temperature.

flow_ratio.note: 0.98 for Bambu Tough+ and eSUN, 0.985 on X1C high flow, 0.96 for PLA Pro, 0.95 for PolyTerra PLA+. Confirm with a flow test.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Bambu Tough+ 12 base, 18 standard and 25 high flow on X1C. eSUN PLA+ 12. Polymaker PLA Pro 15. Start at 12 on an unknown brand.

retraction_mm.note: Bambu Tough+ TDS suggests 0.6 to 1.0 mm at 20 to 40 mm/s. The X1C high flow profile uses 0.4 mm.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: Bambu Tough+ TDS suggests 20 to 40 mm/s. The Bambu printer profile uses 30 and Prusa machine profiles 35 to 45.

pressure_advance.note: No PLA+ specific number exists. Prusa's generic PLA M572 S0.036 at 0.4 mm is a starting point. Calibrate per spool since additives shift PA.

smart_layer.quality_mode: Behaves like PLA for detail. Thin layers on curved tops help, and the toughening additives do not change the safe floor of 0.08 mm.
smart_layer.strength_mode: The point of PLA+ is better layer bonding and impact resistance. Keep layers at or under half the nozzle diameter and print hotter than plain PLA; thin layers alone do not add strength.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: PLA+ blends often run 5 to 10 C hotter than PLA, so thin fast layers keep more heat. Watch overhangs on small parts and allow a slightly longer minimum layer time.

layer_height.note: No PLA+ specific layer height data was found. The band follows PLA and Bambu's tested 0.08 to 0.28 mm range for a 0.4 mm nozzle. Toughening additives are brand specific.

smart_layer.note: PLA+ (tough PLA) prints well from 0.2 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.2 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: No maker wide speed range exists for PLA+. Follow the brand label and stay under the max volumetric speed in extrusion (start at 12 mm3/s on an unknown brand).
speeds.note: print_speed_mm_s is left out because PLA+ is a family of brand blends with no shared range.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Bambu Tough+ and eSUN PLA+ use the PLA bed range: 35 to 45 C on Cool Plate, 45 to 65 C on PEI.
first_layer.squish_note: Same as PLA: 0.2 mm first layer, clean the plate first, then add squish only if lines look round.

walls.note: Impact and layer bonding come from walls. Use 3 or 4 for clips and brackets before adding infill.

infill.density_note: 15 to 25 percent is enough for most parts. Extra infill adds weight and warping risk more than strength.

structure.note: Expert rule of thumb: no maker gives a PLA+ wall count.

soluble_pairing.dissolve: room temperature or warm water (under 50 C), several hours

supports.note: Tougher PLA+ can bond harder to its own supports. Use a support interface filament, or raise the Z gap to 0.25 mm if supports leave scars.

softening_temp_c.note: HDT is 58 to 61 C for Bambu Tough+, 57.6 to 59.3 C for PLA Pro and 53 C for eSUN PLA+. Only a few degrees above plain PLA.

relative.scale: 1 to 5, Bambu star ratings for PLA Tough (the Bambu table groups it with PLA)

safety.note: Ventilate as with any hot plastic. Additives vary by brand.

food_contact.note: Additives are not disclosed by most brands, so do not assume food safety. See the plain PLA notes on layer lines, colorants and nozzles.

failure_modes.symptom: Hairs between features
causes: nozzle too hot for this brand

fixes.why: PLA+ blends can run hot. Step down 5 C at a time.

fixes.advice: Dry the spool at 55 C for 8 h or less if the label says lower.

fixes.why: A little more retraction pulls pressure out before travel.

failure_modes.symptom: Part splits between layers
causes: nozzle too cold for a tough blend
too much cooling on thin parts

fixes.why: Tough blends need more heat to fuse layers. Stay inside the spool's stated range.
Extra walls carry load better than more infill.

failure_modes.symptom: Extruder jams in a warm enclosure
causes: PLA softens in the heat break

fixes.advice: Open the enclosure door or remove the top glass cover when the bed is above 45 C.

failure_modes.symptom: Print quality differs from the same settings on plain PLA

fixes.advice: Read the spool label for temperature range and speed. Run a temperature tower and a max volumetric speed test for each brand.

failure_modes.symptom: Sagging overhangs

fixes.why: Maximum air on overhangs.
Small layers need more cooling time.

disagreements.resolution: Brand specific. Default to 225 C and ask for the brand when it matters. Bambu Tough+ runs 240 to 245 C in its own profile.

data.name: PLA Silk
data.summary: PLA with a glossy, pearly or metallic finish. It prints like PLA but flows more slowly, is weaker between layers, and needs lower speed for a clean surface. Good for decorative parts, poor for anything that carries load.

nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu and Panchroma silk profiles use 230. Orca generic silk uses 220. Prusa Core One silk uses 225. Silk runs 5 to 10 C hotter than Basic to keep the glossy additives flowing.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: 230 for Bambu, Panchroma and Prusa Core One, 220 for Orca generic silk.

bed_temp_c.note: Follows PLA. Bambu Cool Plate 35 to 45, PEI 45 to 65 (profile 55). Prusa Core One silk uses 60.

enclosure.note: Not prone to warping. Open the door or remove the top glass cover when the bed is above 45 C.

plates.note: Bambu groups silk with PLA.
Bambu PLA Silk profile sets the SuperTack temperature to 0, meaning not supported. PLA Silk+ sets 35.
Glue required for PLA on the Engineering Plate.
Smooth PEI gives a shiny bottom that matches silk.
Prusa lists smooth or satin PEI as best for PLA.
Best adhesion per Prusa for PLA.
Texture dulls the silk sheen on the bottom face only.

cooling.note: Bambu uses 100 percent fan and 4 s. Orca generic silk uses 8 s. Prusa Core One uses 85 to 100 percent and 8 s, and 15 s on a 0.6 mm nozzle.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered, flip every 6 hours

drying.note: Bambu lists PLA Silk on its own row: 55 C oven for 8 h, 45 C in AMS for 12 h. Wet silk shows as dull streaks and bubbles.

nozzle.note: Bambu lists PLA Silk as standard PLA. Metallic or sparkle silks from other brands may contain particles, so check the label before using a 0.2 mm nozzle.

flow_ratio.note: 0.98 for Bambu and generic silk, 1.0 for Prusa Core One. Calibrate; silk is sensitive to flow.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Generic silk is 7.5. Prusa Core One silk is 7 (9 at 0.6 mm). Bambu and Panchroma use 12. No source lists a separate high flow value, so 12 is the ceiling. Slower flow gives better gloss.

retraction_mm.note: Orca generic silk uses 0.5 mm. Bowden values come from the printer profile.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: Bambu silk TDS says 20 to 40 mm/s. The Bambu printer profile uses 30 and Prusa Core One 45.

pressure_advance.note: Prusa ships M572 S0.03 for a 0.4 mm nozzle on the Core One, 0.022 at 0.5 mm, 0.018 at 0.6 mm and 0.012 at 0.8 mm. Calibrate per spool.

smart_layer.quality_mode: Silk shine hides layer lines, so the stair step shows up as dull bands on curved and sloped surfaces. Use 0.16 mm and let sleipnir go down to 0.12 mm there. Stay above 0.08 mm: at that height and high speed silk shows a fish scale pattern.
smart_layer.strength_mode: Silk layers are weak already (Z tensile about 18 MPa against 27 MPa in plane). Thinner layers do not fix that. Hotter nozzle and slower flow help the bond more than layer height.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: A thin layer that hits the minimum layer time makes the printer slow down and the surface changes from glossy to matte. Enable Don't slow down outer walls or print several parts at once to keep gloss even.

layer_height.note: Bambu recommends 0.16 mm and lists 0.12 to 0.20 mm as the useful band. Bambu supports silk on 0.2 and 0.4 mm nozzles only and advises against 0.6 and 0.8 mm.

smart_layer.note: Silk shine hides lines, and Bambu keeps silk between 0.12 and 0.20 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: Silk is limited by volumetric speed (7.5 mm3/s generic, 12 Bambu). Speed changes on the outer wall show as gloss bands, so keep the outer wall slow and steady; see extrusion.
speeds.note: Bambu sets outer wall to 40 to 60 mm/s (try 50). TDS says under 250 mm/s overall. Keep the outer wall speed close to the slowest speed on the preview graph.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Bambu TDS: 35 to 45 C on Cool Plate, High Temp Plate or Textured PEI, with glue. Cool Plate SuperTack is not recommended.
first_layer.squish_note: No silk specific rule. Use the PLA first layer and keep the first layer temperature equal to the print temperature (Bambu sets both to 235 in its silk guide).

walls.note: Walls do not add strength to silk that is weak between layers. Use 2 to 3 and print structural parts in PLA, PLA+ or PETG. Print the outer wall first if surface quality matters more than overhang accuracy.

infill.density_note: 10 to 15 percent for display parts. Infill shows through thin walls only on translucent or light colors.

structure.note: Expert rule of thumb. Bambu suggests Archimedean chords or concentric top surfaces and upright orientation of the display face for gloss.

soluble_pairing.dissolve: room temperature or warm water (under 50 C), several hours

supports.note: Bambu lists Support for PLA for silk (55 degree max overhang). Supports leave dull patches on a glossy surface, so orient the display face away from supports and use an interface filament.

softening_temp_c.note: Orca temperature_vitrification is 45 C for Bambu and 58 C for Panchroma Silk.

relative.scale: 1 to 5, Bambu star ratings for PLA (the table groups silk with PLA)

safety.note: Ventilate as with any hot plastic.

food_contact.note: Silk pigments and additives are not certified for food. Do not use for food contact.

failure_modes.symptom: Gloss is patchy, streaks along the wall

fixes.why: Silk needs slower flow for an even sheen.
Hotter silk flows and flattens into a smoother gloss.

fixes.advice: Dry the spool at 55 C for 8 h.

failure_modes.symptom: Part splits between layers

fixes.why: Better fusion between layers.

fixes.advice: Do not use silk for load bearing parts. Print structural parts in PLA, PLA+ or PETG.

failure_modes.symptom: Hairs between features

fixes.why: Silk is runny. A bit more retraction helps.
Faster travel reduces oozing.

failure_modes.symptom: Ugly overhangs and bridges, sagging underside

fixes.why: Full air on overhangs.
Small layers need more cooling time.

failure_modes.symptom: Layer lines look strong in a glossy finish

fixes.why: Thin layers hide lines under a gloss finish.
A slow outer wall gives a smoother, shinier surface.

disagreements.resolution: Default 7.5 for a unknown brand for the best gloss. Raise toward 12 only after a volumetric speed test.

positions.claim: 235 C for first layer and other layers

disagreements.resolution: Start at 230 C. Go to 235 C when layers separate and back to 225 C when gloss goes uneven or the nozzle oozes.

data.name: Polypropylene (PP)
data.summary: Light, tough, chemical resistant plastic that flexes without cracking and floats on water. It sticks to almost nothing except itself, so it needs a PP sheet or PP tape, and it warps hard, so it needs a wide brim and an enclosure or a warm room. Bambu has no PP data, so settings come from Prusa, Polymaker and Orca generic.
avoid_for: printing on bare PEI or glass
large flat parts without a brim
parts that need to be glued
open frame printers in a drafty room
Bambu cool plates without PP tape

nozzle_temp_c.note: Orca generic allows 220 to 250 and prints at 235. Polymaker says 220 to 250. Prusa says 220 to 270. Start at 235 and move in 5 C steps.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: Orca generic uses 235 for the first layer.

bed_temp_c.note: Prusa recommends 85 to 100 C (80 to 105 C by brand) on its PP sheet. Polymaker says 80 to 100 C on PP sheets. Orca generic uses only 55 C on hot and textured plates and 35 C on Cool Plate, probably assuming PP tape on a cooler sheet. Use 85 C for PP sheet and check the spool label.

chamber_temp_c.note: Simplify3D recommends an enclosure or chamber at 45 to 60 C to limit warping. Prusa only says to print in an enclosure. A passive enclosure is the practical target, since no Bambu or Prusa profile heats the chamber for PP.

enclosure.note: Prusa recommends printing in an enclosure because PP is highly prone to warping, and Polymaker recommends one for warping control. A passive enclosure is enough. No chamber heating figure is sourced and chamber heating is not needed. Keep drafts off the print.

plates.note: Best adhesion. Prusa sells a PP sheet and Polymaker recommends PP-specific adhesive sheets. Cardboard is a fallback when PP will not stick.
Prusa: smooth PEI with PP tape works. Bare PEI gives poor adhesion.
Prusa says the powder coated satin sheet is possible but might adhere less.
Prusa reports poor surface adhesion on PEI without PP tape or a PP sheet.
No sourced PP route on glass. PP does not stick to it without a PP surface.
Bambu has no PP row. Bare Cool Plate will not hold PP; apply PP tape.

cooling.note: Orca generic runs the fan at 100 percent with the first layer off and an auxiliary fan at 70 percent. This is a slicer default, not a maker recommendation. Lower the fan to 30 percent or less if the part warps.

oven.note: Prusa figure for glass or carbon filled PP, used as a proxy.

drying.note: No figure for unfilled PP was found in Bambu's table, Prusa's pages or Polymaker's wiki. Prusa's drying table lists only filled PP (70 C for 2 to 4 h), used here as a proxy. Treat drying as optional and follow the spool label. Dry it only if it pops or strings.

nozzle.note: Orca generic requires HRC 3. Glass filled PP is abrasive and needs hardened steel, but no data was sourced.

flow_ratio.note: Orca generic 1.0. Confirm with a flow test.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Orca generic 12.

retraction_mm.note: No PP specific figure. This is the printer default (Bambu 0.8 mm, Prusa MK4S 0.7 mm), not material data. Tune by strings.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: No PP specific figure. Bambu machine profiles use 30 mm/s and Prusa MK4S uses 35.

pressure_advance.note: No PP value in Prusa or Bambu profiles. Calibrate.

smart_layer.quality_mode: PP has a waxy, low gloss finish, so thin layers gain little. 0.16 to 0.2 mm is a good detail setting and keeps warping in check.
smart_layer.strength_mode: 0.2 to 0.24 mm bonds well and keeps the part flexible. PP fuses to itself well when hot, but very thin layers cool and shrink fast.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: Orca generic runs the fan at 100 percent with a 4 s minimum layer time, and Simplify3D says a fan is required. PP warps when cooled hard, so cut the fan to 30 percent or less if corners lift.

layer_height.note: No PP layer height source. Numbers come from Orca machine limits and the standard 0.4 mm presets.

smart_layer.note: Polypropylene (PP) prints well from 0.25 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.25 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: No maker print speed was found. Orca generic allows 12 mm3/s (see extrusion). No source caps outer wall speed. Slow bridges and overhangs, since PP sags and curls.
speeds.note: The 20 mm/s first layer is a rule of thumb that gives PP time to bond to a PP sheet or tape.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Prusa recommends 85 to 100 C on its PP sheet. PP sticks well only to PP, so use the PP sheet or PP tape on smooth PEI. Simplify3D says PP tape can fuse to a part at high bed temperature, so drop the first layer temperature slightly or add a raft.
first_layer.squish_note: Recreus suggests a 0.15 mm first layer at 10 C above normal and 10 percent wider lines for its PP, with a brim. Prusa asks for a 5 to 10 mm brim.
first_layer.note: Orca generic keeps the fan off for the first layer only.

walls.note: Walls set the stiffness of a flexible PP part. Large flat solid areas shrink most, so keep them small.

infill.density_note: 10 to 20 percent. Sparse infill lowers shrink stress and reduces warping on large parts.

supports.note: No maker lists a release or soluble support for PP in the sources found. PP sticks well only to itself, so supports fuse to the part where they touch, and PP bridges and overhangs sag because of its shrinkage. Design out overhangs above 45 degrees, keep bridges short, and widen the top Z gap to 0.25 to 0.3 mm for same material supports.

multi_material.note: Bambu's guide does not list PP.

chemical_resistance.note: Prusa: high chemical resistance and high tenacity. Suitable for lab equipment and engine fluid containers.

safety.note: No fume warning in Prusa's or Polymaker's PP guidance. Ventilate as with any hot plastic.

food_contact.note: PP is used for food storage in industry, but a printed part is not food safe by default. Layer lines trap bacteria and colorants are uncertified.

failure_modes.symptom: First layer does not stick or the part peels off mid print

fixes.advice: Use a PP sheet or apply PP tape to smooth PEI. Polymaker says cardboard can work if PP will not stick.

fixes.why: A slow first layer gives PP time to bond to the PP surface.

failure_modes.symptom: Corners curl and lift, large parts bow

fixes.why: Prusa recommends a brim for PP.
Prusa says to set the brim to 5 to 10 mm depending on model size. Use the top of the range for large parts.
Holds a warmer pocket of air around the part on printers without an enclosure.
Less cooling slows the shrinkage.

fixes.advice: Print in an enclosure or a still room. Prusa recommends an enclosure for PP.

failure_modes.symptom: Strings between features

fixes.why: Cooler PP oozes less.
More retraction relieves pressure before travel.

failure_modes.symptom: Glue does not hold printed PP parts together

fixes.advice: PP resists most adhesives. Design for snap fits, screws or heat welding rather than glue.

positions.claim: 85 to 100 C on the PP sheet
55 C on hot and textured plates, 35 C on Cool Plate

disagreements.resolution: Use 85 C on a PP sheet or PP tape. The Orca generic value is a low default.
Default 235 C and stay under 250 C unless the spool says otherwise.

positions.claim: First layer 10 C above normal printing temperature
Lower temperature for the first layers so the part does not fuse to PP tape
First layer at the same 235 C as the rest of the print

disagreements.resolution: Start at the normal 235 C. Raise it 5 to 10 C if the first layer lacks bonding, and lower it if the part fuses to the tape.

data.name: PVA (water soluble support)
data.summary: Water soluble support material for printing complex overhangs and internal voids in PLA. It dissolves in room temperature water over hours. It is extremely sensitive to moisture: it must be bone dry, printed from a dry container, and stored with desiccant. Prints slowly and clogs nozzles more easily than normal filament. Needs a multi material setup (AMS, MMU or dual nozzle).
use_for: support interfaces and bases under PLA parts
models with tight support contact surfaces
avoid_for: PETG or ABS pairing (BVOH is the usual choice for PETG)
long idle times in a hot nozzle

nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu wiki lists 190 to 240 for dry PVA and BVOH. Bambu PVA profile is 210 to 250 with 220 in base and 240 on X1C. Prusa uses 195 C for PVA+. Orca generic uses 220. Match it to the model filament, since PVA should print near PLA temperatures.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: 220 in base and generic profiles, 240 on X1C.

bed_temp_c.note: Bambu lists 35 to 45 on the Cool Plate and 45 to 65 on other plates. Prusa uses 60. PVA sticks better to a PLA raft than to PEI.

enclosure.note: Not needed for warping. With the bed above 45 C on an enclosed printer, open the door or remove the top cover, since PVA softens below 60 C. A sealed, dry feed path matters much more than the chamber.

plates.note: PVA is usually printed as support on a PLA part, so the plate follows the PLA.
Glue required on the Engineering Plate.
Smooth PEI.
Bambu textured PEI.
Prusa says PVA and BVOH stick much better to a 1 to 2 layer PLA raft than to bare PEI.

cooling.note: Orca Bambu PVA uses 100 percent fan and 7 s. Generic uses 4 s. Prusa MK3.5 uses 7 s.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered by its box

drying.note: Bambu's material table says 55 C for 8 h in an oven, its drying page says 75 to 85 C for 8 to 12 h, and 85 C for 18 h in the AMS HT, which may still not fully dry it. The AMS 2 Pro is not compatible. Put dried PVA into a sealed dry environment right away without letting it cool in open air. Keep below 20 percent RH with calcium chloride desiccant (silica gel is not enough). At about 55 percent RH freshly dried PVA gets damp in 1 to 3 hours. Dry PVA is stiffer than PLA Basic when bent. Damp PVA is soft, sticky and clogs.

nozzle.note: Bambu lists dry PVA and BVOH as not compatible with 0.2 mm nozzles. Prusa warns PVA is more prone to clogging than BVOH. Do not leave PVA sitting in a hot nozzle: purge or retract it when a print pauses.

flow_ratio.note: Bambu base and generic 0.95, X1C and Prusa MK3.5 1.0.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Generic and Bambu base 4, X1C 6, Prusa MK3.5 4. Keep low to avoid clogs and poor interface quality.

retraction_mm.note: No PVA specific retraction is defined. Bambu and Orca profiles inherit the printer setting. Keep retraction short and limit travel to reduce oozing and heat soak in the nozzle.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: No PVA specific value. The Bambu printer profile uses 30 mm/s and filament profiles inherit it.

pressure_advance.note: No PVA specific value is published. Use the printer default or the paired PLA value.

smart_layer.quality_mode: PVA is support only, so sleipnir should follow the model filament. Thin layers on the model do not need thin PVA layers away from the interface.
smart_layer.strength_mode: Strength is not a goal for PVA. Keep it at the model layer height so the interface lines up with the model surface.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: PVA runs slow (4 to 6 mm3/s) and keeps a 7 s minimum layer time, so it is rarely the layer time limit on the part. Keep the nozzle from sitting idle, because PVA degrades and clogs if left hot.

layer_height.note: No maker states a PVA layer band. It prints with the model layer height, within Bambu's tested 0.08 to 0.28 mm range for a 0.4 mm nozzle. Bambu only lists PVA for 0.4 mm and larger nozzles.

smart_layer.note: PVA (water soluble support) prints well from 0.2 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.3 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

speeds.volumetric_note: Keep PVA at 4 to 6 mm3/s; see extrusion. Prusa's soluble interface profile prints the interface at 40 mm/s and the base at 80 mm/s. Bambu suggests grid supports with speeds set for PVA in its example project files.
speeds.note: print_speed_mm_s is left out because no maker sheet with a PVA speed range could be fetched. First layer speed is an expert value.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Prusa uses 60 C on smooth PEI or satin sheets. Bambu profiles use 45 C on Cool Plate and 55 C on PEI.
first_layer.squish_note: Prusa says PVA and BVOH stick much better to PLA than to PEI. Start the support on a 1 to 2 layer PLA raft, or design so PVA never touches the bed.

walls.note: Not applicable. PVA prints only as support base or interface, never as a wall.

infill.density_note: Prusa's soluble profiles use a rectilinear support base at 2 mm spacing with a 0.1 mm interface spacing. Bambu says avoid tree supports with PVA because they are tall, thin and collapse, and use normal grid supports.

soluble_pairing.dissolve: water; several hours to a dozen hours, warm water and agitation help, PLA models under 50 C, about 20 ml per gram

supports.note: Use PVA for the interface only when possible. Prusa's interface profile uses a top Z gap of 0, 3 interface layers and PVA on the interface; the full profile uses 5 layers and PVA for the whole support. Pairs with PLA (similar temperatures). Bambu says PVA is not compatible as support for PETG, so use BVOH there. Bambu lets you set PVA as both base and interface but advises grid, not tree, supports.

multi_material.note: Only when dry. Bambu says dry PVA is hard enough for AMS and AMS lite, but damp PVA becomes soft and sticky and no longer feeds. Bambu Studio recommends setting PVA as both support base and support interface, using normal (grid) supports rather than tree supports. Expect long purge and flush volumes when changing between PVA and PLA.

softening_temp_c.note: Orca temperature_vitrification is 45 C. Bambu groups PVA with filaments that soften below 60 C.

dissolving.water_ratio: About 20 ml of water per 1 g of PVA or BVOH.
dissolving.time: Hours in room temperature water. Warm water is faster but should not be very hot.
dissolving.note: Bambu shows a part after a few hours of immersion and then after complete immersion.

safety.note: Prusa describes PVA and BVOH as non toxic and odorless.

food_contact.note: Not for food contact. Dry PVA absorbs water and additives are not disclosed.

failure_modes.symptom: Extrusion stops, brown or bubbly output, clicking
causes: filament sat in the hot nozzle

fixes.advice: Dry the spool fully and print from a sealed box with desiccant. Cold pull the nozzle afterward.

fixes.why: Slow flow keeps PVA from clogging.

fixes.advice: Do not leave PVA parked hot. Purge or retract it during long pauses.

failure_modes.symptom: Hairs and bubbles on the interface

fixes.advice: Redry the spool. PVA is damp again in 1 to 3 hours at about 55 percent RH.

fixes.why: Cooler PVA oozes less.

failure_modes.symptom: Support does not stick to the plate or to the model

fixes.advice: Start the support on a 1 to 2 layer PLA raft. Prusa says PVA sticks much better to PLA than to PEI.

fixes.why: Prusa recommends 0 mm distance for water soluble supports. The material dissolves away so there is no clean gap needed.

failure_modes.symptom: Tall thin supports fall over

fixes.why: Bambu advises normal (grid) supports over tree supports for PVA.

failure_modes.symptom: Support takes very long to dissolve

fixes.advice: Use about 20 ml of water per gram, refresh the water, and use warm (not very hot) water.

failure_modes.symptom: PLA specks in PVA or PVA in the PLA part after tool changes

fixes.why: Prusa says frequent changes need more purge to avoid PLA contamination.

disagreements.resolution: Both are Bambu figures for their own PVA. Start at 55 C and go up only if the spool label allows. PVA grades differ. AMS HT 85 C for 18 h is a Bambu setting.
Default 220 C, or the paired PLA temperature. Lower for Prusa PVA+ brands.

data.name: TPU 85A
data.summary: Soft, rubbery TPU that stretches a long way and feels like silicone or shoe foam. It is the hardest flexible material to print: flow must stay very low, feeding is prone to buckling, and it is not for AMS or high flow nozzles. TPU 90A sits between 85A and 95A and is easier, with limits noted below. Bambu does not support TPU softer than 85A.

nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu profiles for 85A and 90A run 200 to 240 (225 profile). The Bambu table lists 200 to 250 for TPU 85A and 90A. Prusa's flexible guide says 230 to 245 depending on hardness and brand.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: Both Bambu profiles use 225.

bed_temp_c.note: Bambu 30 to 45 C (profile 35 on PEI, 30 on Engineering plate, no glue needed for 85A and 90A). Prusa runs 60 to 75 C on its sheets.

enclosure.note: Not needed. With the bed above 45 C on an enclosed printer, remove the top glass cover or open the door to keep the filament from softening in the extruder.

plates.note: Bambu's table marks the Cool Plate as not recommended for TPU.
Bambu excludes the Cool Plate SuperTack for TPU.
Works at a low temperature.
Bambu says glue is not required for 85A and 90A.
Prusa says smooth and satin sheets need a separator (glue stick or Kapton).
Powder coated textured sheet needs no separator per Prusa.

cooling.note: Bambu 85A profile: 100 percent fan and a 20 s minimum layer time. Bambu 90A: 100 percent and 0 s. Prusa uses 30 to 50 percent and says to keep cooling low or off.

ams_2_pro.note: Bambu says the AMS 2 Pro may not fully dry TPU. Use the heatbed or AMS HT instead.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered. The spool expands slightly while drying.

drying.note: Bambu groups 85A and 90A: 90 C on the bed for 16 h, 70 C in an oven for 8 h, 75 C in the AMS HT for 18 h. Store with desiccant below 20 percent RH.

nozzle.note: Bambu: 85A needs 0.6 mm or 0.8 mm (or the TPU high flow hotend). It is not compatible with 0.2 or 0.4 mm nozzles or the 0.4 mm high flow nozzle, and 0.6 and 0.8 mm high flow nozzles are not recommended. 90A works with 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 mm nozzles, not 0.2 mm, and regular high flow nozzles are not recommended. Cold pull before TPU if the nozzle printed carbon fiber.

flow_ratio.note: 85A uses 1.0. Bambu 90A uses 1.0, with 1.029 for its first list entry. Confirm with a flow test.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: 85A is 2.2 mm3/s and 90A is 2.8 mm3/s in Bambu profiles. Prusa says flexible filaments usually print at 20 mm/s with a 30 to 40 mm/s maximum. Slower is better for 85A.

retraction_mm.note: Bambu uses 0.4 mm for 85A and for 90A (0.8 mm on one variant). Prusa says use low retraction or disable it to avoid clogs.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: No 85A specific value. Bambu 95A TDS says 20 to 40 mm/s and the Bambu printer profile uses 30. Prusa's TPU profile uses 60 with a 20 mm/s deretraction.

pressure_advance.note: Bambu says to turn off flow dynamics calibration for TPU. Leave PA off unless a calibration shows a clear gain.

smart_layer.quality_mode: Do not go thin with 85A. Thin layers and poor bridging leave holes (Prusa), and flow is very low. Bambu allows 85A only on 0.6 and 0.8 mm nozzles, so use 0.3 mm on a 0.6 mm nozzle and stay above about 0.2 mm.
smart_layer.strength_mode: Layer bonding in TPU is good. Layer height changes softness only through the wall and infill count. Thicker layers reduce how far the soft filament has to be pushed per mm of travel.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: Flow, not cooling, sets the speed. At 2.2 mm3/s a 0.3 mm layer on a 0.62 mm line prints about 12 mm/s. Bambu's profile uses a 20 s minimum layer time.

layer_height.note: Bambu says 85A is not compatible with 0.2 or 0.4 mm nozzles, so the 0.4 mm band does not apply. The band is expert, taken as 0.33 to 0.6 of nozzle diameter with a 0.6 mm nozzle (Bambu 0.6 mm machine limit is 0.12 to 0.42 mm). Speed shown is derived from volumetric speed and line width.

smart_layer.note: Soft TPU feeds poorly at thin layers, so sleipnir stays at a third of the nozzle or more.

speeds.volumetric_note: Prusa says flexibles print at about 20 mm/s and never above 30 to 40, and softer TPU is harder. Bambu's 85A limit is 2.2 mm3/s, which is only about 12 mm/s at 0.3 mm layers on a 0.6 mm nozzle; see extrusion.
speeds.note: No maker range for 85A. Range and first layer speed are expert values that follow Prusa's statement that the softer the filament, the slower it must print.

first_layer.bed_first_layer_note: Bambu profiles use 30 to 35 C. Prusa lists 60 to 75 C for flexibles, higher for large parts.
first_layer.squish_note: Print the first layer very slowly with a light squish. Soft TPU deforms under the nozzle if too close, so tune Z on a first layer test. Use glue stick on smooth PEI.

walls.note: Softness depends on walls and infill. Keep walls and top and bottom layers low to preserve the give, and raise them only where the part must resist wear.

infill.density_note: 10 to 20 percent keeps the part soft. Use rounder patterns that let the walls flex.

structure.note: Pattern and density are expert values. Prusa states only the trade off between flexibility and strength.

supports.note: Prusa asks for a Z gap of 0.3 mm and XY separation of at least 100 percent for flexibles, and lists support removal as difficult. Avoid supports on 85A and design overhangs away. If needed, use PLA and a little alcohol at the joint.

multi_material.note: AMS, AMS lite and AMS 2 Pro are incompatible. The AMS HT works only as a sealed drybox with manual feed through its TPU outlet. For 85A, Bambu says to feed straight into the extruder rather than through the PTFE tube. TPU 85A is not supported on the A1 series.

softening_temp_c.note: Orca temperature_vitrification is 30 C. Bambu groups TPU with filaments that soften below 60 C.

relative.scale: 1 to 5, Bambu star ratings for TPU

safety.note: Operate in a ventilated area, per Bambu.

food_contact.note: Bambu states TPU is not food contact grade. Do not use printed parts for food.

failure_modes.symptom: Filament folds or tangles before the extruder, or no flow

fixes.advice: Raise the spool holder or drybox above the toolhead so the filament feeds downhill. Open the box's side outlet. Feed 85A by hand directly into the extruder.

fixes.why: 85A jams above about 2 to 3 mm3/s.

fixes.advice: Use a direct drive extruder. Softer than 85A is not supported on Bambu printers.

failure_modes.symptom: Strings and blobs

fixes.why: TPU is very fluid when hot.
Bambu pairs a temperature drop with lower flow.
Less travel between models.

fixes.advice: Dry the spool for the full time.

failure_modes.symptom: Gaps and missing layers

fixes.why: Slower flow melts fully.

fixes.advice: Cold pull the nozzle. Use a fresh nozzle if it printed carbon fiber.

failure_modes.symptom: Constant jams with 85A on a 0.4 mm nozzle
causes: 85A is not compatible with 0.4 mm or 0.4 mm high flow nozzles on Bambu

fixes.advice: Use a 0.6 mm or 0.8 mm nozzle, or Bambu's TPU high flow hotend. Use 90A if you must use 0.4 mm.

failure_modes.symptom: Sagging bridges and overhangs

fixes.why: Slow bridges give the line time to set.

fixes.advice: Use PLA as support and remove it with a little alcohol at the joint.

disagreements.resolution: 35 C on Bambu plates. Prusa sheets like a warmer bed.
Default 0.4 mm. Reduce toward zero if the extruder clogs.

data.name: TPU 95A
data.summary: The easiest flexible filament: firm enough to feed reliably, still rubbery and very tough. Prints slowly with almost no retraction, needs a direct drive extruder with a tight filament path, and must be dry. Standard 95A is not for the AMS. Two Bambu variants change the limits: TPU 95A HF is a high flow grade that prints at about 12 mm3/s, and TPU for AMS feeds in the AMS and prints at up to 18 mm3/s.
avoid_for: parts that must hold precise dimensions

nozzle_temp_c.note: Bambu lists 200 to 250 for TPU 95A HF and TPU for AMS (profile 230). TPU for AMS profile range is 220 to 240. Prusament TPU 95A is 220 to 240 and Prusa's flexible guide 230 to 245. Generic Orca uses 240.

first_layer_nozzle_temp_c.note: 230 for Bambu and Prusa, 240 for Orca generic.

bed_temp_c.note: Bambu runs 30 to 45 C (profile 35 on PEI, 30 on the Engineering plate). Prusa runs 50 to 75 C (Prusament TPU 95A 55 to 75). Both work. TPU sticks strongly to PEI, so the low Bambu range keeps release easy.

enclosure.note: Not needed. With the bed above 45 C on an enclosed Bambu printer, remove the top glass cover or open the door because TPU softens below 60 C. Prusa says leave the door open when using high flow nozzles in an enclosure.

plates.note: Bambu's table marks the Cool Plate as not recommended for TPU. Its TPU wiki says only the SuperTack plate is excluded. Orca's profile gives it 30 C. Use another plate to be safe.
Bambu excludes the Cool Plate SuperTack for TPU.
Works at a low temperature.
Bambu uses liquid glue or glue stick for 95A HF and TPU for AMS, no glue for 85A and 90A. Glue also protects the plate.
Prusa says smooth and satin sheets need a separator (glue stick or Kapton) because TPU sticks so hard.
Prusa lists satin among the most recommended surfaces for Prusament TPU 95A, with a separator per the flexible guide.
Prusa needs no separator on powder coated textured sheets. Bambu textured PEI 35 to 45 C.
Prusa lists PP and PA nylon sheets among recommended surfaces for Prusament TPU 95A.

cooling.note: Bambu TPU 95A uses 100 percent fan and 8 s layer time, TPU for AMS uses 20 to 40 or 50 percent and 10 s. Prusa uses 30 to 50 percent and 10 s and says to keep cooling low or off for flexibles. With a slow flow the layers are already cool, so cooling is less critical.

ams_2_pro.note: Bambu says the AMS 2 Pro may not fully dry TPU. Use the heatbed or AMS HT instead.

printer_bed.note: Enclosed Bambu printers only, spool covered. The spool may expand by about 4 mm, which is normal.

drying.note: Bambu lists drying as required with desiccant during printing, storage below 20 percent RH, and 70 C for 8 h in an oven. Prusa says Prusament TPU 95A normally needs no drying, and gives 60 C for at least 4 h if it is damp. Wet TPU strings, bubbles and has weak layer adhesion.

nozzle.note: Bambu says not to use 0.2 mm nozzles. TPU 95A HF and TPU for AMS work with 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 mm nozzles. Standard high flow nozzles are not supported on the X series for 95A HF and TPU for AMS, but Bambu's TPU high flow hotend is. Cold pull before TPU if the nozzle printed carbon or glass fiber.

flow_ratio.note: Bambu TPU 95A 1.0, TPU for AMS 0.97, Prusa generic TPU 1.08. Flow tests matter more here than with rigid materials.

tpu_95a_standard.note: Bambu TPU 95A on X1C is 3.6, base 3.2.

tpu_95a_hf.note: Bambu TPU 95A HF. Needs a 0.4 mm or larger nozzle and no regular high flow nozzle on X series.

max_volumetric_speed_mm3s.note: Standard TPU 95A: Orca generic 3.2, Bambu X1C 3.6, Prusa generic 3 (MK4S) and 2.5 (Core One). Prusa says typical print speed is 20 mm/s with a 30 to 40 mm/s maximum. The HF and AMS variants are much faster because the material is formulated to flow. Do not apply their limits to plain 95A.

retraction_mm.note: Bambu TPU 95A 0.4 mm, TPU 95A HF 0.8 mm, TPU for AMS 0.4 mm (base lists 2 mm for direct drive standard). Prusa says use low retraction or disable it, since retraction can pull flexible filament into the gears and clog. Bowden extruders should not be used with TPU.

retraction_speed_mm_s.note: Bambu TPU 95A and HF TDS say 20 to 40 mm/s and the Bambu printer profile uses 30. Prusa's TPU profile retracts at 60 mm/s and deretracts at 20 mm/s over 2.5 mm.

pressure_advance.note: Bambu says to turn off flow dynamics calibration for TPU. Prusa ships no PA value for its TPU profile. Leave PA off or at a very low value unless a calibration shows a clear gain.

smart_layer.quality_mode: Do not go thin with TPU. Thin layers and poor bridging together leave holes and protrusions (Prusa), and flow is so slow that fine layers take very long. Use 0.2 mm and let sleipnir go no lower than about 0.16 mm.
smart_layer.strength_mode: TPU bonds well between layers already, so layer height is a comfort setting. Slightly thicker layers (0.2 to 0.28 mm) let the extruder push less speed for the same output and reduce jams.
smart_layer.thin_layer_cooling: Cooling is rarely the limit. Volumetric flow is: at 3.2 mm3/s a 0.2 mm layer prints about 38 mm/s and a 0.28 mm layer about 27 mm/s on a 0.42 mm line. Keep cooling low or use Bambu's 100 percent only where the profile says so.

layer_height.note: No maker states a TPU layer height. The band is an expert view built on Prusa's warning about thin layers and on Bambu's tested 0.08 to 0.28 mm range for a 0.4 mm nozzle. Speeds quoted are derived from the volumetric speed and line width, not measured.

smart_layer.note: Thin layers make TPU harder to feed and bond, so sleipnir stays at 40 percent of the nozzle or more.

speeds.volumetric_note: Bambu rates standard TPU 95A for under 80 mm/s and TPU 95A HF for under 200 mm/s. Prusa says typical 20 mm/s and 30 to 40 mm/s at most. Real speed is capped by max volumetric speed (3.2 to 3.6 mm3/s on standard TPU); see extrusion.
