Two different inner and outer wall accelerations in the stock profile are intentional. Change them together.
Sending uses PrusaLink or Prusa Connect.

common_issues.symptom: Extruder jams with PLA after a warm ABS print
common_issues.cause: Chamber heat lingers and softens PLA above the heatbreak.

fix.why: Keep the chamber cool for PLA.

fix.advice: Open the lid or let the chamber cool before switching to PLA.

common_issues.symptom: ABS warps or cracks on tall parts
common_issues.cause: Chamber not up to temperature at start.

fix.why: A warm chamber reduces thermal stress on ABS.
Low cooling keeps ABS layers fused.

common_issues.symptom: Ringing on fast small features
common_issues.cause: Belts or uncalibrated input shaper.

fix.advice: Check belt tension, then run input shaper calibration with the accelerometer set.

fix.why: Lower inner wall acceleration from the 6000 baseline.

data.name: Original Prusa MK4S

extruder.note: Nextruder with load cell nozzle probing.

hotend.stock_nozzle: 0.4 mm brass, E3D V6 compatible thread
hotend.note: A separate MK4S HF variant and high flow nozzles exist. Hardened nozzles for abrasive filament are optional accessories, not stock.

bed.note: Magnetic steel sheets. Prusa ships a smooth or textured PEI sheet depending on the bundle.

enclosure.note: Open frame by default. Prusa says an optional enclosure lets it print ABS and similar.

motion.note: Orca machine profile limits are 300 mm/s and 4000 mm/s2 for stealth off, 160 and 2500 for silent mode. Input shaper is factory calibrated; an optional accelerometer set recalibrates it after hardware changes.

psu_rated_w.note: Custom Delta supply with Power Panic hardware.

printing_typical_w.note: Prusa average measured on an MK series printer at 26 C, with generic PLA and ABS settings.

builtin_calibrations.what: Adjusts live Z from the LCD using the nozzle load cell probe.
Load cell tap mesh before each print.
Accelerometer based, needs the optional accelerometer set.
Firmware motor drive tuning that reduces VFAs and noise. Calibration is listed for CORE One and XL in the Prusa KB; check current firmware notes before promising it on MK4S.

materials.note: Open frame: ABS, ASA, PC and nylons need the enclosure kit or a draft free room, and warp on tall parts otherwise. CF and GF filaments need a hardened nozzle. TPU 85A prints slowly and needs care with the Nextruder gear.

profile_baseline.note: This is the profile Orca lists as default for the MK4S. Prusa's own Quality preset is slower.

pilot_notes: G-code flavor is marlin2. Pressure advance is set with M572 in filament start G-code, not SET_PRESSURE_ADVANCE.
Prusa printers need the vendor filament profile for the right nozzle temperature and PA. Change values as overrides, not by editing the system profile.
Crash detection and input shaper do not work together per the Prusa KB, so do not suggest enabling both.
Real speed is limited by the 290 C hotend and volumetric flow. Do not push filament_max_volumetric_speed above the vendor filament profile without a flow test.
Sending to the printer uses PrusaLink or Prusa Connect, not Moonraker or OctoPrint.

common_issues.symptom: Ghosting or ringing at high accel
common_issues.cause: Loose belts or an uncalibrated input shaper after a hardware change.

fix.advice: Check belt tension first, then recalibrate input shaper with the accelerometer set.

fix.why: Lower outer wall acceleration reduces ringing while the cause is fixed.

common_issues.symptom: PETG or ABS lifts or warps on the open frame
common_issues.cause: Cold room drafts on an open frame printer.

fix.advice: Use the enclosure kit or block drafts. Use a brim for tall or large-footprint ABS and ASA parts.

fix.why: A brim holds corners of ABS and ASA parts.

common_issues.symptom: Nozzle clog or stringy retraction on TPU
common_issues.cause: Too fast and too much retraction.

fix.why: TPU compresses instead of retracting cleanly; keep retraction short.

data.name: Original Prusa MMU3

material_limits.note: Prusa states PLA and PETG are supported and other polymers are not extensively tested. Flexible and abrasive filaments do not feed reliably through the MMU. Also compatible with MK3S+, MK3.5/S and MK3.9/S (not modeled here).

data.notes: CORE One uses the enclosed MMU3 kit. Orca ships 'Prusa CORE One MMU3' machine profiles and separate '+ MMU3' process profiles.

known_issues.cause: The FINDA (SuperFINDA) stays triggered after unload because of debris or a broken filament piece in the selector.

fix.advice: Remove the Festo fitting, slide the selector right and clear debris with the 1.5 mm Allen key, then retry.

known_issues.symptom: Error 04103, filament sensor did not trigger
known_issues.cause: The extruder IR filament sensor did not see filament during load to nozzle. Often an uncalibrated sensor or a filament that stops short.

fix.advice: Recalibrate the IR filament sensor, then check the PTFE path and that the filament tip is clean.

known_issues.symptom: Error 04104, filament sensor still triggered after unload
known_issues.cause: Filament remains in the extruder sensor after the MMU unloaded it.

fix.advice: Clear the extruder path by hand, check for a broken tip, and recalibrate the IR sensor.

known_issues.symptom: Random filament change or spool join in mid print
known_issues.cause: Uncalibrated IR sensor reports no filament while filament is present.

fix.advice: Calibrate the IR filament sensor and keep the sensor clean.

known_issues.cause: Purge volume too small or prime tower too narrow.

fix.why: More flush moves old color out of the nozzle.
Room for full purge lines.

data.name: Original Prusa XL

extruder.note: One Nextruder per toolhead, each with its own load cell.

hotend.note: Single toolhead and 5 toolhead (5T) versions. Nozzles are per toolhead.

bed.note: 16 segment heatbed; only segments under the part are heated. Magnetic steel sheets.

enclosure.note: Open by default. Prusa sells an enclosure bundle.

motion.note: Orca limits 400 mm/s and 4000 mm/s2. Toolheads have an integrated accelerometer, factory calibrated, per Prusa KB.

standby_w.note: Prusa average power draw on stand-by, 5 toolhead XL.

heatup_peak_w.note: Prusa average power draw while heating up before calibration. This is an average, not a peak.

printing_typical_w.note: Prusa states 235 W average while printing PETG. The segmented bed heats only the tiles under the part, so small parts draw less.

power.note: The XL page shows a 240 W PSU line that matches the MK4S table and cannot power 550 W of heat up, so no PSU rating is recorded. The printer plugs into a standard household socket.

builtin_calibrations.what: Automatic toolhead offset calibration on the 5T and multi tool setups.
Integrated accelerometer, factory calibrated.
Introduced on the XL by firmware update.

multi_material.note: Up to five toolheads, each with its own filament. Wipe tower is still used to prime idle toolheads; per-toolhead nozzle and temperature settings are independent.

materials.note: Large open bed: ABS, ASA and nylon need the enclosure and warp on big footprints without it. Abrasive filaments need hardened nozzles on every toolhead that uses them.

pilot_notes: 5T machines use separate Orca profiles (Prusa XL 5T). Confirm which variant the user has before reading limits.
Do not merge plates that need different tools in a way that forces excessive tool changes without saying so: each change costs time and purge.
The bed is segmented. Small parts heat only their segments, so a brim or skirt outside heated segments may not stick.
G-code flavor is marlin2, pressure advance via M572. Sending uses PrusaLink or Prusa Connect.

common_issues.symptom: Large ABS or ASA part warps
common_issues.cause: Open frame and big footprint.

fix.advice: Fit the enclosure and print with the door closed.

fix.why: Wide brim on large footprint ABS.

common_issues.symptom: Oozing color contamination after tool change on multi tool prints
common_issues.cause: Idle toolhead ooze or too small prime tower.

fix.why: The tower primes each toolhead after a change.
A wider tower gives more room to prime.

data.name: Sovol SV08

extruder.note: Direct drive toolhead. The SV08 is a Voron 2.4 inspired CoreXY.

hotend.note: Search summaries disagree on whether the stock nozzle is brass or hardened steel. Ask the user before assuming abrasive filament is safe.

bed.note: Sources report 100 C. Some retail listings mention higher; use 100 unless the user's config says otherwise.

enclosure.note: Sold with a partial enclosure and panels. A SV08 Max variant with heated chamber exists and is a different model. Treat the SV08 as passive.

motion.note: Sovol quotes 700 mm/s and 40000 mm/s2. Orca profile caps extruding acceleration at 20000 and travel at 40000. Input shaper is configured but not tuned per unit, so results vary.

psu_rated_w.note: 24 V supply per the Sovol spec table. The heated bed is an AC bed, so it does not draw from this supply. Bed heater wattage and total maximum draw are not published on the page.

builtin_calibrations.what: Four independent Z motors are leveled with QUAD_GANTRY_LEVEL like a Voron 2.4.
Klipper bed mesh before print.
Available only if an accelerometer is added.

materials.note: Passive enclosure and 100 C bed make ABS and ASA workable with panels and heat soak. High-temp materials such as PC or PA are limited by the 300 C hotend and chamber.

profile_baseline.note: Aggressive baseline. Many users lower it after seeing ringing.

pilot_notes: Orca's baseline acceleration (20000 default, 8000 outer wall) is aggressive for a printer whose input shaper is not tuned per unit. Expect ringing and suggest lowering accel first.
Klipper flavor. Pressure advance via SET_PRESSURE_ADVANCE. Sovol ships PRINT_START macros; confirm their argument names before editing machine_start_gcode.
Bed maximum is 100 C. Do not request 110 C for ABS.
Print quality varies between units; a stated quality issue may be hardware (loose belts, wobbly gantry). Check the machine before blaming settings.
Reachable through Moonraker (Mainsail or Fluidd).

common_issues.symptom: Heavy ringing on outer walls
common_issues.cause: High baseline acceleration without a tuned input shaper.

fix.why: Lower outer wall acceleration from 8000 to clean up ringing.
Lower general acceleration until the shaper is tuned.

fix.advice: Add an accelerometer and run SHAPER_CALIBRATE.

common_issues.symptom: Bed or nozzle temperature not reached for ABS
common_issues.cause: Bed max is 100 C.

fix.why: Stay inside the bed limit.

common_issues.symptom: Under extrusion at high speed
common_issues.cause: Volumetric flow limit of the stock hotend.

fix.advice: Run a max volumetric flow test and cap filament_max_volumetric_speed below the failure point.

data.name: Voron 2.4

build_volume_mm.note: Kit sizes are 250, 300 and 350 cube. This file models the 300. Orca lists 275 mm printable height for the 300 profile to leave room for the bed and nozzle.

extruder.note: Stock design uses the Stealthburner toolhead with a Clockwork 2 extruder. Builders can swap it.

hotend.stock_nozzle: 0.4 mm, depends on the hotend the builder chose (Rapido, Dragon, Revo and others)
hotend.note: Hotend is the builder's choice. The 300 C figure is a common all-metal ceiling, not a Voron spec. Read the actual value from the user's printer.cfg max_temp.

bed.note: Mains powered silicone or aluminum heater with a magnetic PEI sheet is typical. Max temp depends on the build. 110 C is a conservative typical value.

enclosure.note: Fully enclosed. Chamber warms passively from the bed. Active chamber heaters and carbon filters are common mods, not stock.

motion.note: Orca profile limits are 500 mm/s and 20000 mm/s2. Real limits are set by the resonance test result and the user's tuning. Uses ADXL345 or similar with Klipper SHAPER_CALIBRATE.

psu_rated_w.note: The assembly manual names the Mean Well LRS-200-24. The 200 W rating comes from the model number. Builders may fit a larger 24 V supply.

power.note: Depends on the build. The bed heater runs from mains AC through an SSR, not from the 24 V supply, and the Voron docs give no bed wattage. Ask the user for the heater rating. The manual has a supply voltage selector switch that must match local mains.

builtin_calibrations.what: QUAD_GANTRY_LEVEL levels the gantry with four Z motors before each print.
Homing and Z offset routines run from the Voron macros.
Klipper resonance test with an accelerometer.
TUNING_TOWER with SET_PRESSURE_ADVANCE.

materials.note: Enclosed and heat capable, which suits ABS, ASA, PC and nylon. Abrasive filaments need a hardened nozzle. Passive chamber means PLA and TPU need the door or lid opened and the exhaust fan considered. Depends on the user's build.

profile_baseline.note: Generic conservative baseline shared by all Orca Voron profiles. Tuned machines usually run higher accelerations.

pilot_notes: Every Voron is different. Read the user's real limits (max_accel, max_velocity, hotend max_temp, bed max_temp) from the Klipper config via Moonraker before setting speeds or temperatures.
The printer relies on macros. PRINT_START must accept bed and nozzle temperature arguments and machine_start_gcode in Orca must call it with the right parameter names.
Klipper G-code flavor. Pressure advance is SET_PRESSURE_ADVANCE, or Orca's pressure_advance setting emits it. Check the macro does not also set it.
Heat soak ABS and ASA before printing, 10 to 20 minutes with the bed at temperature and the door closed.
The stock Orca profile is conservative. Do not treat 20000 mm/s2 as the safe print acceleration, use the resonance test recommendation.
Reachable through Moonraker (API in moonraker_api guide).

common_issues.symptom: Ringing or ghosting after raising acceleration
common_issues.cause: Acceleration above what the shaper can clean up.

fix.why: Baseline Orca outer wall acceleration for this profile.

fix.advice: Rerun SHAPER_CALIBRATE and keep max_accel at or below the recommended value.

common_issues.symptom: ABS layer splitting or corner lifting
common_issues.cause: Chamber not heat soaked; strong part cooling.

fix.why: Low fan keeps ABS layers fused in the chamber.

fix.advice: Heat soak the chamber before the print starts.

common_issues.symptom: Blobs or missing extrusion after the first layer with a bed mesh
common_issues.cause: Mesh not adaptive or Z offset drifted with chamber heat.

fix.advice: Use adaptive bed mesh and re-run Z offset after heat soak.

data.name: Voron Trident

build_volume_mm.note: Kit sizes are 250x250x250, 300x300x250 and 350x350x250. This file models the 300. Z height is limited by the three lead screw bed design.

extruder.note: Stealthburner toolhead with Clockwork 2 is the stock design; builders can swap it.

hotend.stock_nozzle: 0.4 mm, depends on the builder's hotend
hotend.note: Builder's choice of hotend. Read max_temp from the user's printer.cfg.

bed.note: Typical mains silicone or aluminum heater with magnetic PEI sheet. Depends on the build.

enclosure.note: Fully enclosed, passive chamber warmth from the bed. Active chamber heaters are common mods.

motion.note: Orca profile limits 500 mm/s and 20000 mm/s2. The fixed gantry can be stiffer than a 2.4, but the real limit is the resonance test result.

psu_rated_w.note: The assembly manual names the Mean Well LRS-200-24. The 200 W rating comes from the model number. Builders may fit a larger 24 V supply.

power.note: Depends on the build. The bed heater runs from mains AC through an SSR, not from the 24 V supply, and the Voron docs give no bed wattage. Ask the user for the heater rating. The manual has a supply voltage selector switch that must match local mains.

builtin_calibrations.what: Z_TILT_ADJUST levels the bed on its three lead screws before each print.
Klipper resonance test with an accelerometer.
TUNING_TOWER with SET_PRESSURE_ADVANCE.

materials.note: Same as the 2.4: enclosed and heat capable. PLA and TPU need the door or lid opened. Abrasive filaments need a hardened nozzle.

pilot_notes: Max print height is 250 mm on the Trident. Reject taller models early.
Every Voron differs. Read real limits and hotend max_temp from Klipper before raising speeds or temperatures.
PRINT_START must accept bed and nozzle temperature arguments; the machine_start_gcode in Orca must match its parameter names.
Klipper G-code flavor. Avoid setting pressure advance twice (macro and slicer).
Heat soak ABS and ASA before printing. Reachable through Moonraker.

common_issues.symptom: First layer varies across the bed
common_issues.cause: Bed not tilted flat or mesh stale.

fix.advice: Run Z_TILT_ADJUST and a fresh bed mesh after heat soak.

common_issues.symptom: Ringing after raising acceleration
common_issues.cause: Acceleration above what the shaper cleans up.

fix.why: Baseline outer wall acceleration for this profile.

fix.advice: Rerun SHAPER_CALIBRATE and cap max_accel at its recommendation.

common_issues.symptom: ABS splits or warps
common_issues.cause: Cold chamber and strong cooling.

fix.why: Less cooling keeps ABS layers fused.

fix.advice: Heat soak the chamber before printing.

docs.name: Cornering (jerk, junction deviation, square corner velocity)

data.name: Cornering (jerk, junction deviation, square corner velocity)
data.purpose: Find the fastest cornering setting that keeps corners sharp. Optional if corners already look good.
run_when: Ringing or overshoot at corners after input shaping
Chasing more speed on a Marlin or Klipper printer

firmware_mapping.marlin_2: Junction deviation if enabled (values 0.0 to 0.3 mm), else classic jerk (usually 1 to 20 mm/s)

orca_test.setup: Acceleration and speed high enough to show ringing (for example 2000 mm/s2 and 100 mm/s). Glossy opaque filament shows it best.

read_result: Measure the height where corners start losing sharpness and read the value at that height. Narrow the range and repeat.

camera_reading.look_for: Corner sharpness per height band from a side view.

writes.advice: Save the value in the printer profile's jerk limits, or in firmware (printer.cfg or M205). mimir proposes the change; the user applies firmware edits.

data.bambu_note: Bambu firmware manages cornering itself. Skip this test on Bambu printers.

data.name: Flow ratio
data.purpose: Extrude exactly as much plastic as the slicer plans. Too low leaves gaps and weak parts; too high gives rough tops and tight holes.
run_when: New filament brand or type
Rough or ridged top surfaces
Holes too small and parts too big together

methods.note: Recommended. Archimedean chords pattern, eleven blocks. Range -0.05 to +0.05, step 0.01 (perfectionist: -0.04 to +0.035, step 0.005). New ratio = old ratio + modifier.
Legacy. Pass 1 nine blocks, pass 2 ten blocks from -9 to 0. New ratio = old ratio * (100 + modifier) / 100.

bambu.method: X series printers measure flow ratio with the lidar during flow calibration. Other Bambu printers use the Orca or Bambu Studio manual test with the Flow calibration box unchecked.

klipper.method: Orca test. Flow ratio lives in the filament profile, not in Klipper.

read_result: Pick the block with the smoothest top, no gaps between the arcs, and little or no ridge where the inner spiral meets the outer arcs.

camera_reading.look_for: Gaps between lines are visible under raking light; smoothness is easier to judge by touch. Ask the user to confirm.

writes.why: Best block from the flow test.

data.name: Input shaping
data.purpose: Cancel frame resonance so the printer can accelerate hard without ringing.
run_when: New printer, printer moved, belts tensioned
Ringing after a mechanical change

bambu.method: Vibration compensation runs in the printer's startup calibration. Rerun it after moving the printer.

prusa.method: Input shaping is set at the factory on MK4S, Core One and XL and can be retuned with the accelerometer.

klipper.method: SHAPER_CALIBRATE with an accelerometer, then SAVE_CONFIG. Use the max acceleration it recommends as the ceiling for slicer accelerations.

marlin.method: Orca's input shaping test (ringing tower per frequency and damping) for Marlin builds with input shaping enabled.

writes.why: Stay under the acceleration the shaper recommends, or ringing returns.

data.name: Max volumetric speed
data.purpose: Find how many mm3 of this filament per second the hotend melts before walls fail. Every speed setting is capped by this number.
run_when: Printing fast or with a high flow hotend
Under extrusion that appears only on fast infill or long straight walls
New hotend or nozzle

orca_test.example: Failure at 19 mm with defaults: 5 + 19 * 0.5 = 14.5 mm3/s.

steps: Print the test at the temperature from the tower. Hotter usually allows more flow.
Measure the height where walls first fail, gap, or change sheen from glossy to matte.
Compute the value with the formula, or read the flow color at that height in Orca preview.
read_result: The test is a best case. Set the profile 10 to 20 percent below the measured value for real parts.
Brand and even color change the result for the same material.

camera_reading.look_for: Height where the surface turns matte or rough. Needs a ruler or a known scale in frame.

writes.why: Measured limit minus 15 percent headroom so strength and quality hold.

data.name: Calibration plan
data.summary: Which tests to run, in what order, and when. mimir's calibrate skill reads this to plan a session: it picks only the tests the situation needs, prints them on one plate where it can, and writes results to a new copy of the filament profile after the user approves.

triggers.when: New spool of a brand and type never printed before
Same brand and type, new color
triggers.note: Colors of the same line usually behave alike but not always.

triggers.when: Printing much faster than before or with a high flow hotend
triggers.note: Adaptive pressure advance helps most on fast CoreXY machines with high flow nozzles.

triggers.when: Printer moved, belts tensioned, or ringing appeared
Parts do not fit or holes are tight

triggers.note: Dry the spool first. Retraction tests on wet filament give wrong answers.

firmware_notes.bambu: Flow dynamics calibration measures pressure advance per spool automatically, and X series printers also measure flow ratio with the lidar. mimir uses those first and only prints manual tests when the user asks or results look wrong. In Orca's manual tests on Bambu printers, leave the Flow calibration box unchecked.
firmware_notes.klipper: Pressure advance and input shaper live in printer.cfg or are set per filament through the slicer; Orca's pressure_advance field emits SET_PRESSURE_ADVANCE.
firmware_notes.prusa: MK4S, Core One and XL ship pressure advance per filament and nozzle in the filament start G-code (M572). Input shaping is tuned at the factory and adjustable from the printer menu.

data.approvals: Printing a test plate needs the queue and start permissions. Writing results needs the profile permission. Results go into a new filament profile copy linked to the spool, never over the stock profile.

data.name: Pressure advance
data.purpose: Match extrusion pressure to speed changes so corners are sharp, seams close, and lines have even width.
run_when: New filament brand or type
New nozzle size, hotend or extruder
Input shaper turned on or off
Big temperature change

methods.note: Slower, does not depend on first layer quality. PA = start + step * height_mm (for example 0 + 0.002 * 8 = 0.016).
Ellis pattern method. Fast and easy to read; the recommended method for most printers.
Quickest, but depends on a good first layer. Turn on bed mesh.

orca_test.variants: Each method has a direct drive and a bowden version. Pick the one matching the extruder.

bambu.method: Flow dynamics calibration measures the K value per spool before a print or from the calibration menu. Use Orca's manual test only if auto results look wrong.

klipper.method: Orca test, or TUNING_TOWER COMMAND=SET_PRESSURE_ADVANCE PARAMETER=ADVANCE START=0 FACTOR=.005 (direct drive) or FACTOR=.020 (bowden) after SET_VELOCITY_LIMIT SQUARE_CORNER_VELOCITY=1 ACCEL=500.

prusa.method: Stock profiles already set M572 per filament and nozzle (0.053 for Prusament PETG on a 0.4 mm MK4S nozzle). Tune only for third party filament.

marlin.method: Linear advance (M900) must be enabled in firmware; many stock builds have it off.

read_result: Pick the value with the sharpest corners and no gap or bulge at the corner or seam.
Typical values run 0.05 to 1.0 on Klipper, with the high end only on bowden printers. Modern direct drive printers often land between 0.02 and 0.06.

adaptive.summary: Adaptive pressure advance fits PA to flow and acceleration. It helps most on fast CoreXY printers with high flow nozzles, and is not needed if you print one layer height, speed and acceleration. Tested on Klipper; untested on Marlin and Bambu.
adaptive.never_exceed: Do not calibrate at accelerations above what the input shaper recommends.

camera_reading.look_for: Pattern method: the row with the sharpest corner and even line width. Works well from a top down snapshot.

writes.why: Use the calibrated value from the filament profile.
Best row or height from the test.

data.name: Retraction
data.purpose: Find the shortest retraction that stops stringing and oozing for this spool.
run_when: Stringing on a dry spool after temperature and pressure advance are tuned
data.before_you_start: Dry the spool and check the nozzle is not leaking. Wet filament strings at any retraction length.

orca_test.read_value: Measure the height of the cleanest section and find the Calib_Retraction_tower comment at that height in the G-code preview.

read_result: The best length is the shortest one that gives the cleanest tower.
PLA and ABS often look clean from the bottom; 0.2 to 0.4 mm is then enough.
Stringing all the way up means wet filament or a leaking nozzle, not retraction.

camera_reading.look_for: Strings between the two towers at each height. Backlight helps.

writes.why: Shortest length that printed clean. Saved as the filament's retraction override.

data.name: Shrinkage
data.purpose: Scale parts to cancel the shrink some materials show as they cool. Matters for ABS, ASA, PC and nylon; rarely for PLA or PETG.
run_when: Large accurate parts in ABS, ASA, PC or nylon
Parts consistently undersized in XY after flow and tolerance are tuned
steps: Print a 100 mm reference bar or cube side in the target material with the real profile.
Let it cool fully, then measure. Shrinkage percent is the measured length over the model length, times 100 (94 percent if 100 mm measures 94 mm).
Enter it as the filament's XY shrinkage. The slicer scales the part up to compensate.
data.caution: In multi material prints, every filament on the part needs the same shrinkage value.

data.name: Temperature tower
data.purpose: Find the nozzle temperature that balances stringing, bridging, overhangs and layer strength for one spool.
run_when: New filament brand or type
Stringing or weak layers on a spool that used to print well

orca_test.defaults: Tower of blocks, one temperature per block, inside the filament's range. Auto scale for nozzle is on: the tower scales to the nozzle and uses half the nozzle diameter as layer height.

bambu.method: Orca or Bambu Studio temperature tower. No automatic equivalent.

klipper.method: Orca temperature tower. The tower changes temperature with M104 per block.

prusa.method: Orca temperature tower with the Prusa printer profile.

steps: Take the range from kb.filament(type).nozzle_temp_c, 5 C steps, hottest at the bottom.
Print with the speeds you plan to use; hotter prints tolerate higher flow.
Inspect every block: stringing between the pillars, bridge sag, overhang curl, surface.
read_result: Lower blocks string less; higher blocks bond better and flow faster. Too hot sags bridges.
If several blocks look good, take the middle. If you plan to print fast, take the upper end of the good range.
For strong parts, lean hot: layer adhesion peaked near 230 C for PLA and 245 C for PETG in CNC Kitchen's tests.

camera_reading.look_for: Strings between pillars and bridge sag per block. Layer strength needs a snap test by hand.

writes.why: Start the first layer at the same temperature unless the profile already runs it 5 to 10 C lower.

data.name: Tolerance and hole fit
data.purpose: Measure how much holes and outlines deviate on this printer, nozzle and spool, then compensate.
run_when: Parts that must mate
Bolts or bearings do not fit
After flow ratio is set

orca_test.menu: Add Handy Model > Orca Tolerance Test
orca_test.model: Base with six hexagonal holes at 0.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4 mm clearance, plus a printed hex tester. A 6 mm Allen key also works.

steps: Print with the real profile for the job.
Find the tightest hole the tester or Allen key enters. Measure holes and tester with calipers.
Set hole compensation from the hole error and contour compensation from the tester error. Reprint and repeat until close.

camera_reading.look_for: Needs calipers or a fit check by hand. mimir asks the user for measurements.

writes.why: Positive values open holes up by the measured error.
Corrects outside dimensions by the measured error.

docs.name: Bambu AMS workflows (flushing, mapping, RFID, backup spools)

data.name: Bambu AMS workflows (flushing, mapping, RFID, backup spools)
data.summary: Multi color prints waste filament in flushes and prime towers. Studio and Orca let you scale flush volumes, send waste into infill, support or a sacrificial object, and change fewer times. Mapping ties slicer filaments to AMS slots by type then color, RFID fills in spool data, and auto refill only swaps to an identical spool.

facts.text: A filament change has four stages: flush (purge) the old color, wipe on the wiper, prime on the prime tower, then print. Flush runs at max volumetric speed.
Flush volume depends on the from and to colors. Dark to light needs more than light to dark. Support materials are also handled to avoid sticking.

The Flushing Volumes dialog has a global multiplier. 1.00 is default, and 0.90 cuts every pair by 10 percent. Bambu says defaults run slightly high and 0.8 or 0.9 is a quick saving, but test that colors stay clean. Too low shows discolored layers.
Editing any single pair in the table means Re-calculate resets every pair to the automatic values.
Flush into objects' infill sends purge into hidden infill. It shows through light or translucent colors and thin walls.

Flush into objects' support is on by default and needs the prime tower enabled. Flush into this object is per object and prints the flush as a transition colored part, useful for functional or painted parts.
Orca stores these as flush_into_infill, flush_into_objects and flush_into_support, plus flush_multiplier and enable_prime_tower.
The prime tower must reach the highest layer with a filament change. Turning a part so its color changes sit low shrinks the tower. Bambu's example went from 14.76 g to 9.05 g.

Waste tracks the number of filament changes. Raising layer height from 0.20 to 0.28 mm cut changes by 27 percent and waste from 83 g to 61 g in Bambu's example. Printing many identical multicolor parts on one plate spreads tower cost.

Filament mapping picks the slot by preset first (same type, ideally the same model such as CF versus HF), then by color (exact, then closest). Studio does not auto map external spools, and auto map is off with multi device management.

AMS reads Bambu spool RFID after preloading, on insertion, on startup or per slot on demand. It also estimates remaining filament from the length fed per spool revolution. Reading is unavailable while filament is loaded to the toolhead.

AMS Auto-Refill (backup spool) switches to another slot with the same brand, type, color and nozzle temperature when a spool runs out. If none matches, the slot shows as empty. Bambu suggests Bambu for Bambu and third party for third party. Pausing and unloading mid print can break the backup.
When the tail of a spool has left the spool, the AMS cannot retract it, so on a color change it flushes the tail before feeding the next slot.

Skipping unload and flush between plates of the same filament saves time and waste by editing machine end and start G-code. It hurts RFID reading and can clog, so restore the G-code for any new material.
Catch purged waste in a large container under the chute, keep the chute uncovered, empty during long prints and do not fit covers or ducts.

steps.text: Sync filaments from the printer in Studio or Orca so the project uses the real AMS slots.
Open the flush volumes dialog. Try a multiplier of 0.9. Print a small test to confirm no color bleed.
Enable flush into support. Enable flush into infill only if walls are dark and thick.
Increase layer height and reorient the part if color changes are few and high.
Check the mapping dialog before sending. Confirm type first, then color.
For long jobs load an identical backup spool in another slot and turn on Auto-Refill.

pilot_actions: When the user asks to reduce waste, propose flush_multiplier 0.9 first, then flush into support, then layer height, then orientation. State the risk of color bleed for each.
Never recommend flush into infill for light or translucent filament or parts with one wall.
Read AMS slots through the printer connection before mapping and flag type mismatches (for example CF versus non CF).
Suggest a backup spool only if an identical brand, type and color spool exists.
Do not suggest the no unload G-code edit unless the next plate uses the same filament, and remind the user to revert it.
Check the AMS model limits in the accessory file: no soft TPU in AMS lite, no PET-CF in AMS.

settings.why: Bambu says default flush volumes run slightly high. Test that colors stay clean.
Multi filament single nozzle prints need a prime tower, and flushing into support needs it too.
Fewer layers means fewer filament changes. Bambu's example moved from 0.20 to 0.28 mm.

settings.advice: Turn on Flush into objects' support in Process, Multi material.
Turn on Flush into objects' infill only for parts with thick dark walls.
Load an identical spool in a second slot and enable AMS Auto-Refill in the AMS settings.

docs.name: Bambu community and third party tools

data.name: Bambu community and third party tools
data.summary: Bambu Handy is the official phone app. OrcaSlicer and other tools reach printers through the optional Bambu network plugin, Bambu Connect or LAN plus Developer Mode. Home Assistant, Bambuddy, Spoolman bridges and farm tools mostly read over MQTT, so they keep working read only on new firmware and need Developer Mode for control.

facts.text: Bambu Handy is the official mobile app. It needs the Bambu cloud, so it stops working in LAN only mode.
OrcaSlicer supports Bambu Lab printers. The Bambu networking plugin is optional, and is built on non free libraries from Bambu.
Bambu says third party slicers such as OrcaSlicer can reach printer functions and filament mapping through Bambu Connect and a network plugin, and shows an Orca integration demo.

ha-bambulab is an open source (MIT) Home Assistant integration installed through HACS. It can connect through a Bambu cloud account or LAN mode with serial number, IP address and access code. Local mode gives sensor data and P1 and A1 chamber images.

ha-bambulab read features work on any firmware. Write actions on locked firmware (X1C 01.08.05.00, P1 01.08.02.00, A1 01.05.00.00 and newer) need LAN mode and Developer Mode, which cuts Bambu cloud access.

For H2D, H2S and X2D camera feeds in ha-bambulab, turn on the LAN Only Liveview option on the printer. Cover image, print weight and plate type on newer firmware need Store Sent Files on External Storage and a USB drive or card.

Bambuddy (maziggy) is a self hosted command center for Bambu printers, from one A1 to a farm. Its README warns that on H2 series and P2S, Studio's Print button writes to internal storage that Bambuddy cannot read, so archive entries lack thumbnail and filament totals. Start prints from Bambuddy or slice in OrcaSlicer, or use Send to external storage.
Spoolman is a self hosted filament inventory service that tracks spool weight.

bambu-spoolman (mrkirby153) syncs Bambu usage to Spoolman by watching prints and estimating usage per layer from the G-code. It needs the printer IP, serial and access code. The author lists LAN only prints, external spools and more than one AMS as untested.
SimplyPrint works with Bambu printers. On the 2025 authorization firmware it reads data, and start, stop, move and heat need Developer Mode plus LAN only.
Printago connects Bambu printers through Bambu's cloud or through a local Fuse bridge in LAN plus Developer Mode. This is vendor marketing material.
Bambu has a free print farm manager that works in cloud free LAN mode for an unlimited number of printers. Only the headline was verified.

steps.text: Ask what the user wants: monitoring, notifications, control, inventory or queueing across several printers.
Monitoring or notifications only: any tool with MQTT read works on any firmware, with the printer on the cloud.
Control from a third party tool: enable LAN only plus Developer Mode on the printer.
Inventory: pair Spoolman with a Bambu bridge, and set AMS slot mapping in the bridge.
Farm queueing: Printago, SimplyPrint or Bambuddy, each with its own connection mode.

pilot_actions: When the user asks for a connected tool, ask whether the printer is on the cloud or in LAN plus Developer Mode before choosing.
Name limits exactly as sourced. For example, Bambuddy cannot read the file from H2 and P2S when Studio Print sends to internal storage.
Recommend the self built path first when the user prefers it: MQTT on port 8883 with the LAN access code, per the community MQTT documentation.
Do not send access codes or account tokens to an outside service. Keep them on the local machine.
Flag vendor claims from farm tools as unverified unless a Bambu source backs them.

settings.advice: Need write control from Home Assistant on new firmware: enable LAN only plus Developer Mode. This drops Handy and cloud monitoring.
For H2 and P2S file based tools: turn on Store Sent Files on External Storage and use Send with External storage, not Print.
Read only dashboards can stay on the cloud with no change.

data.name: Bambu flow dynamics (automatic pressure advance)
data.summary: Bambu calls pressure advance flow dynamics and its strength the K value. The printer stores one K per printer and filament combination, and Studio writes it per AMS slot. Automatic calibration exists on X1, A1 and H2D class printers. P1 is manual only. Rerun it when the filament brand, nozzle or temperature changes, not on a schedule.

facts.text: Flow dynamics compensates for lag in extrusion pressure. During acceleration it pushes slightly more filament, and during deceleration it pulls back slightly, which cleans up corners and reduces blobs and gaps at speed.
The K factor is specific to a printer and filament pair. A higher K means more compensation and a more elastic or laggy extrusion path.
X1 series printers run the calibration by printing lines on the plate and scanning them with Micro Lidar. The K values it finds are smaller than the H2D values.
A1 and H2D printers purge at the purge wiper and read extrusion force with the toolhead eddy current sensor. A1 series needs firmware 01.04.00.00 or newer for auto mode.
H2D, X1 and A1 series support auto calibration. P1 supports manual calibration only.
On H2D the automatic K is set higher than a manual pattern value to prevent corner stacking.
Bambu measured about 10 percent jitter between repeat calibrations, so small differences are noise.

Auto results are unreliable with damp filament, transparent filament on X1 (lidar), a plate that is not sticky, a worn or partly blocked nozzle, very soft material such as TPU, or a third party hotend on A1 and H2D.
All printers with a 0.2 mm hotend often produce inaccurate or failed auto calibration. Bambu recommends the manual pattern for 0.2 mm.
Recalibrate for a new filament brand or model, a worn nozzle, a replaced nozzle, and when max volumetric speed or print temperature changes in the filament settings.
Results are saved in the printer. Each result can be named, edited in Manage Results, and picked per slot in the material dialog on the Device page.
Run flow dynamics before flow rate calibration.

steps.text: Dry the spool and wash the plate. On X1 make sure the calibration lines will stick (glue stick if needed).
In Bambu Studio open Calibration, Flow Dynamics, then Auto-Calibration. Pick the printer, nozzle, plate type and the filament (or the AMS slot).
Press Calibrate and wait for the lines (X1) or the purge (A1, H2D).
Read the recommended K value, press Finish to store it, then check it in Manage Results.
For P1, 0.2 mm nozzles or filaments the lidar cannot read, use the manual pattern mode and pick the best line.
Print a test with sharp corners. Compare against the previous K if quality looks worse.

pilot_actions: Ask whether the filament brand, nozzle or temperature changed since the last calibration. If yes, propose a rerun before any other tuning.
Before proposing auto calibration, check the printer id: P1S and P1P are manual only. Other Bambu printers are auto capable.
Refuse auto calibration for TPU, transparent, sparkle, marble, metal or silk filament on X1 series and point to the manual pattern.
Warn that K is stored in the printer, not in the SlicerX project, and that a K from a lidar printer does not transfer to an eddy current printer.
If corners look bulged or gappy after a max volumetric speed change, recommend recalibrating instead of hand editing K.

settings.advice: Recalibrate flow dynamics for each nozzle diameter and each filament brand. Do not copy a K value from a different printer type.
Keep a filament dry while calibrating. A K measured on wet filament is wrong for dry filament.
After changing filament_max_volumetric_speed or the nozzle temperature in a filament preset, rerun flow dynamics. Bambu lists both as recalibration triggers.

data.name: Bambu flow rate calibration
data.summary: Flow ratio scales extrusion volume per filament. Only X1 series printers can calibrate it automatically, with Micro Lidar. Every other Bambu printer uses the manual coarse and fine block tests. Run flow dynamics first, and tune flow only when top surfaces still show over or under extrusion.

facts.text: Auto flow rate calibration uses Micro Lidar to measure printed extrusion lines. Only X1 series printers support it.
Lidar does not work well on sparkle, marble, metal or silk PLA, on transparent or semi transparent filament, or on TPU (calibration lines cannot be printed).
Do flow dynamics calibration before flow rate calibration.
Pick the filament preset that matches the real spool. A wrong max volumetric speed in the preset can cause nozzle clogging during the test.
Manual coarse calibration prints blocks from 80 to 120 percent of the preset flow in 5 percent steps. Fine calibration prints blocks around a custom flow ratio.

In Studio's developer mode tests, pass 1 makes nine blocks and pass 2 makes ten blocks with modifiers from minus 9 to 0. New flow equals old flow times (100 plus modifier) divided by 100. Example: 0.98 with a plus 5 block becomes 1.029.
For a quick manual check on X1, slice a simple model at 0.2 mm layers, 2 walls, 4 top layers, 3 bottom layers and 15 percent infill. Change flow in steps of 0.03 to 0.05.
Over extrusion shows as uneven top layer lines. Under extrusion shows as gaps between top layer lines.
Bambu filament presets are pre tuned. Third party, wood and foaming filament (for example LW-PLA) benefit most from calibration.

steps.text: Confirm the filament is dry, the nozzle is clean and flow dynamics is done.
X1 series with normal opaque filament: Studio, Calibration, Flow Rate, Auto-Calibration. Read the recommended value and save it to the filament preset.
Other printers or lidar unfriendly filament: run the coarse test, pick the smoothest block, then run the fine test around that value.
Apply the formula and save the new flow ratio to the filament preset.
Print a top surface test to confirm.

pilot_actions: Check printer id first. Offer auto calibration only on bambu_x1c and bambu_x1e.
Block the auto test for transparent, sparkle, marble, metal, silk and TPU spools.
When the user reports rough top surfaces after flow dynamics is done, propose a flow change of 0.03 to 0.05 rather than a large jump.
Read the flow ratio and max volumetric speed of the active filament preset before starting a calibration plan.

settings.why: Uneven or bumpy top lines mean over extrusion. Lower flow in steps of 0.03 to 0.05.
Gaps between top surface lines mean under extrusion. Raise flow in steps of 0.03 to 0.05.

settings.advice: Run flow dynamics first, then flow rate.

docs.name: Bambu LAN only mode, Developer Mode and third party access

data.name: Bambu LAN only mode, Developer Mode and third party access
data.summary: LAN only mode runs a printer without the Bambu cloud. Developer Mode, turned on inside LAN only mode, restores open control over MQTT and FTP for third party software. Since the January 2025 authorization firmware, printers without Developer Mode give third party tools read access but block commands unless the tool goes through Bambu Connect. Developer Mode is optional in SlicerX: without it, status shows and prints go through Bambu Connect.

facts.text: LAN only mode works without internet. Remote start from outside the local network, the Bambu Handy app and print history stop working.

Enable it on the printer screen (Settings, LAN Only on X, H2, P2S and A series, or WLAN then LAN Only Mode on P1). The printer shows an access code. Bambu Studio finds it in the Device list with a lock icon, then asks for the code.
X series printers need a Micro SD card in the printer to start a new print from Studio in LAN only mode.
If the printer and computer are on different VLANs, bind with printer IP plus access code. Bambu Studio does not store the IP, so enter both again after every restart.
AI spaghetti detection on X series runs locally. In LAN mode it uses the model in the latest installed firmware.

Developer Mode is a second switch under LAN only mode. It needs the printer screen and a risk acknowledgment. It does not require authorization, keeps the pre 2025 behavior, and disables cloud connection.

Bambu announced an authorization control system on 2025-01-16. A beta firmware (01.08.03.00) followed on 2025-01-17. It restricts third party slicers and tools that start prints, change parameters or view video.

ha-bambulab documents the cutover firmwares: X1C 01.08.05.00, P1 01.08.02.00, A1 01.05.00.00. Read access still works on any firmware. Write actions (temperatures, axis moves) stop working on cloud connected printers unless LAN and Developer Mode are on. Earlier hybrid mode restrictions began around P1 01.07.00.00.

Bambu's third party integration page lists what the authorization does not affect: MQTT status pushes for tools like Home Assistant, starting prints from an SD card, SD card firmware updates and general operations outside the restricted commands. It applies in both cloud mode and normal LAN mode.
SimplyPrint reports the same split: read data continues, while start, stop, move and heat need Developer Mode plus LAN only on new firmware.

Bambu Connect is a beta desktop tool for Windows and macOS (Linux in development) that logs in to the cloud, discovers LAN printers, imports 3MF or G-code and sends prints. Live view is not supported. Third party software can hand a file to it with bambu-connect://import-file and the parameters path, name and version 1.0.0.
Bambu also offers a Bambu Local Server SDK by application for commercial integrations, deployable as a Docker container. It covers printer discovery, status, control and print tasks.
Local MQTT runs on the printer at port 8883 with TLS. Username is bblp. The password is the LAN access code. Messages are JSON. Topics are device/{serial}/report and device/{serial}/request.
File upload to the printer uses FTPS on port 990 with implicit TLS, user bblp and the same access code.
The MQTT and FTP documentation is community reverse engineering, not an official Bambu specification.
The OrcaSlicer Bambu networking plugin is optional and based on non free libraries from Bambu.

steps.text: Decide the need. Slicing only: no network mode needed, export a file. Status in SlicerX: the access code is enough, and SlicerX prints through Bambu Connect. Direct prints and controls from SlicerX or another tool: LAN only plus Developer Mode (optional). Cloud features (Handy, remote start): stay on the cloud and send files through Studio or Bambu Connect.
On the printer open Settings, LAN Only and note the IP and access code. Turn on LAN only mode if the printer cannot be reached. Turn on Developer Mode only if direct third party control is wanted.
For X series, insert a Micro SD card.
Add the printer in the tool by IP address, serial number and access code.
Test read (status) first, then a harmless write such as a light toggle.

pilot_actions: State which of the printer's connection types is available: bambu_lan_mqtt reads status with the access code, and needs Developer Mode (under LAN only mode) for any write. bambu_connect can send files while the printer stays on the cloud. bambu_cloud goes through the Bambu account and the optional Studio network plugin. SlicerX never signs in to a Bambu account.

Developer Mode is optional in SlicerX. Without it the printer connects as monitor only (status, temperatures, progress, AMS), and Print opens the sliced .gcode.3mf in Bambu Connect, where the user presses Print. On Linux, where Bambu Connect does not exist yet, SlicerX saves the file instead. Never tell a user Developer Mode is required to connect.

When a control command is refused on a cloud connected printer with recent firmware, explain the authorization change and offer the two paths: Developer Mode with LAN for direct control, or Bambu Connect for printing.
Never request or store the access code in a project file. Ask the user to enter it in the connection dialog.
On X series in LAN mode, check that a Micro SD card is present before sending a print.
Warn that turning on Developer Mode disconnects the printer from the Bambu cloud, so Handy and remote monitoring stop.
Do not advise downgrading firmware. State the tradeoff and let the user decide.

settings.advice: Read only monitoring works on any firmware and connection type.
Commands (start, stop, heat, move) need Developer Mode plus LAN only on firmware from the 2025 authorization update onward. Without it, print through Bambu Connect.
Use the printer IP plus access code binding on segmented networks and re-enter it after each Studio restart.

data.name: Swapping Bambu nozzles and hotends
data.summary: Bambu nozzles come as complete hotends. A series swaps are toolless. X1, P1 and H2 series need the front cover off and the printer powered down. In Studio the nozzle field is display only, so a swap is a physical change followed by a sync on the printer and a fresh flow dynamics run.

facts.text: X1 and P1 series hotends come with hardened steel or stainless steel nozzles in 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 mm. The complete hotend assembly is sold in separate X1 (X1 and X1C only, not X1E) and P1 versions.
The A1 hotend is toolless and swaps in a few minutes. A1 offers 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 mm hotends plus a high flow hotend.
H2D ships with a 0.4 mm nozzle and takes 0.2, 0.6 and 0.8 mm nozzles plus a high flow hotend. Swap steps include lowering the bed, removing the top glass and the toolhead front cover.
Bambu Studio treats the nozzle information as display only. Studio 02.01.01.52 disabled editing for X1 and P1, and the H2 page says the same, because nozzle replacement must happen on the printer.
After swapping to a different specification, update the nozzle info on the printer screen before printing.
Always power off and let the hotend cool before maintenance to avoid shorting exposed toolhead wires.
Fiber filled filament (PLA-CF, PETG-CF, PA-CF and GF grades, PPS, PPA) needs a hardened steel nozzle. Bambu marks PLA-CF and PETG-CF as not recommended on 0.4 mm high flow nozzles.
0.2 mm nozzles do not accept many wood, marble, PLA-CF, PETG-CF and PA-CF materials. PLA Wood, PLA Marble and PVA are not compatible with 0.2 mm.
TPU 85A is not compatible with 0.4 mm high flow nozzles and not recommended on 0.6 and 0.8 mm high flow. TPU 90A is not recommended on high flow nozzles.
Flush volume depends on nozzle size. A 0.2 mm nozzle extrudes slowly, so each filament change takes much longer.

Recalibrate flow dynamics after replacing a nozzle because of manufacturing tolerances. Bambu says all printers with a 0.2 mm hotend often give inaccurate auto results, so use the manual pattern there.
H2C swaps hotends with an induction hotend rack. Nozzle offset calibration runs for the toolhead hotend and each rack hotend, so it takes longer with more hotends.
X2D has a main and an auxiliary hotend. Bambu recommends the main hotend for PLA Silk, PETG-CF, ASA-CF, PA6-CF and TPU for AMS.

steps.text: Power off. Let the hotend cool to room temperature. Cut or unload the filament.
Open the covers the printer needs: front cover on A1, top glass and toolhead front cover on H2 series.
A1 series: slide the buckle to unlock and lift out the hotend by its heatsink. Insert the new one at a slight tilt, press it in until the buckle locks.
X1, P1, H2: follow the printer's replace hotend page. Handle the silicone sock and wiring with power off.
Power on. Enter the new nozzle diameter and type on the printer screen.
In Studio pick the matching printer variant (for example 0.6 mm nozzle) so layer height, line width and flow limits match.
Run flow dynamics. Consider flow rate calibration for a very different nozzle.

pilot_actions: Match the slicer printer preset variant to the nozzle in use. Do not edit the nozzle diameter as a stand alone setting.
Block CF, GF and other abrasive filament unless the user confirms a hardened steel nozzle.
After a nozzle change, propose flow dynamics calibration.
When the user moves to a high flow nozzle, use the high flow variant of the filament preset and warn about TPU limits.
For 0.2 mm nozzles, recommend the manual flow dynamics pattern and warn that multi color prints flush slowly.

settings.advice: Select the printer preset variant that matches the physical nozzle. Studio no longer lets you edit nozzle info by hand.
Confirm the nozzle material before abrasive filament. Stainless nozzles wear out on fiber filled filament.

settings.why: With a 0.2 mm nozzle keep layers under 75 percent of the nozzle diameter.

docs.name: Bambu build plates, glue and top glass removal

data.name: Bambu build plates, glue and top glass removal
data.summary: Pick the plate by filament, set the bed temperature for that plate, and add glue where Bambu says so. On enclosed X1C, X1E and P1S the top glass lid comes off for PLA, TPU and PVA when the bed is above 45 C, and for PETG when it is above 70 C.

facts.text: Bambu's plate types are Textured PEI, Smooth PEI (also sold as High Temperature Plate), Dual-Texture PEI, Engineering Plate and Cool Plate SuperTack. The older Cool Plate is still listed in the filament guide. Orca also offers a Textured Cool Plate option that Bambu's wiki does not document by that name.
Textured PEI is the standard plate. It grips most filaments without glue and prints release once the bed cools to 35 C or lower. PC, PA, ABS and ASA may need a glue stick layer on it.
Smooth PEI gives a flat matte bottom. Only PLA prints on it without glue. Every other filament needs glue or the PEI sheet can tear.
The Engineering Plate wants a thin glue layer before any filament. Glue stick or liquid glue depends on the material. Use alcohol at the part edge if a print will not release.
Cool Plate SuperTack is for PLA and PETG only. It holds PLA at a 40 C bed. Second generation PETG needs 55 to 60 C, but shared X and P series parameters may still use about 65 C.
Do not print TPU on SuperTack. Bambu PLA Silk sticks too hard and can damage parts. Support for PLA/PETG can damage the plate, so print a raft first. Clean with water and detergent, never acetone.
SuperTack is soft and scratches. Wet the contact area with alcohol before scraping. Warm the plate to about 50 C on the bed to release stubborn prints.

Bed temperature ranges by plate (Bambu, filament guide): PLA 35 to 45 C on Cool Plate and 45 to 65 C on Engineering, Smooth or Textured PEI. PETG and PETG-CF 60 to 80 C on Engineering, Smooth and Textured, not recommended on the Cool Plate. ABS and ASA 90 to 100 C. PC and PA 100 to 120 C. TPU 30 to 35 C on Engineering and 35 to 45 C on Smooth or Textured.
PLA on the Engineering Plate needs glue. The Cool Plate is not recommended for TPU, PETG, ABS, ASA, PC and PA.

Glue stick and liquid glue ranges: PLA 35 to 65 C, PETG 60 to 80 C, ABS and ASA 90 to 100 C, TPU 30 to 45 C, PET-CF/GF 80 to 100 C (glue stick only), PC 100 to 120 C (glue stick), PA 90 to 110 C (glue stick).

Top glass cover removal: recommended for PLA, PLA-CF, PVA and TPU when the bed is above 45 C, and for PETG and PETG-CF when the bed is above 70 C. Do not remove it for ABS, ASA, PC, PA or their fiber grades.

256 x 256 mm Textured PEI, Smooth PEI and SuperTack come in two generations that differ by QR code. P2S and X2D read only second generation plates. X1 series cannot identify second generation plates. A and P series accept both.
Plate sizes: 350 x 320 mm for H2D and H2S, 330 x 320 mm for H2C and A2L, 256 x 256 mm for X2D, P2S, P1, X1 and A1, 180 x 180 mm for A1 mini.

steps.text: Read the filament type and the printer. Check the printer is enclosed or open (see the printer file).
Pick the plate: Textured PEI for most PLA, PETG, TPU. SuperTack for PLA and PETG when the user wants no glue and a low bed temperature. Engineering or Smooth PEI with glue for ABS, ASA, PC and PA.
Set the matching bed temperature key for that plate in the filament preset and set the plate type in the process.
Apply glue where the tables ask for it. Keep glue thin and even.
On X1C, X1E and P1S, remove the top glass for PLA, PLA-CF, PVA and TPU above a 45 C bed, and for PETG above 70 C.
Let the bed cool to 35 C or lower before flexing the plate. Use alcohol or a warm 50 C bed for SuperTack.

pilot_actions: Suggest the plate from the filament first. Refuse PETG, ABS, ASA, PC and PA on the Cool Plate and TPU or PLA Silk on SuperTack.
Set curr_bed_type to match the plate the user says is installed. Then set the matching temperature key only.
When a plate warning about recognition appears on X1 or P2S, tell the user to pick Resolved or turn off build plate detection instead of changing settings.
On X1C, X1E and P1S remind the user to take off the top glass when the bed is above 45 C for PLA and above 70 C for PETG.
Warn that PETG on smooth PEI or the High Temperature Plate needs glue as a release layer.

settings.why: Textured PEI is Bambu's default plate and grips most filaments without glue.
Bambu lists 35 to 45 C for PLA on the Cool Plate.
PLA holds on SuperTack at a low bed temperature. Bambu quotes 40 C.
Bambu lists 45 to 65 C for PLA on textured PEI.

settings.advice: PETG on SuperTack: 55 to 60 C on second generation plates. Older shared profiles use about 65 C.
Use glue stick on the Engineering Plate and on smooth PEI for anything except PLA.
Remove the top glass lid on X1C, X1E and P1S for PLA, PLA-CF, PVA and TPU when the bed is above 45 C, and for PETG when it is above 70 C.

data.name: Bambu time-lapse (smooth versus traditional)
data.summary: Traditional mode shoots right after each layer and can leave an ooze mark. Smooth mode parks the toolhead at the purge chute for every shot, needs a prime tower, and lengthens the print. A series printers also move the bed to a fixed spot for every shot in both modes.

facts.text: Time-lapse takes a snapshot after each printed layer with the chamber camera and compiles the video at the end.
Traditional mode shoots directly after each layer. The nozzle pause can let melted filament leak onto the part.

Smooth mode moves the toolhead to the purge chute for each shot. Because the nozzle pauses there and may leak, a prime tower is required to wipe the nozzle. If none exists on the plate, one is generated.
Smooth mode adds extra travel and purging, so total print time grows.
Orca stores the mode as timelapse_type: 0 is Traditional and 1 is Smooth. Older project files used 2 for Traditional and it is remapped to 0.

On A series printers the bed moves in Y while printing, so the printer parks the bed and the nozzle at fixed positions before every shot, in both modes. Traditional mode tries to hide ooze in infill. If a layer has no infill the defect shows, and Bambu suggests Smooth mode.

On dual nozzle printers the two nozzles differ in height by about 5 mm. To keep the bed steady in the video the printer shoots with a main nozzle per layer and moves to the purge chute to take the picture if another nozzle is active.

Time-lapse needs storage in the printer (Micro SD or USB). Studio downloads the video from the Device, Storage page. Enable it in Studio under Others, Special Mode, Timelapse, or on the printer screen at print start.
An external MakerWorld camera kit plugs into the AMS port. In Smooth mode the firmware waits 500 ms after the photo command. Use the M9711 D parameter for a longer delay in milliseconds.

steps.text: Choose the mode. Smooth for parts with visible top and side surfaces or no infill on some layers. Traditional to save time when a small ooze mark is fine.
For Smooth, keep the prime tower on. Bambu enables it by default.
Confirm storage is inserted.
Turn Timelapse on at send time in Studio, Handy or on the printer screen.
After the print, download from Device, Storage in Studio or the timelapse folder on the card.

pilot_actions: If the user picks Smooth, set enable_prime_tower to true and warn about the longer print time.
Recommend Smooth on A series printers when a layer has no infill.
Do not enable time-lapse for a spiral vase print without warning that every shot pauses the nozzle.
For multi color plans that already use a prime tower, note that Smooth reuses it.

settings.why: Smooth mode parks the toolhead at the chute for each shot so ooze lands on the prime tower, not the part.
Smooth time-lapse needs a prime tower to wipe the nozzle after each shot.
Traditional mode is faster and shoots right after the layer. Expect a small ooze mark.

docs.name: Creality K1 and K2 series workflow

data.name: Creality K1 and K2 series workflow
data.summary: K1, K1C, K1 Max and K2 Plus run Creality's own Klipper build with Moonraker and Fluidd. Root access is available through a printer setting, and community tooling adds features. The CFS multi color system has Orca profiles, but Creality Print is the vendor path for CFS color mapping. Read this before changing start G-code or promising multi color on Orca.

facts.text: K1, K1C and K1 Max use vendor Klipper with Moonraker and Fluidd; the K2 series does too. Guides describe root access as available from the printer's settings rather than needing an exploit.
On the K2 Plus, tap the settings gear and open Root account information to enable SSH. Default credentials are published in community guides and should be changed.
The Creality Helper Script (community) installs Moonraker add ons, macros and camera support on rooted K1 series and other Creality printers. It is unofficial.

K1C is 220 x 220 x 250 mm with a 300 C hotend and hardened steel tip. K1 Max is 300 x 300 x 300 mm with a 300 C hotend. K2 Plus is 350 x 350 x 350 mm with 350 C and an actively heated chamber to 60 C.
Orca ships CFS-C variants of K1, K1C, K1 SE and K1 Max, and K2 Plus profiles. CFS on K2 Plus is a combo product.
Community users report file transfer over the OctoPrint or Klipper protocol from Orca is faster than Creality Print for the K2 Plus, and Creality Print is the recommended slicer.
Creality's Klipper changes are the subject of a forum thread about source release, so vendor Klipper can diverge from upstream commands.
Orca's process defaults for these machines run 10000 to 12000 mm/s2 default acceleration and 200 mm/s outer walls; K1C uses 3000 for walls while K1 Max and K2 Plus use 5000.

steps.text: Identify the exact model: K1, K1C, K1 Max, K1 SE, K2, K2 Plus or K2 Pro. Limits and profiles differ.
Decide slicer path. For CFS color mapping and vendor features use Creality Print. For general slicing, Orca profiles work and send via Moonraker.
If the user wants Moonraker or SSH, walk through the printer's root or SSH switch and warn about warranty and firmware update side effects.
Keep the printer's stock PRINT_START. Only edit machine_start_gcode after reading it through Moonraker or SSH.
For PLA on any of these, open the lid or turn the chamber off. Set chamber temperature only on the K2 Plus and only for ABS, ASA, PC or PA.

pilot_actions: Ask which model and whether CFS is fitted before choosing a profile.
Recommend Creality Print for CFS color mapping and Orca for everything else, with the caveat stated.
Warn that rooting is a user choice; do not do it without an explicit request.
Use chamber_temperature only on K2 Plus; K1 series has no chamber control.
Keep vendor macros; verify a Klipper command exists before calling it.

settings.why: K2 Plus chamber heater tops out at 60 C. Use it only for ABS, ASA, PC and PA.
Lower outer wall acceleration on the K1C profile baseline for cleaner walls.

settings.advice: Open the lid for PLA and TPU on K1 series printers.

data.name: Input shaper on Klipper
data.summary: Klipper measures resonance with an accelerometer, recommends a shaper type and frequency per axis, and prints a maximum acceleration for each shaper. The slicer's acceleration settings must stay under that maximum or ringing comes back. Creality and Elegoo firmware run their own calibration; Voron and SV08 users run Klipper's directly.

facts.text: Klipper supports the ADXL345 (SPI), MPU-9250 family and ICM20948 (I2C), and LIS2DW and LIS3DH (SPI or I2C) accelerometers for resonance testing.
TEST_RESONANCES records raw vibration data for an axis. SHAPER_CALIBRATE runs the test and computes the best shaper and frequency, printing a suggested max_accel for each shaper type.

Shapers from least to most smoothing: ZV, MZV, ZVD and EI (about equal), 2HUMP_EI, 3HUMP_EI. More smoothing tolerates a wider frequency error but rounds small features and lowers the usable acceleration. Klipper default type is mzv.
Klipper advises choosing the lower of the acceleration limits from ringing and from smoothing when setting max_accel. At low frequencies (around 25 Hz) even MZV can smooth too much.
The suggested max_accel is printed per shaper, for example 3500 mm/s2, and you may choose a shaper other than the recommended one if you prefer another smoothing trade off.
max_smoothing can be stored in printer.cfg to limit how much smoothing a shaper may add on later recalibrations.
Klipper notes auto calibration creates intense vibration on each axis and recommends against frequent recalibration because of wear.
Disable dynamic acceleration control in the slicer during resonance testing. Damping ratio defaults to 0.1 and needs no tuning.
Orca's stock profiles for these printers use accelerations of 3000 to 12000 mm/s2 for walls and up to 20000 for travel, so they can exceed a small shaper's recommended max.

steps.text: Mount an accelerometer and confirm it reports with ACCELEROMETER_QUERY.
Warm up the bed and hotend, home, then run SHAPER_CALIBRATE and SAVE_CONFIG.
Read the recommended type and frequency per axis and the suggested max_accel for each shaper.
Set the slicer's default, wall, and travel accelerations at or below the lower of the max_accel values for the chosen shaper.
Print a ringing test at that acceleration. If ringing remains, lower acceleration rather than selecting a heavier shaper.

pilot_actions: Read the current input_shaper and max_accel values from Klipper through Moonraker before advising accelerations.
Cap default_acceleration, outer_wall_acceleration, inner_wall_acceleration and travel_acceleration to the printer's tested limit when the user reports ringing.
Do not recommend rerunning SHAPER_CALIBRATE more than needed; suggest it after belt, toolhead or frame changes.
On Creality and Elegoo stock firmware, tell the user the calibration menu is vendor controlled and Klipper commands may not be exposed.
Never copy shaper frequencies between printers.

settings.why: Orca's Voron baseline uses 5000; use the printer's tested max_accel if it is lower.
Outer walls show ringing first; 3000 is the Voron baseline.

settings.advice: Pick the accelerometer and mounting location per Klipper's docs; a loose mount ruins the measurement.

docs.name: Klipper start and end macros with SlicerX

data.name: Klipper start and end macros with SlicerX
data.summary: Klipper machines do their heating, leveling, purging and meshing in PRINT_START and PRINT_END macros. The slicer should pass temperatures in as parameters, label objects so exclude_object works, and let the macro run an adaptive bed mesh. Heat soak belongs in the macro for ABS and ASA on enclosed machines.

facts.text: BED_MESH_CALIBRATE accepts ADAPTIVE=1 to probe only the area covered by the objects defined in the G-code, and ADAPTIVE_MARGIN to pad it. The [bed_mesh] adaptive_margin option sets a default.
Enabling [exclude_object] in printer.cfg lets a print skip individual objects. The slicer must emit EXCLUDE_OBJECT_DEFINE lines and EXCLUDE_OBJECT_START markers around each object.

Firmware retraction uses G10 and G11 with values from [firmware_retraction] (retract_length default 0, retract_speed 20, unretract_extra_length 0, unretract_speed 10). SET_RETRACTION changes them at runtime.
SET_HEATER_TEMPERATURE HEATER=<name> TARGET=<temp> sets a heater target without waiting, and TEMPERATURE_WAIT SENSOR=<name> MINIMUM=<temp> waits. A macro combines them to heat the bed first and wait.

Orca lets machine start G-code use placeholders such as [nozzle_temperature_initial_layer] and [bed_temperature_initial_layer_single], and has options to label objects and to exclude objects for Klipper.
Pressure advance can be set by the slicer or by the macro; do not do both.
Creality and Elegoo stock firmware keep their own start G-code. Changing machine_start_gcode there can break homing or leveling routines.

steps.text: In Orca machine start G-code, call the macro with parameters: PRINT_START BED=[bed_temperature_initial_layer_single] EXTRUDER=[nozzle_temperature_initial_layer] CHAMBER=[chamber_temperature]. Match the parameter names the user's macro reads.
In the macro, read params.BED, params.EXTRUDER and params.CHAMBER with defaults. Heat the bed, home, level (QGL or Z tilt on Voron), run BED_MESH_CALIBRATE ADAPTIVE=1, then heat the nozzle and prime.
Enable object labels in Orca (label objects, Klipper) and add [exclude_object] to printer.cfg.

Add heat soak for ABS and ASA on enclosed machines: heat the bed early, close the door, and wait in the macro until the chamber sensor reads the target or a set soak time ends. Community practice is 10 to 20 minutes.
If using firmware retraction, enable it in the slicer, add [firmware_retraction] to printer.cfg, and stop the slicer from emitting its own retract lengths.
PRINT_END should retract a little, park, turn off heaters and fans, and leave the bed warm only if the user wants it.

pilot_actions: Read printer.cfg and the macro source through Moonraker before editing machine_start_gcode, and match parameter names.
Never invent a PRINT_START. If the macro is missing, tell the user and offer a template for review.
For ABS or ASA on enclosed Klipper machines, recommend heat soak and add chamber temperature only if the printer has an actual chamber control.
Turn on object labeling and exclusion only if [exclude_object] is enabled.
When firmware retraction is on, warn that slicer retraction length and z hop values are ignored or conflict.

settings.why: Single material prints do not need a tower on Klipper machines.

settings.advice: Enable Orca's label objects and exclude object options for Klipper. They are stored under gcode_label_objects and exclude_object, which the settings catalog does not list yet.
Enable Orca's firmware retraction (use_firmware_retraction) only when [firmware_retraction] is configured.
Put machine_start_gcode and machine_end_gcode edits under user review; they change hardware behavior.

data.name: Pressure advance on Klipper
data.summary: Pressure advance adds extra filament on speed up and removes it on slow down to counter nozzle pressure. It sharpens corners and reduces bulging. Tune it per filament and per nozzle with Klipper's tuning tower. Retraction and pressure advance work together; keep retraction small once PA is set.

facts.text: Klipper's command is SET_PRESSURE_ADVANCE [EXTRUDER=<name>] [ADVANCE=<value>] [SMOOTH_TIME=<seconds>]. In printer.cfg the extruder options are pressure_advance (default 0, which disables it) and pressure_advance_smooth_time (default 0.040 s).
Typical pressure advance values are 0.050 to 1.000, with the high end normally only on bowden extruders.
Tuning tower for direct drive: TUNING_TOWER COMMAND=SET_PRESSURE_ADVANCE PARAMETER=ADVANCE START=0 FACTOR=.005. For bowden: the same with FACTOR=.020.
Compute the value as pressure_advance = start + measured_height * factor. Example from the docs: 0 + 12.90 * .020 = .258 for a bowden tower.
Klipper suggests a small slicer retraction (for example 0.75 mm), wipe on retract enabled and z lift on retract disabled during and after tuning.
Pressure advance is filament and nozzle specific. Prusa ships M572 S0.053 for PETG on MK4S, showing how much values differ from a Klipper default.
Orca can emit its own pressure advance value from the filament profile. If the machine's PRINT_START macro also sets it, the later command wins and the two can conflict.

steps.text: Set the printer to a fast but normal speed, 0.2 mm layers, and no input shaper changes during the test.
Reset PA: SET_PRESSURE_ADVANCE ADVANCE=0. Keep SMOOTH_TIME at the default 0.040 unless a specific problem points at it.
Run TUNING_TOWER with the direct drive or bowden command above and print the tower.
Measure the height where corners look best. Compute start + height * factor.
Store the value in the filament profile in the slicer, not printer.cfg, so each material keeps its own. Re-test on a corner heavy part.
Lower retraction to about 0.75 mm and confirm stringing did not worsen.

pilot_actions: Ask whether the printer is direct drive or bowden before choosing a tower factor. All printers in this list are direct drive.
Enable pressure advance in the filament profile and write the measured value, within 0 to 1.5.
Check that start G-code or PRINT_START does not also set pressure advance.
Reduce retraction length on direct drive once PA is on; do not raise it as the first stringing fix.
Adaptive pressure advance is an Orca feature that varies PA with flow; only suggest it after a single tuned PA value works.

settings.why: Turns on pressure advance so the tuned value is written to G-code.
Klipper suggests a small retract once pressure advance is set.
Wipe on retract helps stringing while retraction is small.
Klipper advises disabling z lift on retract during tuning.

data.name: Moonraker API for SlicerX
data.summary: Moonraker is the web API in front of Klipper. It exposes file upload, a job queue, printer object status, G-code execution and webcams over HTTP and websocket. SlicerX can upload and start prints, read status, manage the queue and read webcam URLs. It is present on Voron and Sovol builds and on Creality and Elegoo stock Klipper firmware, but not on the Elegoo Centauri Carbon's stock firmware.

facts.text: Moonraker supports HTTP, websocket (/websocket), a unix socket, MQTT and JSON-RPC over HTTP. Successful HTTP responses return {"result": ...}.

Upload is POST /server/files/upload with form fields file (required), root (default gcodes), path, checksum (SHA256) and print (default false). Roots are gcodes, config, logs, config_examples and docs; only gcodes and config are writable.

Other file endpoints: GET /server/files/list?root=, GET /server/files/directory?path=, GET /server/files/metadata?filename=, POST /server/files/metascan, GET /server/files/thumbnails, DELETE /server/files/{root}/{filename}.
Job queue: GET /server/job_queue/status, POST /server/job_queue/job with filenames and reset, DELETE the same to remove by job_ids or all, POST /server/job_queue/pause, /start and /jump.
Starting the queue loads the next job if Klipper is ready; otherwise it waits and loads after the current job. Pausing prevents the next job from loading.

Webcams: GET /server/webcams/list, GET and POST /server/webcams/item, POST /server/webcams/test. Entries include stream_url, snapshot_url, target_fps, rotation and flip flags. Cameras defined in moonraker.conf are read only through the API.
Printer state is available through the printer objects query, which returns toolhead position, print statistics and webhooks state. G-code can be sent through the printer G-code script endpoint.
Creality K1 series and K2 series run Klipper with Moonraker and Fluidd. Elegoo Neptune 4 series does too. Whether a given Creality printer exposes SSH depends on its Root account switch and firmware.

steps.text: Find the Moonraker URL (usually the same host as Fluidd or Mainsail on port 7125, or the vendor's port) and test GET /server/info.
Add the printer in SlicerX as a Moonraker host. Use an API key or a trusted client entry in moonraker.conf if the network is not trusted.
Upload the sliced G-code with POST /server/files/upload. Set print only after the user confirms the bed is clear.
Poll printer objects for progress and temperatures. Use the job queue for batches.

pilot_actions: Upload G-code and start a print after user confirmation.
Read status: state, progress, temperatures, current file and layer where exposed.
Read Klipper config values (max accel, shaper, hotend max temp) to ground advice.
Enqueue several plates and pause or start the queue on request.
Fetch a webcam snapshot_url to help diagnose a failing print.
Write to the config root only with explicit user approval; config edits can stop a printer from starting.
Do not assume Moonraker exists on a printer with vendor closed firmware such as the stock Elegoo Centauri Carbon.

settings.advice: Use trusted_clients or an API key in moonraker.conf; do not expose Moonraker to the public internet.

docs.name: Input shaper and phase stepping on Prusa printers

data.name: Input shaper and phase stepping on Prusa printers
data.summary: Prusa firmware ships an input shaper that is factory calibrated, so most users never touch it. An optional accelerometer set recalibrates it after hardware changes. Phase stepping is a separate motor drive feature that cuts noise and fine surface ripples. Both matter mainly when mimir is asked to raise acceleration or diagnose ghosting.

facts.text: Input shaper reduces ghosting by filtering the motion commands so that resonance vibrations cancel. It is available on the CORE One family, MK4/S, MK3.9/S, MK3.5/S, XL and MINI/+ (firmware 5.0.0 or newer on MK4, 5.1.0 or newer on the others).
Prusa exposes it as the M593 G-code with F (frequency, default 0 Hz meaning off), D (damping ratio, default 0.1), T (type, ZV through 3HUMP_EI) and R (vibration reduction, default 20).
