The CORE One L and XL have an integrated accelerometer and are pre-calibrated. The MK4S and base CORE One use an optional accelerometer set that is only needed after hardware changes and is meant for experienced users.
Prusa says crash detection is not compatible with input shaper. Do not suggest enabling both.
Belt maintenance comes before calibration. A failed phase stepping calibration usually points to belt tension.

Phase stepping customizes the drive signal for each motor to reduce visible fine artifacts (VFAs) and noise. On the CORE One the calibration option needs the accelerometer set; on the CORE One L the accelerometer is built in.

Prusa's PrusaSlicer profiles are split into Speed and Structural presets. Speed presets assume input shaper is on; Orca's bundled Prusa process profiles use the Speed values (170 mm/s walls, 4000 mm/s2 on MK4S).

steps.text: Check belt tension and that the toolhead and bed move freely. Do this before any calibration.
On MK4S or CORE One: connect the accelerometer set. On the XL and CORE One L: no hardware is needed.
Run the calibration from the LCD menu: Settings, Input Shaper, Calibration. For phase stepping use Settings, Phase Stepping, Calibration.
Read the type and frequency shown at the end. Keep the result the firmware stores; do not copy numbers from another printer.
Print a ringing tower or a known part at the profile's acceleration. If ghosting remains, lower outer wall acceleration before changing shaper values.

pilot_actions: Ask whether the printer has had hardware changes (new belts, toolhead swap, new mount) before suggesting recalibration.
Suggest lowering outer_wall_acceleration first when the user reports ringing. Only suggest the accelerometer calibration when acceleration cannot be lowered.
Do not write M593 values from a table. Only read them or ask the user to run calibration.
Never combine advice to use crash detection with input shaper.

settings.why: The CORE One Speed profile uses 3000 for outer walls; a lower value cleans up ringing while the shaper is not recalibrated.

settings.advice: Belts and frame rigidity limit input shaper more than any setting does.

data.name: PrusaLink and Prusa Connect
data.summary: PrusaLink is the local web API built into Prusa printers with a documented OpenAPI spec. Prusa Connect is Prusa's cloud service for remote control and a print queue. SlicerX can drive PrusaLink directly for upload, start, pause, stop, status and camera snapshots. Prusa Connect has no public automation API, so treat it as a manual or PrusaSlicer path.

facts.text: PrusaLink's API is documented as OpenAPI (spec/openapi.yaml in Prusa-Link-Web). Endpoints live under /api/v1 and use HTTP digest authentication. Older API key style X-Api-Key still exists and is off by default.
Status and control endpoints: GET /api/v1/status, GET /api/v1/info, GET /api/v1/job, PUT /api/v1/job/{id}/pause, PUT /api/v1/job/{id}/resume, DELETE /api/v1/job/{id} to stop.

Upload is PUT /api/v1/files/{storage}/{path} with headers Content-Length, Content-Type (default application/octet-stream), Print-After-Upload (?0 or ?1) and Overwrite (?0 or ?1). POST to the same path starts printing a stored file.
Storage listing is GET /api/v1/storage, transfer state is GET /api/v1/transfer, and camera snapshots are GET /api/v1/cameras/snap or /api/v1/cameras/{id}/snap.
PrusaSlicer sends G-code to PrusaLink from the G> button, with upload and print options. For Prusa Connect it has its own tab, which Prusa recommends over the older physical printer entry.
Prusa Connect can accept uploads with three choices: start now, add to the print queue, or store in cloud storage. It also handles remote monitoring.
I found no official public Prusa Connect automation API. A Prusa forum thread asks for one. Treat cloud automation as unsupported.

steps.text: Enable PrusaLink on the printer and note the address and the digest credentials from the printer's network settings.
In SlicerX, add the printer as a PrusaLink host by IP or hostname and test with GET /api/version.
Slice, then upload with PUT and Print-After-Upload set to ?0 unless the user confirms the plate is clear.
Poll /api/v1/status for progress. Use pause and resume by job id.

pilot_actions: Upload sliced G-code to a chosen storage and folder, and optionally start it after the user confirms the bed is clear.
Read printer state, job progress, temperatures and current job before advising mid print changes.
Pause or stop a job when the user asks or a failure is detected, with confirmation first.
Fetch a camera snapshot when the user asks mimir to look at a failing print.
Never send Print-After-Upload=?1 without explicit user confirmation.
Do not attempt to edit printer settings over PrusaLink; the documented API covers files, jobs, storage, cameras and updates only.

settings.advice: Use digest authentication and a strong password on PrusaLink; do not expose the port to the internet.

data.name: Prusa MMU3 multi material workflow
data.summary: The MMU3 feeds up to five filaments into one nozzle. It works best with PLA and PETG, relies on the extruder's IR filament sensor and its own FINDA, and makes prime tower and purge settings the main quality lever. Most failures are sensor or path problems, not slicer settings.

facts.text: The MMU3 is compatible with MK3S+, MK3.5/S, MK3.9/S, MK4/S and CORE One. Up to five filaments.
PLA and PETG are the materials Prusa officially supports; other polymers may work but are not extensively tested.
CORE One uses an enclosed MMU3 kit. Orca ships 'Prusa CORE One MMU3' machine profiles and separate '+ MMU3' process profiles.
An uncalibrated IR filament sensor can report no filament while filament is present, which can trigger a filament change or spool join mid print.

Error 04102 means the FINDA stayed triggered after unload, usually debris or a broken piece in the selector. 04103 means the extruder filament sensor did not trigger during load to nozzle. 04104 means the extruder sensor still sees filament after unload.

steps.text: Calibrate the IR filament sensor before the first multi color print and after any extruder service.
Load each filament into its slot from the MMU menu and let it feed to the FINDA. Trim the tip flat and clean.
Slice with the MMU3 machine and process profile for the printer. Assign colors per object or by painting.
Keep the prime tower (wipe tower) enabled and wide enough to purge the color change.
If colors bleed, raise the flush multiplier in small steps rather than shrinking the tower.
If a load error appears, follow the error code guidance: clear debris for 04102, recalibrate the sensor for 04103 and 04104.

pilot_actions: Confirm the printer has an MMU3 before applying MMU settings; refuse MMU advice on a single extruder printer.
Warn when a filament outside PLA and PETG is assigned to a slot, especially TPU or CF filament.
Enable the prime tower and raise flush_multiplier when the user reports color contamination.
Map an MMU error code to the causes above and give the fix; do not change slicer settings for a sensor fault.
Advise recalibrating the IR sensor when spurious filament changes or spool joins appear.

settings.why: A single nozzle multi material print needs a tower to purge between colors.
A wider tower gives each color change room to purge fully.
More flushing removes leftover color from the nozzle.

settings.advice: Keep filament tips clean and flat; a blobbed tip is the most common cause of a load failure.

data.name: Brim, raft and draft shield
data.summary: How mimir keeps parts on the plate: the right plate and temperature from the filament file first, then brims, mouse ears, rafts and draft shields for warp prone materials and tall thin parts.

facts.text: Auto brim sizes the brim from part geometry, speed and material. Reference thermal lengths: ABS, PA-CF and PET-CF 100, PC 40, TPU 1000. Adhesion coefficient 2 for PETG and PCTG, 0.5 for TPU. Capped at 20 mm; under 5 mm it adds no brim.
Outer brims are easiest to remove. Inner brims hide the removal mark but are harder to remove. Mouse ears add small brims only at corners and sharp features.
A draft shield protects ABS and ASA from drafts on open frame printers; enclosed printers rarely need one.
Consider a raft for complex models or difficult materials.

settings.why: Lets the slicer size the brim from the part and material.

pilot_actions: Offer mouse ears (brim_type brim_ears) instead of a full brim on boxy ABS or ASA parts: corners only, less cleanup.
For ABS, ASA, PC and nylon parts larger than about 100 mm across, suggest a brim or mouse ears and a closed enclosure.
For tall thin parts, suggest a brim and slower travel.
Always check the plate choice against the filament file before adding a brim.

data.name: Ironing
data.summary: A second pass over flat top surfaces with very little flow, which smooths them. Good for nameplates, lids and badges. Useless on curved tops, and it adds time.

facts.text: Ironing reprints the top at the same height with low flow. Types: top surfaces, topmost surface only, or all solid layers (slowest).
Orca defaults: 10 percent flow, 0.1 mm line spacing, 20 mm/s.
Line spacing should be at or below the nozzle diameter. Lower layer heights may need more ironing flow.
Filament moves very slowly while ironing, which raises the risk of heat creep and clogs, especially with PLA.
PLA irons well, PETG irons well but can stick to the nozzle, ASA irons very well, wood filled filaments iron poorly.

settings.why: Smooths every flat top surface.
Orca default.
Orca default.
Orca default.

pilot_actions: Suggest ironing only when the model has large flat top faces; say how much time it adds after slicing.
On an open printer printing PLA in a warm room, mention heat creep risk and keep the enclosure lid open on Bambu enclosed printers.

data.name: Seams
data.summary: Every layer of a normal print starts and ends somewhere, and that point is the seam. mimir picks where it goes (hidden, at the back, or scattered for strength), whether to scarf it, and how to fix bulges or gaps at it.

facts.text: Aligned, aligned back and back usually look best. Aligned back keeps the seam off the front of figurines and other models with a clear front.
Random spreads the seam's weak point across layers, which suits parts that need strength, such as a pin through a hole.
Nearest saves travel but scatters seams around the part.
Seam gap of 0 to 15 percent of the nozzle is typical on a printer with tuned pressure advance and retraction. A larger gap reduces bulges; a smaller gap hides the seam.

Scarf joint seams ramp the start and end of a loop to hide the seam and make it stronger. The conditional scarf applies only to loops without sharp corners (threshold 155 degrees by default); default scarf length is 20 mm.
Staggered inner seams move inner wall seams away from the outer seam so they do not stack into one weak line.

settings.why: Hide the seam at the back of display models.
Scarf the outer wall seam so it nearly disappears.
Keeps inner seams from lining up behind the outer one.
Middle of the typical 0 to 15 percent range on a tuned printer.

pilot_actions: For display models, pick aligned back and scarf seams; offer seam painting when a specific face must stay clean.
For strength goals, prefer random or staggered seams over aligned ones.
If the user reports a bulge at the seam, check pressure advance first (see troubleshoot seam_zits), then raise seam gap.

data.name: sleipnir (adaptive layer height)
data.summary: sleipnir changes the layer height through the part. Thin layers go where the surface is shallow or curved, where stair stepping shows most. Thick layers go on vertical walls, where thin layers only add time. Quality mode spends thin layers on looks. Strength mode keeps layers in the band that bonds best. Every layer stays inside the printer's layer height limits and the material's floor, the first layer is never touched, and cooling slowdowns are recomputed for the new profile.

facts.text: Layer height is the main driver of print time and vertical resolution. It does not change horizontal resolution: embossed text parallel to the bed looks the same at any layer height.
Bambu's example print took 1 h 19 min at 0.08 mm, 36 min 14 s at 0.20 mm and 28 min 27 s at 0.28 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle.
A shallow slope or a dome top shows the stair step most. Lowering the layer height only there keeps the finish while saving most of the time of a thin layer print.
Thinner layers also let overhangs go steeper before they sag, because each layer steps out less.
Bambu Studio does not support variable layer height with organic tree supports. A prime tower is only allowed when every object on the plate uses the same variable layer height profile.

rule_of_thumb.text: Keep layer height between about 25 and 75 percent of the nozzle diameter.
rule_of_thumb.origin: The 75 percent ceiling is the fallback that Slic3r, PrusaSlicer and OrcaSlicer use for adaptive layers when a printer profile leaves the maximum layer height unset. A 2023 peer reviewed review gives the same 25 to 75 percent band. Printer makers draw the band a little differently: Bambu 20 to 70 percent, the OrcaSlicer wiki 20 to 80, Prusa below 80, Cura warns above 80. SlicerX Easy mode clamps to 20 to 75 percent.

low_end.text: Below about 20 percent of the nozzle, flow gets uneven and fish scale patterns can show, especially at high speed. Prusa does not suggest going below 0.10 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle because 0.07 or 0.05 mm layers look only slightly better and take much longer.

high_end.text: Above about 80 percent of the nozzle, layer adhesion and quality suffer. Layer height can never exceed the nozzle diameter.

first_layer.text: Bambu presets use a first layer of 50 percent of the nozzle diameter (0.2 mm on 0.4). Prusa profiles use 0.20 mm. The OrcaSlicer wiki recommends 0.25 mm on 0.4 and a maximum of 65 percent. Variable layer height in Orca starts after the first layer and leaves it fixed.

engine_behavior.text: min_layer_height and max_layer_height live in the printer (extruder) profile and are only used for adaptive or variable layer height.
Orca defaults: min_layer_height 0.07 mm, max_layer_height 0 (unset). An unset max falls back to 0.75 times the nozzle diameter. The minimum is never below 0.01 mm.
Orca widens the limits to include the base layer_height if it lies outside them, and with supports it also applies the support and interface extruders' limits.
Bambu says its 0.08 to 0.28 mm range for a 0.4 mm nozzle comes from lab tests and should not be changed.

vendor_limits.note: min_layer_height and max_layer_height from OrcaSlicer machine profiles, inheritance resolved. Fractions are of the nozzle diameter.

rows.note: The maximum is above the nozzle diameter, which looks like a profile error. Do not trust it.
Prusa ships 0.25 mm nozzles instead: 0.05 to 0.15 mm on MK4S and Core One.

rows.printers: MK4S, Core One, Core One L
K1, K1C, K1 Max, K2 Plus
K1, K1C, K1 Max, K2 Plus

vendor_limits.takeaway: Bambu and the Creality K1 family use exactly 20 to 70 percent. Prusa and Voron sit at 25 to 80 percent on larger nozzles, and Prusa allows 0.07 mm on 0.4. The floor is mostly 17.5 to 25 percent (MK3S and K2 Plus 0.6 go to about 13) and the ceiling mostly 67 to 80 percent, with outliers on 0.2 mm nozzles. That brackets the 25 to 75 percent rule.

rows.note: 0.20 mm Standard is the default. 0.20 mm Strength keeps the layer height and adds walls (6) and infill (25 percent).
The 0.4 high flow nozzle adds 0.25 and 0.28 mm. Soluble support presets exist only at 0.20 mm.
The 0.6 high flow nozzle adds 0.40 mm.

z_step.text: A full step on a common Z axis (1.8 degree motor, 8 mm per turn leadscrew) is 8 / 200 = 0.04 mm. Prusa's calculator picks layer heights that are whole full steps because a Z motor that is switched off between microsteps jumps to the nearest full step. Klipper's endstop phase feature can put every layer on a full step, but only if the layer height is a multiple of a full step. OrcaSlicer's adaptive code has a Z gradation (rounding) step, but it is commented out, so adaptive heights are not rounded to steps. Cura steps between heights in 0.01 mm increments by default.
z_step.why_it_matters: Full step alignment matters when Z motors are idled mid print or when Klipper endstop phase is in use. Printers that hold Z energized and use microstepping position fine layers well, so full steps are a nice to have there, not a limit. No maker states a Z quantum for Bambu printers.

positions: CNC Kitchen: strength drops past 50 percent
disagreements.resolution: Use the printer profile maximum, capped at 75 percent. Strength mode caps at 50 percent.

positions: Prusa MK4S profile: 0.07 mm (17.5 percent) on 0.4
Prusa KB: not below 0.10 mm (25 percent)
disagreements.resolution: Use the printer profile minimum, never below 20 percent of the nozzle.

cusp_height.text: Cusp height is the largest gap between the stair stepped print and the true surface. It equals the layer height times the vertical part of the surface normal: zero on a vertical wall, the full layer height on a nearly flat top. The classic adaptive rule picks, for each layer, the tallest height that keeps the cusp under a limit, capped by the printer maximum.
cusp_height.formula: layer height = min(max layer height, cusp limit / nz), where nz is the vertical component of the surface normal (0 for a vertical wall, 1 for a flat top)
cusp_height.limits: Cusp alone never thins vertical walls, yet FDM walls are rough even when vertical because each bead is rounded (bead height to profile depth about 3.3). Thinner layers still smooth vertical walls, just less.

prusaslicer.text: Variable layer height tool with Adaptive (Quality/Speed slider), Smooth (filter radius, can be applied repeatedly), Keep min (thinnest layers are not smoothed) and manual painting. The metric limits the cross section area between the stepped surface and the model. Prusa advises starting from a base profile close to what most of the print will use.

orcaslicer_and_bambu.text: Same tool family: Adaptive with a quality and speed slider, Smooth with a Gaussian filter radius, Keep min, and manual raise or lower with the mouse. For each facet the code computes the allowed height from its slope using an error area measure, capped on near vertical surfaces, and takes the smallest over all facets that cross the layer. The slider maps to an allowed deviation that runs from min_layer_height through the base layer_height to max_layer_height. The smoothing radius defaults to 5. The first layer stays fixed. Bambu Studio labels the slider detail and speed.
inputs: surface slope of every triangle crossing the layer

cura.text: Adaptive layers vary the height around the base layer height. Maximum variation (default 0.1 mm) sets how far it may move. Variation step size (default 0.01 mm) sets how much one layer may differ from the previous one. Topography size (default 0.2 mm) is the target horizontal distance between the edges of two adjacent layers; a smaller value uses thinner layers. Cura keeps horizontal stepping constant, where Prusa and Orca limit an error area.

lessons.text: Users judged sudden jumps from thin to thick layers as worse than uniform thick layers, so the profile must be smoothed.
Taller layers get wider extrusions in PrusaSlicer's variable layer height, so pick a base profile near the typical height.

strength_evidence.summary: Most tests find parts get weaker once layers exceed about half the nozzle diameter, and that going thinner than about 0.15 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle gains little or nothing. Across 0.05 to 0.3 mm the published drops run from about 5 to 23 percent, and some studies see the opposite trend. Build orientation, temperature and wall count move strength far more than layer height inside the normal band.

studies.text: Prusament PLA hooks, 0.4 mm nozzle. Lying hooks from 0.05 to 0.2 mm all failed near 80 kg, 0.3 mm earlier, 0.4 mm far worse. Standing hooks (layer bond): 0.15 mm strongest, 0.3 mm about half, 0.4 mm almost nothing. Thin layers did not bond better. Past a nozzle to layer ratio of 2, strength drops.
studies.note: Single hobby test with one filament, weight normalized.

studies.text: Average tensile strength at 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 mm: PLA 32, 30.2, 28.8 MPa; PETG 33.5, 30.4, 29.5 MPa; PETG-CF 28.5, 24.4, 22.5 MPa. Thinner was stronger for all three; the drop from 0.1 to 0.3 mm was about 10 percent for PLA and 12 for PETG.

Flat PLA tensile bars at 0.05 to 0.20 mm. Strength fell as layers thickened for all four colors, by 4.77 percent (grey) to 23.41 percent (black) across the range. Filament color mattered more than layer height.
Upright PLA: 0.16 mm layers gave 67 percent more tensile strength than 0.24 mm, at 91 percent more print time.
studies.note: Read through the Stojkovic review table, not the original paper.

studies.text: PLA tensile strength 60.4 MPa at 0.2 mm, 48.5 at 0.3 and 54.9 at 0.4 (a V shape). ABS showed the same trend with a smaller effect.
studies.note: Read through a review; the review notes the original omitted standard deviations.

studies.text: 0.06 to 0.24 mm layers. Thicker layers raised tensile strength of upright samples; thinner layers helped flat and on edge samples. Upright samples were weakest overall.
Build orientation explained 98.16 percent of tensile strength variation. Layer thickness was not significant; the optimum was 0.16 mm.
Layer height significantly affected ABS interlayer fracture resistance. Nozzle temperature was the stronger lever: 20 C hotter raised apparent fracture resistance 38 percent.
studies.note: Direction of the layer height effect not stated in the abstract.

studies.text: 0.4 mm layers on a 0.4 mm nozzle gave up to 36.2 percent higher ultimate strength than 0.2 mm and halved print time.
studies.note: One specimen per condition; authors say it cannot show significance.

disagreements.topic: Do thinner layers make stronger parts?
positions: Thinner is stronger, most studies (Stojkovic, Frunzaverde, Szust and Adamski).
No gain below 0.15 mm on a 0.4 nozzle, and a clear loss above half the nozzle (CNC Kitchen).
Thicker helps upright samples or all samples (Chacon for upright, Aldawood with weak statistics), or a V shaped curve (Tymrak).
disagreements.resolution: Strength mode keeps layers between 30 and 50 percent of the nozzle. It never goes above 50 percent for load bearing parts and does not chase very thin layers for strength.

no_data: No peer reviewed layer height study was found for ASA, nylon, TPU or PVA. Their Strength mode bands are expert rules.

surface_quality.stair_step: Cusp height = layer height x nz. A 0.2 mm layer on a surface tilted 30 degrees from horizontal (nz about 0.87) leaves a step about 0.17 mm deep; on a 60 degree slope (nz 0.5) about 0.1 mm; on a vertical wall none from stepping.

diminishing_returns.text: Prusa: below 0.10 mm on 0.4 mm the gain is small for a large time cost.
CNC Kitchen: 0.15 mm on 0.4 mm gave the best overhangs and bridges. At 0.05 mm the color went patchy because the plastic stayed molten so long.
Frunzaverde: best dimensional accuracy at 0.10 to 0.15 mm on 0.4 mm; 0.05 mm had larger deviations, likely from many more heat cycles.
Below about 20 percent of the nozzle, flow turns uneven and fish scale patterns appear.

vendor_guidance.text: Bambu: lower layers make interlayer lines less visible but take longer; use variable layer height on domes and slopes rather than a thin layer for the whole part.
Prusa: a standard 0.15 mm profile on 0.4 mm suits most prints; layer height does not affect XY detail.

cooling.how_it_interacts: The slicer slows a layer down when its estimated time is under the minimum layer time, but never below the minimum print speed. At a fixed mm/s a thin layer takes about as long as a thick one, so layer time does not drop by itself. It drops when a thin layer is allowed to run faster because it needs less plastic per second, and on small cross sections. Every change to the layer profile needs the slowdown recomputed.

facts.text: Orca defaults: minimum layer time 5 s, minimum print speed 10 mm/s. Cura uses the same 5 s and 10 mm/s.
Ellis uses at least 15 s for ABS and says PLA and PETG on open printers can generally use less. Layers printed too fast go down on layers that are still soft.
Printing several parts at once, spread out, gives each part a break between layers.
Don't slow down outer walls keeps outer wall speed constant when layer time slowdowns kick in, which avoids gloss changes and banding lines.
Very low flow lets filament sit in the hotend long enough to soften above the melt zone. Orca warns of heat creep and clogs when ironing for this reason, and PLA is the most prone.

Example of low flow: a 0.08 mm layer, 0.4 mm wide, slowed to Orca's 10 mm/s minimum, extrudes 0.32 mm3/s. At Bambu PLA's 20 mm/s minimum it is 0.64 mm3/s, about 3 percent of that profile's 21 mm3/s limit.
facts.note: Simple arithmetic from profile values. No published flow threshold for heat creep was found.

by_family.note: Silk PLA runs 8 s in Orca generic and 15 s on the Core One with a 0.6 nozzle.

by_family.fan: 20 to 40 percent on Bambu, up to 100 in Orca generic

by_family.note: Orca generic uses 3 s, Bambu 12 s, Ellis at least 15 s.
Flow is capped near 3.2 to 3.6 mm3/s in Orca and Bambu TPU profiles, so TPU already prints slowly.
PVA flow caps are low (4 mm3/s generic, 6 on Bambu). HIPS uses 6 s and 0 to 60 percent fan.

modes.frac_note: Floors and ceilings are fractions of the nozzle diameter. The final bound is the tighter of this, the printer's min_layer_height and max_layer_height, and the SlicerX clamp of 0.2 to 0.75.

quality.goal: Hide stair stepping and layer lines where the eye sees them, and save time where it does not.
thin_where: shallow slopes and dome tops (surface within about 45 degrees of horizontal)
the last layers under a top surface
steep overhangs that need smaller steps
thick_where: vertical walls, where stepping is zero
straight internal sections with no visible slope
quality.reasoning: Stair step depth scales with layer height times the surface's vertical normal, so shallow surfaces gain the most. Vertical walls gain only a little from thin layers. Keep the ceiling at the base layer height from the Detail slider so walls do not get coarser than what the user picked, and never above 50 percent of the nozzle.

strength.goal: Keep every layer in the band that bonds well and let the rest of the strength come from walls, temperature and orientation.
thin_where: steep overhangs and bridges where sagging would weaken the section
small cross sections that would otherwise hit the minimum layer time
thick_where: vertical walls and straight sections, up to half the nozzle
strength.reasoning: Strength drops past half the nozzle diameter and gains little below about 0.15 mm on 0.4 mm. Orientation and nozzle temperature move strength more than layer height does inside that band. Bambu's own Strength preset keeps 0.20 mm and adds walls and infill instead.

cooling_guard.note: Use 8 s for silk and on printers whose profiles use it (Prusa Core One).

pla_family.reasoning: PLA takes strong cooling well, so thin layers are safe for looks. CNC Kitchen saw patchy color at 0.05 mm, which the 20 percent floor avoids on 0.4 mm. PLA is the material most prone to heat creep when thin layers get slowed down in a warm enclosure.

petg.reasoning: PETG lost about 12 percent tensile strength from 0.1 to 0.3 mm in one study, a bit more than PLA. Bambu runs it at 20 to 40 percent fan for layer bonding, so short thin layers need the full minimum layer time.

cooling_guard.note: Ellis uses at least 15 s for ABS. Orca generic uses 3 s, which is too short for small parts.

abs_asa.reasoning: Layer bond in ABS follows heat more than layer height: a hotter nozzle raised fracture resistance far more than any layer height change. Keep fan low and the chamber warm, and let Strength mode avoid very thin layers that stack many cool bonds on small parts.

pc.reasoning: PC runs low fan (10 to 40 percent on Bambu). The only PC layer height study found favored thicker layers but used one specimen per condition, so Strength mode leans thick without going past half the nozzle.

nylon_and_composites.thin_where: avoid thin layers; slopes only when the user asks
nylon_and_composites.reasoning: Prusa asks for at least 0.2 mm layers and a 0.4 mm nozzle with carbon, glass or kevlar filled filament, because higher layers and wider nozzles clog less. PETG-CF lost the most strength with thicker layers in the Stojkovic tests (28.5 to 22.5 MPa from 0.1 to 0.3 mm), so Strength mode stays near the floor for filled PETG. No layer height data was found for unfilled nylon.

tpu.reasoning: TPU is flow limited to about 3.2 to 3.6 mm3/s and Prusa's typical speed is 20 mm/s, so thin layers multiply an already long print. Keep a narrow band and let Quality mode add only a few thin layers on visible tops.

soluble_supports.thin_where: follow the model material; supports do not need thin layers
soluble_supports.thick_where: support body when layers are allowed to be independent

cooling_guard.note: Generic PVA uses 4 s, BVOH 8 s, HIPS 6 s.

soluble_supports.reasoning: Soluble interfaces print with zero Z gap, and Prusa ships its soluble presets only at 0.20 mm on 0.4. With supports enabled Orca also clamps the object's adaptive range to the support extruders' limits. Independent support layer height does not work with a prime tower, which multi material prints usually need, and Bambu needs the same variable profile on every object to keep the prime tower.

settings.why: Thin, fast layers can finish before the last one has cooled. This slows them down to the minimum layer time.

pilot_rules.rule: Clamp every sleipnir height to the tightest of: the printer's min_layer_height and max_layer_height, the SlicerX clamp (0.2 to 0.75 of the nozzle), the mode and material band in modes.families, and any absolute material floor. If max_layer_height is 0, treat it as unset and use 0.75 of the nozzle, as Orca does.
Treat a printer max_layer_height above 0.8 of the nozzle as a likely profile error (the Creality K2 Plus 0.2 nozzle profile lists 0.30 mm) and fall back to 0.7 of the nozzle.
Clamp the base layer_height from the Detail slider before running sleipnir. Orca widens its adaptive limits to include the base height, so an out of range base height would leak through.
Never change the first layer. Keep initial_layer_print_height as the profile sets it (Bambu 50 percent of the nozzle, Prusa 0.20 mm, at most 65 percent per the Orca wiki).

Never go below the material floor. For carbon, glass or kevlar filled filament that is 0.2 mm absolute on a nozzle of at least 0.4 mm; refuse sleipnir thin zones on a smaller nozzle and suggest a 0.6 mm hardened nozzle.

Round each height to 0.01 mm. When the printer's Z full step is known and the user runs Klipper endstop phase or idles Z motors, round to whole full steps instead (0.04 mm on a 1.8 degree motor with an 8 mm lead screw). Re-check the clamp after rounding.

Smooth the profile before slicing (Orca's default filter radius is 5) and keep the thinnest layers in Quality mode (keep min). Avoid jumps between neighbors; users see sudden thin to thick changes as worse than uniform layers.

After building the profile, recompute each layer's speed against filament_max_volumetric_speed, then its time against slow_down_layer_time, using the material's slow_down_min_speed as the floor. Show the new estimated time next to the old one.
Apply the family cooling_guard minimum layer time from modes.families, and for ABS offer 15 s. If many thin layers still fall under it, suggest printing more parts at once instead of more slowdown.

Warn when a thin layer combined with a cooling slowdown drops flow to a few percent of the filament's max volumetric speed (see the 0.32 to 0.64 mm3/s example in cooling.facts), especially with PLA, PETG or TPU in a closed printer. No published threshold exists, so this is a warning, not a block. Suggest opening the door or raising slow_down_min_speed.

In Strength mode, cap at half the nozzle diameter and put extra effort into walls, nozzle temperature and orientation rather than thinner layers. Tell the user orientation matters more than layer height.

Before enabling sleipnir on Bambu printers, switch organic tree supports to normal or classic tree, and give every object on a prime tower plate the same layer profile. Keep soluble interfaces synced with object layers.
Tell the user where thin and thick layers went and why, in one line each (for example: thin on the dome top to hide steps, thick on the straight sides to save time).

disagreements.resolution: Printer profile maximum capped at 75 percent of the nozzle; 50 percent in Strength mode.
Stay in 30 to 50 percent of the nozzle for strength; thinner is not reliably stronger.
12 s default, offer 15 s on small parts.

open_questions: No published volumetric flow threshold for heat creep; the warning in pilot_rules is qualitative.
No maker states the Z full step or leadscrew lead for Bambu printers.
Orca keys min_layer_height, max_layer_height, dont_slow_down_outer_wall and infill_combination_max_layer_height are not in settings.yaml; mimir can only read or mention them.

data.name: Supports
data.summary: When to add supports, which kind, and how to keep them easy to remove. Orientation comes first: turning the part often removes the need for support entirely.

facts.text: Normal supports are a grid under overhangs: stable and good for large flat overhangs. Tree supports branch from trunks and use less material.

Organic is the default tree style and saves material. Tree slim is lighter, tree strong is sturdier for heavy overhangs, and tree hybrid behaves like normal support under large flat overhangs. Snug normal supports reduce scarring.
Overhangs whose slope is below the threshold angle get support. A smaller threshold means steeper overhangs print without it.
Orca's default gaps are 0.2 mm between support top and part, and 0.35 mm in XY.
Higher branch density at the tips gives better overhangs but harder removal; use top interface layers instead when a dense surface is needed.
Bambu's presets change the threshold with layer height: 15 degrees at 0.08 mm, 30 at 0.20 mm, 40 at 0.28 mm.

settings.why: Trees for figures and organic shapes.
Default tree style, least material.
Stops supports from starting on the part and scarring it, when the geometry allows.

material_notes.text: PETG bonds hard to its own supports; raise the top Z gap slightly or use an interface in a different material (Support for PLA/PETG).
Soluble PVA or BVOH interfaces give clean undersides on multi material printers; see the pva and bvoh filament files.

pilot_actions: Run orient with minimum support before enabling supports.
Report support volume and removal risk; offer manual support painting for critical faces.

docs.name: AMS load and unload failures
aliases: filament will not load from AMS

data.name: AMS load and unload failures
aliases: filament will not load from AMS
camera_signs: Filament stopped partway in the PTFE tube, bent or kinked at the AMS outlet, the buffer or the toolhead inlet
Filament stuck at the AMS hub or the AMS lite hub with a tangled or loose loop on the spool
Scraped, flattened or dented filament section near the feeder wheel
The buffer slider or spring at rest at one end and not moving as filament feeds
A spool that has slipped off its holder or an overwound spool that will not turn
log_signs: Bambu HMS 0700-4000-0002-0004: filament buffer signal abnormal (spring stuck or filament tangled)
Bambu HMS 0700-xx00-0002-0014: AMS slot odometer no signal (connector or odometer failure)
Bambu HMS 0700-0100-0002-0011: AMS motor assist parameter lost. Pull filament from the hub and restart the AMS
Bambu HMS 0700-2x00-0002-0001: slot filament has run out. Not a jam, but the spool may be tangled or stuck when the AMS cannot pull it
Bambu HMS 1200-2000-0002-0006 family: failed to extrude AMS lite filament, or air printing detection cut the filament (A1 series)
Prusa MMU3 error codes such as 04101 (FINDA did not trigger), 04102 (FINDA filament stuck), 04104 (filament sensor filament stuck), or a load failure into the extruder

q_system.ask: Is this a Bambu AMS, AMS 2 Pro, AMS HT or AMS lite?

q_stage.ask: Does the filament fail to leave the AMS slot or feeder, as opposed to jamming further down the tube or at the toolhead?

q_slot.ask: Is the filament worn, kinked or flat at its tip, or is the spool tangled or turning hard when you pull by hand?

q_wheel.ask: Does the feeder motor turn, but the filament slips and shows dents, or does the LED not change when you insert filament?

q_odometer.ask: Does the printer report an odometer, motor assist or sensor fault (HMS 0700 codes), or is the AMS reading the RFID and then pulling filament back with a clicking sound?

q_tube.ask: Is the PTFE tube between the AMS, buffer and toolhead bent, deformed, loose in a fitting or not fully seated?

q_buffer.ask: Does the buffer spring or slider stick, or does the filament tangle at the buffer or spool?

q_toolhead.ask: Does the filament reach the toolhead but not extrude, click at the extruder, or does printing from an external spool also fail?

causes.name: Worn, kinked or poorly wound filament
checks: Pull the filament out of the slot and look for wear marks, dents or a bent tip.
Turn the spool by hand. It should spin freely without tangles or an overwound loop.

fixes.advice: Cut off the worn section, straighten and trim the tip to a clean angle, and reload. Try a different spool. If several spools show the same wear, clean the feeder or hub next.
Rewind or replace a spool with tangles. Check the spool is seated on its holder and the spool holes are not catching.

causes.name: Slipping feeder wheel or dirty internal hub
checks: Filament shows dents after a failed attempt and you hear the motor rotating while nothing moves.
Check the knurled teeth on the hub for debris and confirm the odometer wheel turns freely.
On AMS, the LED should stay white after filament is inserted and turn off when it is removed.

fixes.advice: Try another spool first. Tighten the 4 screws on the hub described in the Bambu guide, and clean the knurled teeth and the odometer wheel. If the hub still slips, replace the extrusion wheel assembly, feeder unit or internal hub as the wiki directs.
For a feeder unit that does not react when filament is inserted, clean the Hall sensor and check the magnet for grooves.

causes.name: Odometer, sensor or assist motor fault
checks: Read the HMS code in the printer log. 0700 codes with 0014 mean no odometer signal, 0011 means the motor assist parameter is lost.
During RFID read the filament is fed out, then pulled back. A clicking feeder with no RFID data points at the odometer.

fixes.advice: For a lost motor assist parameter, pull the filament out of the hub and restart the AMS as the HMS page directs.
For an odometer with no signal, reseat the connector and replace the odometer or hub if it persists. Contact Bambu support with the log if the fault remains.

causes.name: Bent, loose or deformed PTFE tube
checks: Disconnect each tube segment and feed filament through by hand. Note where it sticks: between the AMS and the buffer, or between the buffer and the toolhead.
On AMS lite and the A1, check the 4-in-1 hub adapter is holding the tube.

fixes.advice: Replace a bent or deformed PTFE tube and press it fully into the pneumatic fitting. Bambu recommends a new tube if filament sticks between the AMS and buffer or the buffer and toolhead.
If it sticks at the same spot after replacing the tube, check the AMS internal hub for a piece of broken filament.
For AMS lite, fix a filament hub or 4-in-1 adapter that will not hold the PTFE using the A1 guide. Route tubes without tight loops.

causes.name: Stuck or bent AMS buffer, or tangled spool
checks: Open the buffer window. The slide and spring should move smoothly side to side as filament feeds. The buffer has a hall sensor that detects the slide position.

fixes.advice: Pick the spring back into its normal position through the buffer window with a screwdriver so the slide moves freely, as Bambu's HMS page directs. If the error persists, check for tangled filament or a stuck spool and send the log to support.
Power cycle the printer after clearing the jam, and check the hub PTFE fittings for debris.

causes.name: Clogged nozzle or extruder
checks: Bambu suggests removing the AMS from the path and printing from an external spool. If quality is acceptable, look at the AMS internal hub. If it also under-extrudes or cannot extrude, the nozzle is at fault.
Check the extruder resistance HMS (0300-0900-0002-0004) and the filament type set in the slicer against the real filament.

fixes.advice: Clear the clog using the printer's official unclogging guide and replace the nozzle if the external spool test still fails. See the clog troubleshooter.
Set the filament type in the slicer to the real filament. A mismatch can trigger resistance faults.

causes.name: Extruder sensor, cutter or gripping problem
checks: Filament reaches the toolhead but the printer says it is not detected, or unloading fails because the cutter no longer cuts.

fixes.advice: Test the extruder filament sensor with Bambu's sensor inspection guide (Hall switch). For an unload that cannot pull out of the inlet, check for a worn filament cutter blade or a blockage in the extruder.

causes.name: Prusa MMU3 or Creality CFS feed problem
checks: MMU3: read the error. 04101 is FINDA did not trigger, 04102 is FINDA filament stuck, 04104 is filament sensor filament stuck, and there is a separate load failure into the extruder.
CFS: check the PTFE between the CFS and the toolhead for kinks and the buffer for a stuck spring or pin, and feed a filament directly to see if the CFS or the buffer is at fault.

fixes.advice: MMU3: heat the nozzle, open the idler screw and pull the filament out by hand before retrying. Look for a string or broken filament stuck in the selector if FINDA stays triggered. If FINDA did not trigger, check that the idler and pulley grabbed the filament. Only the Prusa KB summaries were read, so follow the article for the exact code.
CFS: replace a kinked or collapsed PTFE loop, trim a clean straight tip after any failed print or manual unload, and update the CFS firmware. Community reports, low confidence.

data.name: Bed adhesion failure
camera_signs: First layer lines are not attached, lift when touched, or are dragged around by the nozzle
Part is loose, shifted or gone from the plate in a snapshot mid print
Lines are round, thin, or spaced apart on the first layer, or peel at the corners
A dull or shiny patch on the plate where prints keep failing
log_signs: Bambu HMS prompts that point at the plate: force sensor disturbance (for example 0300-0A00-0001-0004 for a plate not seated or debris under it)
Bambu spaghetti detection or first layer inspection alerts
Klipper: a print that continues with no part on the bed is not logged as an error. Check the camera

q_clean.ask: Was the plate washed with dish soap and water (or 90 percent IPA on Prusa sheets) and handled only by its edges?

q_plate_match.ask: Does the plate type and temperature selected in the slicer match the plate installed and the filament?

q_first_layer_look.ask: Do first layer lines look round and separated, with gaps, instead of flat and joined?

q_material.ask: Is the material wet, or one that needs glue or a special plate (PETG on smooth PEI, nylon, ABS, PC)?

q_speed.ask: Is the first layer speed above 30 mm/s (Bambu's recommended ceiling), or was the print sped up during the first layers?

q_plate_condition.ask: Is the plate old, worn or scratched, or a cheap or fake PEI sheet, with adhesion getting worse over weeks?

causes.name: Grease or residue on the plate
checks: Fingerprints, hand cream, glue stick residue or dust on the surface. Water beads on greasy spots.

fixes.advice: Wash the plate with warm (not hot) water and dish soap, using a fresh sponge, rinse and air dry or use paper towel. Do not touch the print surface. Ellis notes IPA is fine for maintenance but does not clear oils well. Prusa recommends 90 percent IPA, never acetone on textured or satin sheets.

causes.name: Wrong plate type or temperature in the slicer
checks: Bambu says a wrong build plate type selection often causes adhesion failure and lowers the bed temperature.

fixes.advice: Set the plate type in the slicer (curr_bed_type) to the plate that is physically installed. Bambu's bed temperature changes with the plate selected.
Use the plate's recommended temperature for the filament. Ellis lists first layer temperatures around 60 C for PLA, 80 C for PETG and 90 to 100 C for ABS as a rough reference.

causes.name: First layer too high or bed not level
checks: Print the squish test. Lines that are round with gaps mean the nozzle is too far. On Bambu, first layer too high shows sparse lines and poor adhesion.

fixes.advice: Run automatic bed leveling (Calibration, Print Calibration, Auto Bed Leveling), check the back of the plate for debris, and confirm the plate lies flat. Then use the first_layer troubleshooter for Z offset.
Ellis suggests a first layer line width of 120 percent or more, which raises pressure against the surface. Lean toward slightly more squish, but do not over squish.

causes.name: Material needs glue or a different surface
checks: PETG, ABS, ASA, nylon, PC and other PET based materials bond hard to smooth PEI or barely at all to some surfaces, and wet filament weakens adhesion.

fixes.advice: Use a thin layer of PVA glue stick. Prusa recommends it for PETG, ABS, ASA, PC, nylon, flexible and PET based materials, and it also protects the sheet. Bambu uses glue on the Engineering and High Temp plates for these materials.
Dry the filament. Bambu notes moisture causes uneven extrusion that hurts first layer adhesion.

causes.name: First layer printed too fast
checks: Speed on the first layer above what the plastic needs to bond.

fixes.why: Bambu recommends an initial layer speed of 30 mm/s or less.
Bambu recommends an initial layer infill speed of 60 mm/s or less.

fixes.advice: On Prusa, reduce speed to about 75 percent for the first three layers using the speed knob.

causes.name: Worn, fake or wrong plate
checks: Adhesion degraded gradually. Clear rather than yellowish PEI is likely fake per Ellis. Some two sided plates are only printable on one side.

fixes.advice: Refresh smooth PEI by scuffing with a kitchen scouring pad or fine sandpaper (about 400 to 600 grit on Prusa's guide, 800 to 1000 in Ellis), then wash again. Prusa says acetone once a month restores smooth PEI but never on textured or satin sheets.
Replace the plate if scratched or from an unknown seller. Use a well known brand.

causes.name: Small footprint or high shrink part
checks: Tall, thin or narrow base part, or a large flat part in ABS, ASA, PC or nylon.

fixes.why: A brim adds contact area. Bambu recommends 5 to 8 mm for small footprints.
Bambu suggests brim width 5 to 8 mm.

fixes.advice: See the warping troubleshooter for enclosure, cooling and drafts.

data.name: Nozzle clog
camera_signs: Nothing comes out of the nozzle, or the print shows missing layers and gaps that get worse
Filament curls sideways or up around the nozzle when extruding by hand
A small blob of plastic stuck to the outside of the nozzle or a ball of plastic around the tip
Ground or flattened filament visible at the extruder gear, or a thin neck on filament that entered the hotend
log_signs: Bambu HMS 0300-1A00-0002-0002: the extrusion force sensor repeatedly detected excessive force and judged the nozzle is clogged (A1 series)
Bambu HMS 0300-0900-0002-0004: extrusion resistance abnormal (jam in the toolhead, clog, wrong filament type in the slicer, tangled external spool)
Bambu HMS 12xx-2000-0002-0006 family: failed to extrude AMS lite filament, extruder may be clogged or filament too thin
Klipper: no clog error exists. Look for a print that ran with no extrusion, or heater warnings if the hotend is the problem

q_manual_extrude.ask: Heat the nozzle a little above the filament's usual temperature and extrude by hand. Does the plastic come out straight and steady?

q_high_temp_history.ask: Did you recently print a high temperature material (PAHT-CF, PPA, PPS, PC) and then a low temperature one (PLA, PETG, TPU) without a purge?

q_chamber_hot.ask: Was the chamber or room hot, the bed above 70 C with the top glass on, or is the hotend fan weak or stopping?

q_debris.ask: Is the filament abrasive, glitter or fiber filled, or a cheap spool with variable diameter, or do you see debris on the filament?

q_feed.ask: Does it extrude fine by hand but still click or under-extrude in the print?

q_gear.ask: Is the filament worn, dented or ground at the extruder gear, or does the spool or AMS path have drag?

q_speed.ask: Do the problems only appear when printing fast, thick layers or a cold nozzle?

causes.name: Residue from a high temperature material
checks: Clog appears right after changing from a high temperature filament to PLA, PETG or TPU.

fixes.advice: Follow Bambu's switch procedure: set the nozzle to 250 to 300 C, unload the hot material by hand, load the new filament and let it push out the residue while cooling, then lower to 220 to 240 C and keep extruding until it flows cleanly.

causes.name: Heat creep
checks: Filament is soft or swollen above the heatbreak, and clogs return after warm prints. See the heat_creep troubleshooter.

fixes.advice: For PLA and PETG, open the door or remove the top cover, and lower the bed temperature where possible. Bambu recommends keeping the chamber at least 10 C below the filament glass transition.
Check the hotend cooling fan spins at full speed all the time. Replace it if it stops or slows.

causes.name: Debris or abrasive particles in the nozzle
checks: Partial clog with filament coming out curled. Particulates in carbon fiber or glitter filament can be larger than the nozzle hole.

fixes.advice: Clear it with the official procedure for your printer: manual extrude at higher temperature, pin tool, then cold pull. For abrasive filaments use a hardened nozzle and replace it when worn.
Use quality filament with tight diameter control. Bambu recommends 1.75 plus or minus 0.03 mm and checking the cross section for impurities.

causes.name: Damaged or worn nozzle or heater
checks: Repeated clogs after a proper clean, or the same spot that keeps failing.

fixes.advice: Replace the nozzle. Ellis says to try a new nozzle first because it is often a partial clog. Bambu notes persistent extrusion problems can point to a worn or damaged heater cartridge.
On Bambu machines, re-tighten the two hotend screws and check the hotend for skew.

causes.name: Wet filament
checks: Popping at the nozzle, bubbles in the strand or rough walls.

fixes.advice: Dry the filament and store it sealed with desiccant. Water vaporizing in the nozzle causes bubbles, stringing and poor flow, and engineering materials with carbon or glass fiber are more sensitive.

causes.name: Extruder gear or feed path drag
checks: Feel for drag pulling filament from the spool to the extruder. Check the gear for filament dust or dents.

fixes.advice: Clean the feed gear. Replace kinked PTFE, clear a stuck AMS buffer spring and untangle the spool. If several AMS spools have wear marks, clean the internal hub knurled teeth and odometer wheel per the AMS guide.

causes.name: Printing too fast or too cold for the hotend
checks: Bambu warns printing too fast (for example Ludicrous mode) may not let the plastic melt fully, and printing too cold can under-melt and clog.

fixes.advice: Print within the filament's recommended temperature range and lower speed or the filament max volumetric speed until extrusion is steady.

fixes.why: A little more heat helps at high flow. Stay inside the filament range.

data.name: Dimensional accuracy
camera_signs: Holes and shafts that measure smaller than the model, so screws, pins or magnets do not fit
Parts that need force or sanding to mate, or that are too loose
A flared base (elephant foot) or a bulge on outer walls that changes the measured width
Parts that are the wrong size in one axis only, or all sizes wrong by a similar percentage (shrinkage)

q_pattern.ask: Are all dimensions off by about the same percentage (large parts wrong the most), rather than just holes or the base?

q_hole.ask: Are holes undersized while outside dimensions are about right (screws, pins or magnets do not fit)?

q_extrusion_ok.ask: Have you calibrated flow and pressure advance for this filament, and is the filament dry?

q_base.ask: Is the base wider than the rest of the part (a flare in the first 1 to 3 layers)?

q_outer.ask: Are outside dimensions too large or walls bulging at corners and seams?

causes.name: Material shrinkage
checks: Measure a large part in X, Y and Z with calipers. A uniform percentage error points at shrinkage.
Bambu names material shrinkage as a factor to check before adjusting XY compensation.

fixes.advice: Use the filament shrinkage compensation (filament_shrink) only with a value found from a measured calibration part, never a guess. 100 percent means no compensation.

Print a calibration cube with the same filament, temperature, plate and enclosure conditions as the final part. Measure it and set the compensation to the ratio of the target size to the measured size.
High shrinkage materials (ABS, ASA, PC, nylon, and carbon fiber filled versions) vary the most. Print them enclosed and use the same conditions every time.

causes.name: Flow or pressure advance not calibrated, or wet filament
checks: Bambu lists moist filament and flow dynamics not tuned as causes to fix before compensating.

fixes.advice: Dry the filament, run flow dynamics (pressure advance) calibration, then flow ratio calibration, and only then compensate sizes. Ellis says tune pressure advance first, then the extrusion multiplier.
Ellis notes the extrusion multiplier is an aesthetics first method. For true to CAD dimensions read the rationale and dimensional accuracy section of his extrusion multiplier page.

causes.name: Holes need XY hole compensation
checks: Print a hole gauge model with the same profile and filament. Bambu suggests an M6 screw size test where the actual thread diameter is often about 5.9 mm. Holes under 1 mm are hard to tune.
Add chamfers or lead-in features to holes in CAD, since lack of chamfer is a listed factor.

fixes.why: Increase the hole compensation in small steps and re-test. Bambu's worked example measured a hole 0.24 mm undersized and applied about half of that as compensation.
Polyholes correct the tendency of circular holes to print smaller than modeled.

fixes.advice: Calibrate per filament and repeat when changing material. The seam can also affect hole precision, so place it away from tight fits.

causes.name: Elephant foot flare
checks: The first layers are wider than the rest. Bambu says this affects fit on assemblies, snaps, rails and shaft holes.

fixes.advice: Follow the elephant_foot troubleshooter: measure a test cube and enter the elephant foot compensation. Bambu's X1C Standard profile uses 0.15 mm.

causes.name: Over-extrusion inflating outer dimensions
checks: Outside dimensions are oversized and walls look wide. Corners bulge.

fixes.why: Lower flow in 1 to 2 percent steps after pressure advance is tuned.
Orca's precise wall setting sets the overlap between the outer and adjacent inner wall to zero to improve dimensional accuracy.
Shrinks the outer contour without changing holes. Calibrate on a measured part, since Bambu treats hole and contour as separate settings.

causes.name: Axis scale, belts or squareness
checks: One axis is consistently wrong, or a square part measures as a parallelogram.

fixes.advice: Check belt tension, pulley set screws and gantry squareness, and check rotation_distance and steps per mm on Klipper machines. On Bambu printers run the built in calibrations after a move. Klipper also has skew correction for a printer that is slightly out of square.

data.name: Elephant foot
camera_signs: The bottom layers flare outward as a lip wider than the layers above, most visible on the first 1 to 3 layers
A part sits fine on the plate but a lid or mating part will not seat because of the ridge at the base
Shiny, squashed first layer lines with a ridge at the edge

q_squish.ask: Does the first layer look glassy or squashed, with ridges pushed out at the edge of the lines?

q_bed_heat.ask: Is the bed temperature at the high end for the material, or higher than the plate needs?

q_compensation.ask: Is elephant foot compensation set to 0, and do you need tight tolerances at the base?

q_compensation_high.ask: Is there a step or gap in the wall just above the base (perimeters printing over nothing)?

causes.name: Nozzle too close to the plate
checks: Print the first layer squish patches. If lines merge with no gaps and ridges at the edges, the nozzle is too close.

fixes.advice: Raise the Z offset a little. On Bambu textured plates the default G29.1 Z-0.04 adds pressure. Bambu's suggested range is -0.06 to 0 mm on textured plates and -0.01 to 0.01 mm on smooth plates; a value closer to zero raises the nozzle.
Lower the flow of the first layer only if the rest of the part is correct, and do not fix adhesion by squishing. Prusa warns that too low a Z offset can damage the sheet.

causes.name: Bed too hot for the first layer
checks: The first layers stay soft while upper layers press on them. Bambu names bed heat as one of the two causes.

fixes.advice: Drop the bed temperature toward the low end of the plate and filament range. Keep it high enough for adhesion, since warping is the opposite failure.

causes.name: No elephant foot compensation
checks: Print a 25 x 25 x 10 mm cube with compensation at 0 and no brim. Let the bed cool to room temperature before removing, then measure the base against the upper walls with calipers.

fixes.why: Add a little compensation and re-measure. Bambu's example uses 0.2 mm and the Bambu X1C Standard profile ships 0.15 mm. Use the measured flare for tight parts.

causes.name: Compensation set too high
checks: A visible groove or a perimeter that prints over nothing above the base. Ellis notes this is common with high values combined with bottom chamfers.

fixes.why: Reduce, disable or fade the compensation. Too much makes the upper perimeters print over an undersized base.

causes.name: Large or heavy base on soft first layers
checks: Larger models and wider bases show more flare because more weight sits on the soft base.

fixes.advice: Add a small chamfer to the bottom edge of the model in CAD. That removes the flare without touching slicer settings.
Keep the first layer at the recommended first layer height, and print the first layers slower so the plastic sets. Bambu recommends 30 mm/s or less for the initial layer.

data.name: First layer problems
camera_signs: Sparse, thin or see-through lines on the first layer, with gaps between lines
Glassy, squashed lines, ridges, or a nozzle that scrapes the plate and leaves scratches
One side of the plate good and the other side too high or too low (a tilt or mesh problem)
Lines start well then thin out or blob, or the first layer has holes at some spots
log_signs: Bambu HMS 0300 family: heatbed force sensor prompts such as 0300-0A00-0001-0004 (external disturbance during sensitivity test). Bed leveling or first layer inspection failures
Klipper: probe accuracy errors, 'Probe triggered prior to movement', or a bed mesh that looks very different hot and cold

q_height.ask: Is the first layer too high everywhere (round, spaced lines) or too low everywhere (scraping, glassy, no extrusion)?

q_uneven.ask: Is the first layer good in some areas of the plate and bad in others (a high or low patch, or a tilt left to right)?

q_hardware_tight.ask: Are the hotend, nozzle and toolhead screws tight, and is the plate seated with nothing under it?

q_mesh.ask: Was bed leveling or a bed mesh run just before this print, while the bed and chamber were at print temperature?

q_extrusion.ask: Do lines start and stop with thin spots or blobs, or is the filament wet or the nozzle partly clogged?

causes.name: Z offset wrong
checks: Print the square patches from Ellis' squish test. Lines should touch with no gaps, still be visible on the underside, and not fade.
On Bambu printers the default G29.1 offset is Z-0.04 on textured plates.

fixes.advice: Adjust Z live while a squish test prints. On Klipper use SET_GCODE_OFFSET Z_ADJUST=0.01 MOVE=1 or the Tune menu. Ellis leans toward slightly more squish. Prusa uses Live Adjust Z, and warns against squishing to solve adhesion problems.

On Bambu, edit G29.1 in the printer start G-code as a temporary fix. Suggested ranges are -0.06 to 0 mm on textured plates and -0.01 to 0.01 mm on smooth plates. A value of Z0 on a textured plate raises the nozzle by 0.04 mm from the default. Fix the root cause afterward and restore defaults.

fixes.why: Ellis prefers a first layer height of 0.25 mm or more because thicker first layers are less sensitive to bed variation.

causes.name: Loose hotend, nozzle or plate
checks: On Bambu, remove the silicone sock and look for a skewed hotend or contamination.
Look for debris under the plate or a bent sheet.

fixes.advice: Re-tighten the two hotend screws on Bambu printers and replace a skewed hotend assembly. On Klipper, make sure everything in the toolhead and across the X extrusion, including hotend and nozzle, is tight.
Check the back of the plate for filament debris and ensure the plate sits flat. Bambu's HMS page lists an unseated plate and an unstable surface as causes of force sensor prompts.

causes.name: No bed leveling or a stale mesh
checks: A cold mesh is different from a hot one. The bed and gantry warp with heat.

fixes.advice: On Bambu, run Automatic Bed Leveling from Calibration, Print Calibration after a move, a long storage or a heatbed change, and enable bed leveling in the print preparation screen.

On Klipper, run BED_MESH_CALIBRATE in the print start macro while the bed is hot. Ellis suggests bicubic for meshes larger than 3 by 3, and a mesh above 5 by 5 is usually overkill. Klipper needs a calibrated probe Z offset before meshing.

causes.name: Gantry, bed or Z belts out of square
checks: A mesh cannot fix mechanical problems. If the pattern stays the same after a fresh mesh, the gantry, bed mounting or Z drive is at fault.

fixes.advice: Square and de-rack the gantry. Check bed mounting screws (Ellis heat soaks and hot tightens three of four and leaves the fourth snug), Z belt tensions being equal (about 140 Hz over 150 mm for his machines), and an inductive probe's PEI bubbling.
Klipper's bed mesh cannot compensate for a skewed axis or an inaccurate probe. Verify the probe accuracy first.

causes.name: Inconsistent extrusion on the first layer
checks: Popping or bubbles, or a partial clog that gives a thin or inconsistent line.

fixes.advice: Dry the filament. Bambu says wet filament makes extrusion uneven and hurts first layer adhesion. Check for a partial clog, since Bambu notes insufficient first layer extrusion can lead to a clogged tip.

causes.name: First layer speed, width or temperature
checks: First layer speed is high, line width is narrow, or the first layer temperature is conservative.

fixes.why: Bambu recommends 30 mm/s or less on the first layer.
Orca's Bambu profiles use 0.5 mm for a 0.4 mm nozzle. Ellis suggests 120 percent or wider for grip.

fixes.advice: Use standard first layer temperatures if the filament maker's are conservative. Ellis gives about 60 C for PLA, 80 C for PETG and 90 to 100 C for ABS. Prusa suggests 5 to 10 C hotter bed for stubborn materials.

docs.name: Heat creep
aliases: clog that appears after an hour

data.name: Heat creep
aliases: clog that appears after an hour
camera_signs: The print starts fine, then under-extrusion or a full stop appears after a period of time
Filament above the nozzle is swollen, soft, bent or thicker at the bottom when pulled out
Clicking extruder late in the print, gaps in walls, then nothing extruding
log_signs: Bambu HMS extrusion resistance prompts (for example 0300-0900-0002-0004) or clog detection (0300-1A00-0002-0002) appearing late in a warm print
Klipper: hotend fan or heater warnings, or a temperature sensor on the heatsink reading high if you have one

q_material.ask: Is the filament PLA, TPU or PETG (low glass transition), or PETG with the bed at 70 C or more inside a closed enclosure?

q_enclosure.ask: Is the printer enclosed with the door and top cover on, or in a room that is hot (summer, small closed room)?

q_fan.ask: Is the hotend cooling fan spinning at full speed all the time, with clean heatsink fins and an intact duct?

q_retraction.ask: Do long retractions or many stop and start retractions sit near the clog, or is the print slow with very little extrusion per minute?

q_heatbreak.ask: Is the heatbreak seated properly with no gap, thermal paste on threads where the maker calls for it, and no cracked or loose heatsink?

causes.name: Chamber or room too hot for the material
checks: Bambu says the most common reason for hotend and extruder clogs on X1 Carbon and P1S is heat buildup in the enclosure.
Keep the chamber at least 10 C below the filament glass transition.

fixes.advice: Open the front door and remove the top glass or lid for PLA, TPU and PETG. Ellis suggests at minimum opening the door, or taking the panels off, for PLA in an enclosure.
Print PLA on a cooler plate at a low bed temperature. Bambu notes the Cool Plate at about 35 C lets PLA print with the door closed.
In a hot room, add airflow around the printer and avoid printing at the hottest time of day. Bambu names outside heat as a cause.

causes.name: Hotend fan weak, stopped or ducted wrong
checks: Watch the fan during a print. A fan that stops and starts can be a wiring fault. Some vendor Klipper configs cap the hotend fan at 40 percent power.

fixes.advice: Replace or rewire the fan and run it at 100 percent. Bambu names a malfunctioning hotend cooling fan as a cause of an overheated heatsink.
Clean dust from the heatsink fins and check the fan duct is seated.

causes.name: Slow extrusion lets heat climb the filament
checks: Filament that moves slowly through the hotend has more time to soften above the melt zone.

fixes.advice: Extrude faster than the heat can creep up, or improve cooling at the top of the hotend. Reduce very long retractions, which drag molten plastic up into the cold zone.
Keep retraction at or under 1 mm on direct drive. Ellis notes high retraction can cause skipping and jams.

causes.name: Bed temperature and top glass cover
checks: Bed above the guideline for the material with the top glass cover fitted (Bambu table).

fixes.advice: Follow Bambu's table for the top glass. PLA 45 to 60 C, TPU 35 to 45 C, PVA 45 to 60 C should print with the upper glass removed. ABS, PETG, ASA, PC and PA keep the glass on in that table. Bambu recommends removing the top glass for PETG when the bed is above 70 C.
For soft filaments, lower the bed temperature when the plate allows it.

causes.name: Poor heatbreak contact or hotend assembly
checks: Prusa says stringing and clogs can come from poor heat dissipation between heatbreak and heatsink after a hotend change.

fixes.advice: Reassemble the hotend to the maker's instructions. On Prusa hotends, reapply thermal paste on the threads between the heatbreak and the heatsink, and confirm every part is in place.
On V6 style hotends, do not bottom the nozzle against the heater block. Reseat the heatbreak so it makes full contact.

data.name: Layer separation and cracking
camera_signs: Clean horizontal cracks along layer lines, often with an upward bend at the edge
Layers pulling apart on tall parts, especially on corners and thin walls
Gaps between the outer walls and inner walls (perimeter separation) on part of the print
Splits get worse higher up the part or near an open window or vent

q_material.ask: Is the material ABS, ASA, PC or nylon (high shrinkage), or printing in a cold room or a draft?

q_enclosure.ask: Is the printer enclosed with the door closed, part fan off or very low, and no draft?

q_temp.ask: Is the nozzle at the low end of the filament's range, or did you print fast without raising the temperature?

q_fan.ask: Is the part cooling fan high for this material, or did you raise it recently?

q_flow.ask: Do the walls have gaps between them or does the surface look thin, with flow not calibrated?

q_wet.ask: Is the filament wet (popping, rough surface) or a recently opened old spool?

causes.name: Cold room, draft or open chamber
checks: Prusa says ABS is highly susceptible when cold air blows on the print before it has cooled down.
Layers crack higher up as the part gets taller and cools faster than the layers below.

fixes.advice: Print ABS, ASA, PC and nylon in an enclosure with the door closed and no draft. Prusa suggests fans off completely for ABS. Consider PETG or ASA if the part is large, since ABS is prone to cracking.
Keep a stable ambient temperature. An open window or AC blowing at the printer increases splitting.

causes.name: Nozzle temperature too low
checks: Prusa says PLA can crack at too low a temperature. Ellis says high speed printing often needs a temperature bump.

fixes.why: Prusa raises the temperature in 5 C steps until the layers bond well. Stay inside the filament's range.

fixes.advice: If you raised part fan speed and layers started splitting, raise the nozzle temperature to compensate, per Prusa's warping guide.

causes.name: Too much part cooling
checks: Prusa says too high a fan speed can lift the part and reduce layer to layer adhesion.

fixes.advice: Lower the maximum part fan in steps. Less cooling keeps layers hot long enough to bond. Bambu's PETG profile runs the fan between 10 and 40 percent, and Prusa suggests turning the fan off completely for ABS.
Ellis says constant fan speed avoids banding and inconsistent bonding. Use a stable speed rather than big swings.

causes.name: Low flow or narrow wall lines
checks: Ellis says perimeters separate with narrow line widths, especially with layer heights above 50 percent of the nozzle diameter.
Under-extruded lines bond less. Prusa says more material creates a stronger bond between layers.

fixes.why: Prusa raises the extrusion multiplier in 5 percent steps for better layer bonding. Confirm with a flow test so you do not over-extrude.

fixes.advice: Check the outer wall line width is wide enough. A 100 percent line width does not work well above 50 percent layer height, per Ellis.
If the gaps are at the bottom, lower or disable elephant foot compensation. Too high a value makes perimeters print over nothing.

causes.name: Wet filament
checks: Popping at the nozzle and rough or pitted walls.

fixes.advice: Dry the filament for its material. Moisture weakens layer bonds and makes extrusion inconsistent. Bambu notes PETG and engineering materials are more sensitive.

causes.name: Hotend heat transfer or partial clog
checks: Layers bond poorly even at a correct temperature. Check the heater cartridge and thermistor, and look for a partial clog.

fixes.advice: Verify the nozzle temperature with a known good reading and run PID calibration on Klipper. Replace a worn heater cartridge, which Bambu says can cause persistent extrusion issues. Try a new nozzle, per Ellis.

data.name: Layer shift
camera_signs: The upper part of the print is offset sideways from the lower part along X, Y or both, as a sharp step on one side
Every layer above a certain height is shifted the same way (a single event), or the print drifts each layer (a rubbing belt)
A lifted corner or blob at the height where the shift begins, which points to a nozzle strike
Purge waste or a cable sitting in the toolhead path in a snapshot
log_signs: Bambu prints that report step loss and auto-recover (Auto-recovery from step loss option), or repeated motor or axis HMS prompts
Bambu HMS 0300 family motor faults such as 0300-0700-0001-0002 (motor short circuit) point at a motor or wiring problem
Klipper TMC driver errors such as 'Unable to read tmc uart' or a driver over temperature or reset in klippy.log
Klipper 'Lost communication with MCU' during the print, which can also cause a shifted or stopped print

q_axis.ask: Look at the shift. Is it a single sharp step at one height (rather than a gradual drift)?

q_strike.ask: Is there a curled corner, blob, purge waste or a loose cable at the height where it shifted?

q_speed_change.ask: Did you change speed mid print (for example Bambu Ludicrous mode) or print with very high acceleration or in a quiet or stealth mode?

q_gradual.ask: By hand with the motors off, does one axis feel rougher, or do belts show dust, fraying or rubbing on a pulley flange?

q_belts.ask: Are the belts noticeably loose or very tight, or does a pulley set screw move when you touch it?

q_electrical.ask: On Klipper or a printer with visible wiring, do the logs show TMC or MCU errors, or is the motor or driver hot to the touch?

causes.name: Nozzle strike or obstruction
checks: Move the toolhead by hand through X and Y with the printer off and watch for cable chains, tubes or purge waste in the path.
Look for a curled part or a blob at the failure height.

fixes.advice: Clear purge chute waste and tidy tubes and cables so nothing blocks the toolhead. Bambu lists purge waste, damaged toolhead cable chains and loose tubes as known causes.

fixes.why: Ellis says about 0.2 to 0.3 mm of z lift is usually enough to clear curling. Too much causes stringing.

fixes.advice: If the model warps, fix the warping first (see the warping troubleshooter). For PETG, drying the filament or enabling the prime tower reduces nozzle sticking.

causes.name: Speed or acceleration too high for the printer
checks: Check whether speed was raised during the print or acceleration is above what the machine can hold.
Prusa recommends normal mode rather than stealth mode for large or complex prints.

fixes.advice: Lower the default and outer wall acceleration in steps and re-test. Ellis and Prusa both point at speed and acceleration when a machine with sound belts still shifts.
Start the print at the speed profile you want to finish it at. Bambu notes that switching to Ludicrous mode mid print can cause a shift.
On Bambu printers, enable the Auto-recovery from step loss option so the printer re-homes and continues after a detected shift.
On Prusa, switch from stealth to normal mode for large prints.

causes.name: Belt tension, pulleys or axis binding
checks: Pull each belt and compare resistance. Look for belt dust that indicates rubbing or mis-routing. Belts should not ride against bearing flanges.
Check each motor pulley set screws. One of the two must sit on the flat of the motor shaft.
On CoreXY, move the toolhead along both diagonals. A rough diagonal points at that motor or its pulley.

fixes.advice: Set belt tension to the maker's method. Ellis measures about 120 Hz over a 150 mm span on Voron style machines and warns most people over tighten belts, while too loose can cause tooth skipping. On Prusa CORE One use the belt adjustment guide and keep the CoreXY square.
Tighten pulley grub screws with one on the flat of the shaft. Prusa lists loose pulleys as a common cause.
Loosen the belts, lift them off each bearing stack and spin every bearing by hand to find a rough one.
On Bambu X1 and P1 printers, clean the carbon rods, which Bambu lists as a way to reduce shifts.

causes.name: Motor current, wiring or driver overheating
checks: Check the Klipper log for TMC errors or MCU disconnects.
Wiggle-test wires in drag chains. Broken strands inside the insulation are invisible.
Confirm stepper drivers have heatsinks and airflow.

fixes.advice: Check the run_current for the X and Y motors against the motor datasheet and confirm the driver cooling. Ellis recommends high strand count wire of 24 AWG or thicker in drag chains, and checking crimps and continuity.
If Klipper reports 'Lost communication with MCU', check for host serial interference and cabling before touching print settings.

causes.name: Dirty or dry guide rails
checks: The toolhead or bed feels gritty when moved by hand, or makes noise at the same position each pass.

fixes.advice: Clean and relubricate rails or rods using the maker's instructions. Bambu lists cleaning the carbon rods on X1 and P1 machines as a way to reduce shifts.

data.name: Over-extrusion
camera_signs: Rough, ridged or bumpy top surface with lines merged together or humped
Walls look wider than the design, corners bulge outward, small holes closed up
Solid infill lines pushing into the walls from the inside, with bumps on the outer wall
Rounded, blobby corners and first layer that looks glassy and squashed with ridges at the edges

q_where.ask: Is the extra plastic mainly on the first layer (squashed, ridged, elephant foot), rather than on every layer?

q_corners.ask: Do bulges show mainly at corners, seams or where the walls change direction, rather than along straight lines?

q_small_areas.ask: Is it mostly small infill areas, single top layer patches or areas right next to walls?

q_flow_calibrated.ask: Have you calibrated the flow ratio for this exact filament, and does the extruder distance check out (100 mm requested equals 100 mm extruded)?

q_temperature.ask: Is the nozzle running hot for this filament, or is the filament wet so it foams and swells?

causes.name: First layer squished too hard
checks: Bottom layers look glassy with raised ridges at line edges, and the first layer is much wider than the part.

fixes.advice: Raise the Z offset slightly (nozzle further from the plate) until the first layer lines just touch without gaps. Ellis says leaning toward slightly more squish is fine, but too much causes ridges and elephant foot. See the first_layer troubleshooter.

fixes.why: Orca's Bambu profiles use 0.5 mm as the first layer line width for a 0.4 mm nozzle. Ellis suggests 120 percent or more for adhesion, so go wider only if adhesion needs it.

causes.name: Pressure advance too low
checks: Bulges at every corner and at line starts, but straight walls look correct.

fixes.advice: Run pressure advance (Bambu: flow dynamics) calibration for this filament, temperature and speed. Klipper and Ellis both say to tune pressure advance before the flow ratio.

fixes.why: Pressure advance must be on for calibrated values to apply.

causes.name: Solid infill over-filling small areas
checks: Bumps on the outer wall line up with where solid infill meets it, or small top patches look over-filled. Ellis notes some of this is normal.

fixes.advice: Lower the infill and wall overlap. Bambu's layer line guide gives a change from 15 percent to a lower or even negative value as an example, and Ellis suggests roughly 20 to 25 percent encroachment as a floor before infill disconnects from the walls.
Slow the top surface speed and top surface acceleration. Ellis saw diminishing returns below about 2000 mm/s2 on his printer.

fixes.why: Printing the outer wall first can help with bulging layers and extrusion consistency. It can hurt steep overhangs.

causes.name: Flow ratio too high
checks: Print a flow test cube with several top layers and look for ridges on the top surface. Any gaps mean too little flow, ridges and pillows mean too much.

fixes.why: Lower flow in 1 to 2 percent steps until top lines just touch. Ellis tunes after pressure advance.
