fixes.advice: Run the slicer's built in flow rate calibration and keep the result per filament and per brand, or per spool if the diameter varies.

causes.name: Nozzle too hot or wet filament
checks: Popping or steam at the nozzle, or filament that oozes and looks glossy and swollen.

fixes.why: Runny plastic spreads wider. Prusa suggests 5 to 10 C lower for stringing, the same fix applies here.

fixes.advice: Dry the filament. Moisture vaporizes in the nozzle and causes bubbles and uneven flow.

causes.name: Extruder not calibrated
checks: Mark 120 mm of filament, extrude 100 mm, and measure what was consumed. Klipper printers use rotation_distance for this.

fixes.advice: Calibrate the extruder so 100 mm requested is 100 mm extruded before tuning flow. Ellis says do this first, and adjust backlash or gear wear if patterns repeat along the walls.

data.name: Pillowing and top surface holes
camera_signs: Top surface has holes, pits or gaps between lines, with sparse infill pattern showing through
Top surface is bumpy or pillow shaped, humping between infill lines
Top layer lines look thin or separate, and some areas are shiny while others are rough
Ridges and blobs on the top surface, with a rough finish after ironing

q_sparse.ask: Are the holes or pillows only over sparse infill, with solid areas fine?

q_top_layers.ask: Are there fewer than 5 top shell layers, or is the infill density very low (under about 15 percent)?

q_cooling.ask: Is the part cooling fan low, off, or blocked on the top layers, or is the layer time very short?

q_flow.ask: Do gaps show even over solid areas, with lines that do not touch each other?

q_wet.ask: Is the filament wet, or is the top pattern making bumps or ridges (over-extrusion)?

causes.name: Too few top layers or too little infill support
checks: The first top layers bridge across sparse infill gaps. Bambu's standard 0.20 mm profile uses 5 top layers, the Orca default is 3.

fixes.why: Bambu's 0.20 mm Standard profile uses 5 top shell layers, the Orca default is 3. Thinner layers need more of them to cover the same height.

fixes.advice: Raise the infill density or use a pattern with less open area under the top. More top layers and denser infill are the standard cures for pillowing, per vendor guides (low confidence).

causes.name: Top layers cooling too slowly
checks: Fan is low on the last layers, small tops have very short layer times, or the fan is blocked.

fixes.advice: Increase part cooling on the top layers and check the fan and duct are clear. Prusa says to check the print fan works and the shroud is not obstructed or melted.

fixes.why: Small tops need time to cool. Bambu PETG and Prusa PETG profiles use a minimum layer time near 8 to 12 seconds.

fixes.advice: Print more parts at once or add a sacrificial part to lengthen layer time. Ellis notes short layers are printed onto soft layers.

causes.name: Flow too low or under-extrusion on top
checks: Gaps between top lines even where solid layers sit underneath. Ellis says there should be no gaps or holes in top solid surfaces.

fixes.why: Ellis tunes the extrusion multiplier with cubes in 1 to 2 percent steps until the top closes with no gaps.

fixes.advice: Check for a partial clog or extruder skipping if the gaps come and go. See the under_extrusion troubleshooter.

causes.name: Wet filament or over-extruded top
checks: Pockmarks and pits with popping at the nozzle point to moisture. Ridges and humps point to too much flow.

fixes.advice: Dry the filament. Ellis says pockmarks are caused by moisture turning to steam and popping, and sealed spools can be wet.
Run a flow test and lower the flow ratio if the top is ridged. See the over_extrusion troubleshooter.

causes.name: Top surface line width, pattern or speed
checks: A monotonic top pattern with a narrow top line width and slow top speed gives the cleanest top, per Ellis' extrusion test setup.

fixes.why: Ellis tests top surfaces with a monotonic pattern, which gives consistent line direction.

fixes.advice: Slow the top surface speed. Ellis uses about 60 mm/s for top solid infill in his flow test and says keeping it low to moderate helps surface finish.
Ironing does not repair a bad top surface. Fix holes and flow first, then use ironing for polish (low confidence vendor guidance).

data.name: Poor overhangs and bridges
camera_signs: Underside of an overhang or an arch looks rough, droops or has loose strands
Bridges sag in the middle, or bridge lines are separated and stringy
Outer edges of steep overhangs curl upward into the nozzle path
Surface above supports is rough or has gaps
log_signs: A print that stops with extrusion resistance or spaghetti detection after a curled overhang is struck by the nozzle

q_angle.ask: Is the overhang shallower than about 45 degrees from the bed (more horizontal), with no supports under it?

q_bridge.ask: Is the problem mainly on flat bridges that span a gap, rather than on angled walls?

q_bridge_length.ask: Is the bridge long (more than a few centimeters), fast, or printed with high flow?

q_fan.ask: Is the part cooling fan weak, blocked or set low on overhangs, or the nozzle above the material's usual range?

q_curling.ask: Do the overhang edges curl upward and get hit by the nozzle?

causes.name: Overhang too shallow for no support
checks: Bambu treats overhang angles below 45 degrees from the bed as needing supports, and above 45 degrees as fine without.

fixes.why: Bambu recommends enabling supports when the overhang angle is under 45 degrees.

fixes.advice: Reorient the part so the overhang is steeper, or split the model. Prusa's rule of thumb is to rotate the part until bridges and supports are avoided.
Use normal supports for heavy overhangs and tree supports for detailed or irregular models, per Bambu's guide.

causes.name: Bridge speed, flow or length
checks: Sag in the middle of a long bridge, or lines pulled apart.

fixes.advice: Lower the bridge speed and the bridge flow ratio so the line is pulled taut behind the nozzle. Prusa advises printing a bridging test with several flow values in one plate to find the best value.
Lower the bridge flow ratio in small steps. Prusa says the first bridging layer should print with lower flow, and to test several values on one plate.
Lower the bridge speed. Prusa recommends slower bridges and lower bridge flow together.
For a very long bridge, add a support enforcer partway across so the span is shorter, as Prusa suggests.

causes.name: Weak cooling or nozzle too hot on overhangs
checks: The fan is running, its duct is clear, and the fan is set high on overhangs. Prusa says to check the fan is working and the shroud is not obstructed.

fixes.why: Bambu profiles run the overhang fan at 90 percent for PETG and Bambu's overhang guide uses 100 percent for PLA. Keep it high where the material allows.
Bambu suggests lowering the nozzle temperature by about 5 to 10 C for steep overhangs, staying inside the filament's range.
Bambu's overhang guide recommends slowing down for overhangs so cooling has time to work.

fixes.advice: On Prusa, check the print fan and shroud are not melted or blocked. On Bambu, check the aux fan and door or lid settings.

causes.name: Curling edges strike the nozzle
checks: Edges of overhangs curl up, and the nozzle hits them on the next pass.

fixes.why: Ellis says about 0.2 to 0.3 mm of z lift is usually enough to clear curling. Too much causes stringing.
Slows the nozzle over curled edges so it is less likely to knock the part.

fixes.advice: Cool the layer more and lower the nozzle temperature a little. Ellis also lists overheating as a cause of curling and shifts.

causes.name: Rough surface above supports
checks: Prusa treats the surface above supports like a bridge, so it needs the same care. Check the support z gap, interface layers and fan on the interface.

fixes.advice: Tune the support top Z distance and the number of interface layers. A smaller gap and denser interface give a smoother underside but make removal harder. Change one at a time.
On Prusa, make sure detect bridging perimeters is on and raise the fan on those surfaces. Prusa notes the bridge fan has material limits.

data.name: Ringing and ghosting
camera_signs: Repeating ripples or echoes of a sharp corner, letter or hole trailing along the wall behind it
Ripples follow the shape of the feature and fade over several millimeters
Worse on one axis or at the far side of the bed
Vertical lines with steady spacing (VFAs) or wood grain that do not follow the feature shape are a different problem
log_signs: Klipper: no error. Check that [input_shaper] exists in printer.cfg and SHAPER_CALIBRATE or the ringing tower has been run
Bambu: none specific. Motion accuracy or vibration compensation calibration can be run from the printer menu

q_pattern.ask: Do the ripples follow the outline of a corner or letter and fade with distance from it?

q_tight.ask: Are belts, pulleys, frame screws and the printer feet tight, and is the printer on a firm surface?

q_speed_accel.ask: Do you print at high speed and acceleration (above what the machine profile normally uses), or with heavy moving mass?

q_shaper.ask: Is input shaping, vibration compensation or motion calibration available and already tuned for this printer?

causes.name: Loose belts, pulleys or frame
checks: Klipper says ringing usually has a mechanical origin: an insufficiently rigid frame, belts that are loose or too springy, misalignment or heavy moving mass. Fix those before tuning input shaping.
On Prusa, pluck the belt like a guitar string. It should make a low bass tone. On MK3 style machines the LCD belt status between 240 and 300 is fine.

fixes.advice: Set belt tension per the maker's guide, tighten pulley set screws and frame screws, and place the printer on a heavy, stable surface. Ellis warns against over tightening: very tight belts cause VFAs, and CoreXY belts of about 110 Hz over 150 mm are a starting point on Voron machines.

causes.name: Speed or acceleration too high
checks: Prusa says ghosting comes from vibrations that grow with print speed. If ringing is only on outer walls, lower acceleration there.

fixes.advice: Lower the outer wall acceleration in steps and re-test. Klipper's ringing tower makes ringing worse on purpose by raising acceleration every 5 mm of height, so the same sensitivity shows in normal prints.
Reduce outer wall speed to see if the ghosting disappears. Prusa says ghosting is caused by vibrations that increase with print speed.
Ellis lists reducing perimeter accelerations for bulging and ringing at corners. Do not raise Klipper square_corner_velocity above 5 mm/s when using input shaper, since it adds smoothing.

causes.name: Input shaping not run
checks: No [input_shaper] section in Klipper, or default values that were never measured for this printer.

fixes.advice: Klipper: print the ringing tower, measure the ringing frequency on each axis, and set shaper_freq_x and shaper_freq_y. MZV or EI are the usual choices. Compare them on a second tower, then pick max_accel from the ringing and smoothing balance. Re-tune pressure advance afterward.
Bambu: run the motion or vibration compensation calibration from the printer menu after moving or servicing the machine. Only the wiki page title was confirmed.
If the resonance frequency is very low (about 20 to 25 Hz), stiffen the printer or reduce moving mass before shaping. Klipper says shaping alone will smooth too much at those frequencies.

causes.name: Shaper smoothing or wrong shaper
checks: Klipper: an EI shaper smooths more than MZV. Rounded corners with little ringing mean too much smoothing.

fixes.advice: Klipper: choose the shaper by test, not habit. MZV is recommended if no ringing shows, EI is more robust to changing bed mass, and 2HUMP_EI only makes sense above about 50 to 60 Hz. Set max_accel from the point where the 0.15 mm gap in the test wall starts to widen.
Ellis notes input shaper conflicts can cause bulges at STL vertices. Disable and retune it if you see those.

causes.name: VFAs, extruder patterns or axis mechanics (not true ringing)
checks: Klipper says if the pattern does not follow the curved notches of the test, it is not ringing. Vertical stripes about 2 mm apart point at belt, pulley or idler teeth.

fixes.advice: For vertical stripes, check belt tension (Ellis says belts too tight cause VFAs), belt rubbing on flanges, dirty or poor quality pulleys, idlers and bearings. Diagonal or wood grain patterns can be extruder gear backlash or axis mechanics. See the z_banding troubleshooter.
Inspect extruder gear backlash and gear wear when the pattern repeats along extrusion lines.

data.name: Seam, blobs and zits
camera_signs: A vertical line or row of small bumps (a seam) running up one side of the part
Small blobs or pimples at layer starts and ends, or at corners
A gap or divot at the seam, or an outward bulge where the loop closes
Random pimples scattered across walls (seam set to random, moisture, or a dirty nozzle)

q_random.ask: Are the blobs scattered all over the walls rather than lined up in one column?

q_wet_nozzle.ask: Is the seam set to random, or do you hear popping, or is there burnt plastic stuck on the nozzle?

q_type.ask: Is the seam a raised blob at the start of the loop, or a gap or dent where it starts?

q_pa.ask: Has pressure advance (flow dynamics) been calibrated for this filament, and is travel speed and acceleration set high for the printer?

q_retract_threshold.ask: Do small travel moves trigger retraction (minimum travel under about 2 mm), and is wipe before the external wall off?

causes.name: Random seam, wet filament or dirty nozzle
checks: Ellis says pockmarks come from moisture turning to steam, and that the seam should not be random.
Look for a burnt brown crust on the nozzle.

fixes.why: A random seam scatters blobs over the whole wall. Aligned lines them up so they are easier to hide. Orca lists random as best for strength only.

fixes.advice: Dry the filament (extrude in the air and listen for popping). Clean the nozzle and replace it if pockmarks persist, as Ellis suggests.

causes.name: Pressure advance not calibrated
checks: Orca says a too low pressure advance leaves excess pressure at the end of the previous extrusion, which increases ooze during travel and makes a blob at the seam start.

fixes.advice: Run pressure advance (Bambu: flow dynamics) calibration for this filament. On Klipper, Ellis says tune pressure advance before extrusion multiplier.

fixes.why: Calibrated values only apply when pressure advance is on.

causes.name: Retraction, wipe and travel around the seam
checks: Orca notes the start of a seam depends on extrusion control after a travel move. Short travels that retract and de-retract add variation.
Klipper says not to use coasting, which makes blobbing worse. Retract, wipe and wipe on retract are fine.

fixes.advice: Raise the travel distance threshold so small moves do not retract, Orca suggests 2 to 4 mm as a starting point when pressure advance is tuned.

fixes.why: Orca suggests a 2 to 4 mm travel threshold so short moves skip retraction.

fixes.advice: Enable wipe before external perimeters, which moves the de-retraction inside the part so a blob is less visible. Raise travel speed and travel acceleration as far as the printer allows.

fixes.why: Wiping while retracting helps hide ooze at the seam.

causes.name: Seam position or scarf joint not used
checks: The seam is in a visible spot, or on a curved face where it cannot be hidden.

fixes.why: The scarf joint seam ramps the flow at the start and end of each loop for a smoother overlap. Orca documents it as a seam appearance option.
Aligned back prefers hidden spots away from the front. Orca says aligned, aligned back or back work best for looks.

fixes.advice: Use seam painting to place the seam in a concave corner or on the back, and check the wall order since outer wall first or last changes the seam look.

causes.name: Seam is where the loop meets itself
checks: A column of bumps is in the same place on every layer. That is normal to some degree, since every loop starts and ends somewhere.

fixes.advice: You cannot remove a seam in normal printing, only hide or tune it. Use aligned back, seam painting, or a scarf joint, and consider staggered inner seams if the seam is strong enough to show.

fixes.why: Spreads the inner wall seams so they do not stack into a weak line.

data.name: Spaghetti (detached print)
camera_signs: A tangled pile of filament where the part should be, with extrusion continuing in the air
The part has fallen over, is loose on the plate or is missing from the plate
Corners lifting with the nozzle crashing into them, or a collapsed overhang or support
Filament wrapped around the nozzle or a large blob on the hotend
log_signs: Bambu spaghetti detection alerts and pauses
Bambu HMS 1200-2000-0002-0006 family on A1 series with AMS lite: air printing detected, the printer cuts the filament and pauses
Bambu HMS 0300-0900-0002-0004: abnormal extrusion resistance during a print
Klipper: a print that keeps running after the part fell off has no error. Use the camera or a filament runout sensor

q_when.ask: Did it fail in the first few layers (rather than after the part had grown for a while)?

q_first_layer_state.ask: Did the first layer look loose, thin or dragged around before it failed?

q_feed.ask: Did the extruder click or the filament stop feeding when it started to fail?

q_mid_cause.ask: Did you see a corner lift or the base peel before it fell?

q_support.ask: Did an overhang, bridge or support collapse (an unsupported or steep part)?

q_clunk.ask: Did the nozzle knock the part or a tall thin part topple over (a clunk, or a small contact area)?

causes.name: First layer did not stick
checks: Bambu says the direct cause of first layer spaghetti is that filament does not stick firmly to the plate.
Clean the plate, match the plate type, run bed leveling, and check filament moisture.

fixes.advice: Wash the plate with warm water and dish soap and handle it by the edges. Confirm the plate type in the slicer matches the plate installed. Run Auto Bed Leveling and check the plate sits flat with no debris behind it.

fixes.why: Bambu recommends an initial layer speed of 30 mm/s or less.
Bambu recommends 60 mm/s or less for first layer infill.

fixes.advice: Dry the filament. Water vapor in the nozzle causes uneven extrusion that hurts first layer adhesion.

causes.name: Corner lift or detachment mid print
checks: Bambu says corners slowly lift and the nozzle finally knocks the model loose. High shrinkage filaments (ABS, ASA, PC, PA) are the most common.

fixes.why: A brim gives more first layer adhesion. Bambu recommends it for spaghetti caused by warping.

fixes.advice: Clean the plate, verify the plate type, run bed leveling, and see the warping troubleshooter for enclosure and cooling.

causes.name: Overhang or support collapse
checks: Bambu says overhangs with more than 45 degrees of unsupported angle without supports, or with too little cooling, can collapse.

fixes.why: Enable supports where overhangs are under 45 degrees from the bed, as Bambu advises.
Slows the nozzle on overhangs. Bambu lists this as a spaghetti fix.

fixes.advice: Slow the support and support interface speeds, and switch to normal (auto) support for a better interface if needed.

causes.name: Nozzle knocks the part or the model is unstable
checks: A clunk during the print, or a tall thin model or one with a small contact patch that tips over.

fixes.why: Bambu says a Normal z hop lift can clear the part when the nozzle scrapes it in travel.
A brim widens the contact area. Bambu recommends 5 to 8 mm and wider for smaller footprints.
Bambu suggests 5 to 8 mm.

fixes.advice: For thin or branching parts, paint extra support to stabilize them. Bambu suggests paint-on supports for tall or unstable shapes.

causes.name: Feed failure or clog leaving air printing
checks: The extruder clicks or stops feeding, the spool tangles, or the AMS does not feed. Bambu A1 series with AMS lite detects air printing from the extruder distance and the AMS odometer.

fixes.advice: Check the spool for tangles, the PTFE for kinks, and the nozzle for a clog. See the clog and ams_jam troubleshooters.
Use Skip Objects on Bambu printers to cancel only the failed part on a multi-part plate and let the rest finish.

data.name: Stringing
camera_signs: Thin threads or wisps stretched between separate towers, posts or islands
Fine hairs across open gaps, holes or the inside of an arch
Small blobs or a fringe of hair at the start of travel moves and at the seam
Threads that are worse on one spool or one material (PETG, TPU and wet spools string most)

q_wet.ask: Did you hear popping or hissing at the nozzle, see tiny bubbles in the strands, or has this spool been open for weeks (more so if it is PETG, nylon or TPU)?

q_idle_ooze.ask: When the hot nozzle sits idle, does plastic keep dripping, or is there melted plastic leaking around the nozzle threads or heatbreak?

q_retraction_on.ask: Is retraction enabled with a length above zero in the active printer profile (Bambu, Prusa and Orca profiles turn it on by default)?

q_hot.ask: Is the nozzle temperature in the top half of the filament's range, or above the maker's recommendation?

q_travel.ask: Are the strings mostly across long open travel moves, with a low travel speed or a high minimum travel threshold?

q_extruder_play.ask: With the nozzle cold and the extruder motor off, is there a dead zone when you reverse the filament by hand, or does the motor shaft turn without moving filament?

causes.name: Wet filament
checks: Extrude a few centimeters in the air at the print temperature and listen for popping or watch for steam.
Look for rough, pitted walls in the same print. Sealed spools can also arrive wet.

fixes.advice: Dry the spool using the drying table for its material, then print from a dry box or a sealed AMS slot. Wet filament can cause near unfixable stringing.

causes.name: Leaking or loose hotend
checks: Heat the nozzle and look for plastic seeping at the nozzle to heater block joint or around the heatbreak.
A nozzle that is bottomed out against the heater block on a V6 style hotend means the heatbreak is not seated far enough.

fixes.advice: Hot tighten the nozzle to the maker's torque spec and reseat the heatbreak so it makes full contact. Clean off old plastic first. On Bambu printers, re-tighten the two hotend screws and check the silicone sock area for skew or contamination.
After many hours of one material such as PETG, clean the nozzle exterior thoroughly. A film of old plastic on the tip drags strings onto the part.

causes.name: Retraction disabled or far too low
checks: Check the printer profile retraction length. Zero or a value copied from a bowden profile onto a direct drive machine (or the reverse) is the usual mistake.
In Klipper, do not use coasting or extra restart distance. Klipper's slicer notes say retract, wipe and wipe on retract are fine.

fixes.why: On direct drive Ellis starts at 0.5 mm at 35 mm/s and tries to stay under 1 mm. Bowden machines start near 1 mm.
Wiping while retracting is recommended by Prusa and helps hide ooze.

causes.name: Nozzle too hot
checks: Compare the nozzle temperature with the filament's recommended range. A second spool of the same brand at a lower temperature is the cleanest test.

fixes.why: Cooler plastic is less runny while the nozzle travels. Prusa suggests trying 5 to 10 C lower.

causes.name: Slow travel or long crossing moves
checks: In the slicer preview, look for travel lines crossing open air between the stringing features.

fixes.why: Routes travel inside the part where any ooze is hidden. Ellis notes it costs slicing and print time, so it is worth turning on mainly for PETG.

fixes.advice: Raise travel speed and travel acceleration to what the printer profile allows so the nozzle spends less time oozing. Orca's seam guide says to make travel as fast as the printer can manage.

fixes.why: Ellis found z hop above about 0.3 mm makes stringing worse.

fixes.advice: A high minimum travel after retraction lets short hops skip the retraction and ooze. Prusa notes a preset of 1 mm is low and that raising it increases oozing.

causes.name: Extruder backlash or loose gear
checks: Turn the extruder by hand and reverse. A clear dead zone points at gear backlash, a loose grub screw or a worn gear.
Check that the tension screw is not over or under tightened.

fixes.advice: Tighten the extruder gear grub screw onto the flat of the motor shaft and set a small amount of gear backlash. Too much backlash upsets retraction and pressure advance.
On Bambu printers, inspect the extruder idler and feed gear for wear or filament dust and clean it. If the gear is worn, replace the extruder.

causes.name: Pressure advance too low or not calibrated
checks: Bulged corners, or a pressure blob after each corner or seam, suggest pressure is not being controlled.

fixes.advice: Run pressure advance (Bambu: flow dynamics) calibration for this exact filament. A too low value leaves excess pressure in the nozzle at the end of each line.

data.name: Under-extrusion
camera_signs: Visible gaps between wall lines, thin or see-through walls, sparse or stringy infill
Top surface not fully covered, with gaps between the lines
Missing or partial layers at random heights, or a print that gets worse as it goes
Filament curling to the side or sticking to the outside of the nozzle when extruding by hand
Ground or flattened filament near the extruder gear
log_signs: Bambu HMS 0300-0900-0002-0004 (extrusion resistance abnormal) and 0300-1A00-0002-0002 (force sensor detects clog) on printers with those sensors
Bambu HMS 12xx-2000-0002-0006 family ('failed to extrude AMS filament, extruder may be clogged') on A1 series with AMS lite
Klipper heater warnings such as 'not heating at expected rate' point to a temperature problem instead of a flow one
Flow dynamics or pressure advance calibration giving very different K values run to run, which Bambu links to an inconsistent flow from a partial clog

q_extruder.ask: Do you hear clicking or see the extruder gear skipping or grinding the filament?

q_partial_clog.ask: When you extrude by hand at print temperature, does the filament come out curled or sideways, or is there strong resistance?

q_spool_path.ask: Does the spool turn freely, with no tangle, kink in the PTFE tube, or bent buffer or AMS path?

q_grip.ask: Is the filament worn or dented at the gear, or is the extruder tension or idler too loose or too tight?

q_hotend_fan.ask: Is the hotend cooling fan running at full speed, and does it stop and start?

q_wet.ask: Does the filament pop, or has it been out of dry storage for weeks?

q_speed.ask: Are you printing fast with thick layers, wide lines or a filament that needs more heat (near the maximum volumetric speed)?

causes.name: Partial nozzle clog
checks: Heat the nozzle a little above the filament's normal temperature and extrude by hand. It should come out straight and steady.
Bambu notes a partial clog can make flow dynamics calibration give an inconsistent K value.

fixes.advice: Clear the nozzle using the printer's official unclogging guide (manual extrude, pin tool, then a cold pull). If it clogs again quickly, replace the nozzle. Ellis says try a new nozzle first, since it is often a partial clog.
Check the filament diameter with calipers along the length. Bambu recommends 1.75 plus or minus 0.03 mm and clean, impurity free filament.

causes.name: Restricted feed path
checks: Pull filament by hand from the spool to the extruder and feel for drag. Look for kinked or collapsed PTFE, a jammed AMS buffer spring, or a spool catching on a holder.
With an AMS, print once from an external spool. If quality is fine, the AMS path or internal hub is at fault.

fixes.advice: Replace any bent or deformed PTFE tube between the AMS, buffer and toolhead. Check the buffer spring moves freely and the filament is not tangled on the spool.
Print from an external spool to isolate the AMS. Bambu suggests checking the internal hub if the external spool prints fine.
With direct drive, use a reverse bowden tube from the spool if pulling from a dry box adds drag.

causes.name: Extruder grip or tension
checks: Look for filament dust or worn dents at the drive gear.
Yank on the filament while it feeds. If it slips easily, tension is too loose. Too tight also causes skipping.

fixes.advice: Clean debris out of the feed gear grooves. On Prusa, set the idler tension screws so the tips are level with the front of the idler nut. On DIY extruders tighten the tension screw until the filament stops slipping, then about 1 to 2 more turns.
Check the gear grub screw is tight on the motor shaft. If the motor turns normally but the filament does not move, the gear or screw is the likely fault.

causes.name: Hotend fan not cooling the heatbreak
checks: Confirm the hotend fan spins at full speed and does not start or stop. Some vendor Klipper configs cap max_power at 0.4 for the hotend fan.
Touch test the heatsink after a long print. It should not be hot to hold.

fixes.advice: Replace or rewire a slow or stopping hotend fan and make sure it runs at 100 percent. See the heat_creep troubleshooter.

causes.name: Wet filament
checks: Extrude in the air and listen for popping or watch for steam. Sealed spools can be wet.

fixes.advice: Dry the filament for its material and print from a dry box. Bambu notes moisture vaporizes in the nozzle causing bubbles, poor flow and rough surfaces.

causes.name: Volumetric flow limit exceeded
checks: Under-extrusion appears only in fast, wide, thick parts such as infill and solid layers, and improves when you slow the same model.
Bambu warns printing too fast (for example Ludicrous mode) may not leave enough time to melt the plastic.

fixes.advice: Lower the filament max volumetric speed, or run a max flow test to find it for this filament and nozzle, so fast thick sections slow down enough for the hotend to keep up.

fixes.why: A little more heat lets the filament melt faster at high flow. Stay inside the material range. Ellis notes high speed printing often needs a temperature bump.

causes.name: Flow ratio too low or pressure advance off
checks: Top surface has gaps even at slow speeds and the extruder sounds normal.

fixes.why: Nudge flow up. Ellis tunes extrusion multiplier with cubes in 1 to 2 percent steps after calibrating the extruder and pressure advance.

fixes.advice: Redo pressure advance (Bambu: flow dynamics) calibration for this filament, since a wrong value causes thin starts and bulged ends of lines.

data.name: Warping and corner lift
camera_signs: Corners or edges of the first layers curl up off the plate, leaving a visible gap under the part
The base looks bowed or rounded in a side view of a flat part
The part sits at an angle or has detached from the plate
Bulges on the outer wall above a lifted corner where extra plastic squeezed sideways
log_signs: Bambu HMS 0300 family prompts about a heatbed force sensor disturbance (for example 0300-0A00-0001-0004) can point at the plate not seated or debris under it, which also causes lift
Klipper or Bambu logs may show a print that stops with a nozzle collision or extrusion resistance error after a corner lifts into the nozzle path

q_material.ask: Is the material a high shrinkage type (ABS, ASA, PC, PA, and carbon fiber filled versions), or is it a large flat part?

q_enclosed.ask: Is the printer enclosed or in a stable warm room, with no draft, open window or air conditioner blowing on it?

q_plate_clean.ask: Was the plate washed recently (dish soap and water, or 90 percent IPA) and handled by the edges?

q_plate_setting.ask: Does the plate type and bed temperature in the slicer match the plate and filament you are using?

q_first_layer.ask: Does the first layer look flat, continuous and slightly squished with no gaps between lines?

q_cooling.ask: Does the lift start at thin corners, small overhangs or supported contact points while the part fan is high?

causes.name: Drafts or cold chamber air
checks: Check for open windows, air conditioning, or a fan pointed at the printer.
On printers with adaptive airflow (P2S, X2D), cold chamber air blowing straight on the part in cooling mode can drive first layer and support interface warping.

fixes.advice: Close the door and top lid for ABS, ASA, PC and PA. Keep PLA and PETG in a cooler, open setup, since they need strong part cooling. Prusa says an enclosure is not a good idea for PLA or PETG.
On P2S and X2D, print and fit the Bambu air deflector when printing PETG, so cold chamber air is not aimed at the part.

fixes.why: A draft shield or skirt holds heat around high shrinkage prints, which Prusa recommends for PC blend, ASA and ABS.

causes.name: Dirty or oily build plate
checks: Fingerprints, hand cream, glue residue or dust show as a dull or shiny patch where the part lifted first.

fixes.advice: Wash with warm water and dish soap, dry or air dry, and hold the plate by its edges afterward. Ellis notes IPA does not remove oils well. Prusa recommends 90 percent IPA for routine cleaning and a dish soap wash when adhesion fades.

causes.name: Wrong plate type or bed temperature
checks: Bambu heatbed temperature depends on the plate type chosen in the slicer, and a wrong choice leaves the bed too cool.

fixes.advice: Set the plate type in the slicer to the plate actually installed, then use that plate's temperature for the filament.
If the material still lifts, raise the bed temperature slightly. Prusa suggests 5 to 10 C hotter for stubborn materials.

causes.name: Poor first layer squish
checks: Look for sparse, thin or rounded first layer lines. That means the nozzle is too high or the bed is not level at that spot.

fixes.advice: Run automatic bed leveling and check the plate is seated flat with nothing under it. See the first_layer troubleshooter for Z offset and mesh steps.

fixes.why: Bambu recommends a first layer speed of 30 mm/s or less to help bonding.

fixes.advice: Do not over squish to fix adhesion. Prusa warns that too low a Z offset can damage the sheet.

causes.name: Too much part cooling on small features
checks: Lift starts high on the part or at thin, tall corners rather than at the very first layer.

fixes.advice: Lower the maximum part fan in steps. Prusa warns too much fan can lift the whole object, and suggests 10 to 20 percent fan even for ABS or PC blend when small overhangs warp.
If layer bonding weakens after lowering the fan, raise the nozzle temperature a little instead of restoring the fan.
Print more parts at once or add a small sacrificial part to lengthen layer time, and use a constant fan speed to avoid banding.

causes.name: No brim or too little contact area
checks: Small footprint, sharp corners or tall thin walls on a large part with high shrinkage lift first.

fixes.why: A brim adds first layer grip. Bambu recommends an outer brim 5 to 8 mm wide for small contact areas.
Wider brims hold small footprints better. Bambu suggests 5 to 8 mm.

fixes.advice: Orient the problem corners toward the center of the bed and slow the print down, since Prusa reports slower speed reduces warping in high shrinkage materials.
Use a thin layer of glue stick on the plate. Prusa notes it helps adhesion and also acts as a separation layer for PETG, ABS and ASA.

data.name: Z banding
camera_signs: Horizontal ridges or bands that repeat at a regular height along the Z axis, on all sides of the part
Bands only on one side of the part or a single visible line at a fixed height (a cooling or geometry event, not the Z axis)
Alternating thick and thin layers, visible on tall smooth walls
Sudden ring or ridge right after a bridge, an infill to solid transition or a color change
log_signs: Klipper: no errors are expected. Check the config for the Z motor rotation_distance, microsteps and lead screw pitch
Bambu: none specific. Flow dynamics or bed mesh warnings do not usually explain regular banding

q_regular.ask: Do the bands repeat at a steady spacing on every side of the part?

q_z_hardware.ask: Does the Z lead screw or rod look bent or dirty, or does the bed or gantry wobble sideways as it moves?

q_layer_height.ask: Is the layer height not a whole multiple of the Z motor step distance, or is this a Klipper machine with an unverified rotation_distance or lead screw pitch?

q_one_place.ask: Do the ridges start at a fixed feature (after a bridge, where infill turns solid, or where the wall thickness changes)?

q_flow_temp.ask: Do the bands look like alternating thick and thin lines regardless of height, with uneven top surfaces?

causes.name: Z axis lead screw or alignment
checks: Remove the lead screw and roll it on a flat surface. Wobble means it is bent.
Look for dry threads, a loose coupler, or a lead screw nut that binds when the gantry moves.

fixes.advice: Replace a bent lead screw, clean and relubricate the screw, and align the Z axis so the screw carries no sideways load. Tighten the coupler and the lead nut mounting.
On Klipper machines with belts on Z, check Z belt tension is roughly equal across the drives. Ellis tensions his Z belts to 140 Hz over a 150 mm span.

causes.name: Layer height not matched to Z motor steps
checks: Compare the layer height with the Z motor full step size. A layer height that is not a whole multiple of it makes layers slightly uneven.

fixes.advice: Use layer heights that are whole multiples of the Z motor full step distance, and check the lead screw pitch, rotation_distance and microstep values in the printer configuration.

causes.name: Cooling and layer time change at a feature
checks: Ridges sit right after a bridge, at an infill to solid layer change, or at the transition from a wide base to thin walls. Prusa's Benchy hull line has the same cause and is usually not hardware.

fixes.advice: Lower the overhang and bridge fan speed a bit, use a gyroid or concentric infill, and reduce infill and wall overlap. Bambu reports these reduce the shrinkage ridge but may not remove it.
Print several parts at once to lengthen layer time, or add small fillets or chamfers inside a box model so the bridge does not touch the outer wall.
Use a constant fan speed. Ellis notes varying fan speed during the print causes inconsistent layers and banding.

causes.name: Inconsistent extrusion
checks: Wood grain or repeating patterns along walls, sounds of gear backlash during retractions, or a filament diameter that varies along the spool.

fixes.advice: Check extruder gear backlash and gear wear, and the filament tension screw. Ellis says too little backlash wears the plastic gear and causes permanent patterns, too much upsets pressure advance.
Measure the filament diameter along its length. Bambu recommends 1.75 plus or minus 0.03 mm. Dry the filament if walls are rough or pitted.

causes.name: Temperature or fan fluctuation
checks: Bands line up with a fan that ramps between layer times, a draft, or PID temperature swings.

fixes.advice: Stabilize the environment (no drafts) and keep the fan speed constant. If Klipper shows large temperature swings, run PID calibration on the hotend.

skills.name: Check on a print
skills.purpose: Take a fresh camera frame of a running print, say what it shows, and propose fan, speed, temperature or pause changes, each behind an approval card.
inputs: printer, or the only one printing
outputs: a reading of the frame and the status

skills.name: Diagnose a failure
skills.purpose: Explain a failed or bad print from photos, camera snapshots and printer logs, and propose fixes.
outputs: fixes as settings or hardware steps
questions the evidence could not answer

skills.name: Tune a profile from a failed print
skills.purpose: Turn a diagnosis into a tested profile change, print a small check part, and save the fix to a new profile version.
skills.example: Fix the stringing in my PETG profile for good

skills.name: Resume from a layer
skills.purpose: After a failure with the part still on the bed, find the last good layer and build a resume file at the right height.

skills.name: Settings from a request
skills.purpose: Turn a plain request (strong, fast, watertight, by Friday) into a settings diff with reasons and sources.
skills.example: 12 functional brackets in PETG, strong, by tomorrow

skills.name: Recommend a material
skills.purpose: Pick the material for a use case (heat, sun, flex, chemicals, food contact) from what the user owns first.
skills.example: What should I print a car phone mount in? It sits on the dashboard in summer.

skills.name: Optimize to a target
skills.purpose: Hit a target such as under 2 hours, under 40 g, or strongest within 3 hours by slicing hundreds of real candidates over layer height, walls, infill, speed and orientation, then show the best few with their tradeoffs.
inputs: target and constraint (time, grams, cost, strength proxy)
limits the user will not trade (walls, surface)
outputs: best 3 to 5 candidates with time, grams, cost and strength proxy
settings diff for the chosen one
skills.example: Make this under 2 hours but as strong as possible

skills.name: Compare two setups
skills.purpose: Slice the same plate two ways and compare time, grams, strength proxies and risk before choosing.
skills.example: Is a 0.6 nozzle worth it for this batch?

skills.name: Split to fit the bed
skills.purpose: Cut an oversized model into parts that fit the printer, with dovetail, pin or dowel connectors and seams placed where they hide.
skills.example: This helmet is too tall for my A1 mini, split it

skills.name: Make a multi-color model
skills.purpose: Build a multi-color model from a request (boxes, cylinders, extruded text, the SlicerX mark or an SVG), map the colors to filament slots with matching presets, add it to the project on its own plate, slice it and report time and grams per color. Optionally write a 3MF project.
skills.example: Build me a SlicerX logo in SlicerX black and X pink

skills.name: Part from a description
skills.purpose: Generate a simple functional part from a description as parametric geometry, show it for review, then slice it.
skills.example: 40 mm L bracket, two M3 holes, 3 mm thick

skills.name: Answer printing questions
skills.purpose: Answer material, printer and technique questions from the knowledge base with sources, and fall back to a cited web lookup.
skills.example: Can the AMS 2 Pro dry nylon?

skills.name: Printer setup
skills.purpose: Walk a new user through adding a printer: optional look and feel, brand, model, nozzle, connection method, test connection, first calibration suggestion. One question at a time, asking before each printer action, never taking access codes in chat.

skills.name: Calibration suites
skills.purpose: Plan and print only the tests a situation needs (temperature, max volumetric speed, pressure advance, flow, retraction, tolerance, shrinkage), then save results to a new profile for that spool.
inputs: situation: new spool, new nozzle, fit problem
outputs: results read from camera or entered by the user
skills.example: Tune a profile for this new PETG spool

skills.name: Schedule by due date and cost
skills.purpose: Plan plates across the chosen printers (or a saved fleet group) to meet due dates at the lowest machine cost, using printers that already have the material loaded.
inputs: printers or a fleet group (default: all printers)
outputs: levers used if a deadline is at risk
skills.example: Get these three orders done by Friday, cheapest printers first

skills.name: Queue, start, pause, cancel
skills.purpose: Send plates to printers and control running jobs, always behind the approval gate.
skills.example: Send plate 2 to Bay 3 and start it
